metadata.title: EAU Guidelines on Urethral Strictures
metadata.summary: This guideline addresses the definition, causes, prevention, diagnosis and management of urethral strictures in male, female and transgender patients. It covers conservative, endoluminal and reconstructive approaches, including tissue transfer and management of posterior urethral stenosis. It also addresses peri-operative care and follow-up after urethral surgery.

target_population: Male patients with urethral strictures or posterior urethral stenosis

toxicities.event: Catheter-related urethral injury, stricture or erosion
toxicities.incidence: In the meta-analysis by Hollingsworth et al., stricture or erosion occurred in 3.4% (CI: 1-7%) after short-term catheterisation (< 3 weeks) in higher-quality studies and in 8.7% (CI: 0.0-18.7%) in studies mainly involving men with spinal cord injury and indwelling urethral catheters. Urethral injury occurred at a rate of 3.2 per 1,000 inpatients. In a follow-up study of 37 patients with catheter-related urethral trauma, 78% developed a stricture.
recognition: Catheter insertion may create a false passage or inflate the balloon inside the urethra; these mechanisms accounted for 29.7% and 70.3%, respectively, of insertion injuries in the cited study.
The bulbar and posterior urethra are the most frequent sites of catheter-related trauma.
prevention: Avoid catheterisation when it is unnecessary.
Provide catheterisation training to physicians and nurses.
When drainage is the sole purpose, do not use a catheter larger than 18 Fr.

toxicities.event: Catheter-associated urethritis and possible urethral stricture
recognition: Comparative cardiac-surgery studies associated non-coated latex catheters with more urethritis and stricture formation than silicone catheters, although other studies found no difference.
prevention: Avoid non-coated latex catheters.

toxicities.event: Urethral stricture after transurethral prostate surgery
toxicities.incidence: Urethral stricture occurs in 4.5-13% after transurethral prostate surgery. After monopolar TURP, a 26 Fr rather than 24 Fr sheath was associated with bulbar stricture in 11.4% vs. 2.9% (p=0.018). Following combined transurethral resection and vaporisation, room-temperature rather than body-temperature irrigation was associated with stricture in 21.3% vs. 6.3% (p=0.002).
recognition: The bulbomembranous urethra is the most frequent location, followed by the fossa navicularis and penile urethra.
prevention: Do not perform routine urethrotomy in the absence of a pre-existing urethral stricture.
The clinical efficacy and safety of additional preventive surgical procedures require confirmation in larger prospective RCTs before they can be recommended.

toxicities.event: Bladder neck stenosis after transurethral prostate surgery
toxicities.incidence: Bladder neck stenosis occurs in 0.3-9.7% after transurethral prostate surgery. In the retrospective study by Lee et al., incidence at a median 38 months was 12.3% with TURP and 6.0% with TURP plus TUIP (p < 0.001); for glands < 30 g, it was 19.3% and 7.7%, respectively (p < 0.05).
recognition: The condition occurs more frequently in smaller prostate glands after monopolar and bipolar TURP.
prevention: The clinical efficacy and safety of additional surgery intended to prevent bladder neck stenosis require confirmation in larger prospective RCTs before recommendation.

toxicities.event: Vesico-urethral anastomosis stricture after radical prostatectomy
toxicities.incidence: Reported in 0.5-30% after radical prostatectomy, with most modern series reporting 1-3%; after salvage RP, the reported risk is 22-40%. In the cited UK national cohort, rates were 3.3% after robotic RP, 5.7% after laparoscopic RP and 6.9% after open RP.
recognition: Most cases develop during the first two years.

toxicities.event: Urethral stricture after prostate irradiation or ablative treatment
toxicities.incidence: At around four years, stricture occurred in 1.5% after EBRT, 1.9% after BT and 4.9% after EBRT-BT. Reported incidences were 1.1-3.3% after cryotherapy and 10.3% after HIFU; in salvage settings, 3-10% after EBRT, 5-12% after cryotherapy and 15-30% after HIFU.
recognition: These strictures typically involve the bulbomembranous urethra; incidence after irradiation increases over time.
prevention: Delaying adjuvant or salvage EBRT by nine months was associated with less stricture formation (HR: 0.6), but this must be weighed against the potential effect of postponement on cancer control.
For BT, the document attributes a possible reduction in strictures to combined measures addressing the “hot spot”, needle placement, midline insertion and needle material.

toxicities.event: Complications of “cold knife” direct vision internal urethrotomy
toxicities.incidence: The SR by Jin et al. reported an overall complication rate of 6.5% in twelve articles including 1,940 patients. Its reported event rates were urinary extravasation 2.9%, urinary incontinence 4.1%, urinary tract infection 2.1%, urinary retention 0.4%, haematuria 2%, epididymitis 0.5%, fever 2.3%, scrotal abscess 0.3% and erectile dysfunction 5.3%. Graversen et al. reported erectile dysfunction in 11/104 (10.6%).
recognition: The risk of erectile dysfunction appears higher when the stricture lies in the penile urethra.
prevention: Do not use DVIU for penile strictures.

toxicities.event: Complications of laser direct vision internal urethrotomy
toxicities.incidence: The SR by Jin et al. reported an overall rate of 11.8% (39/330); its individual rates were urinary extravasation 3.1%, urinary incontinence 2.1%, urinary tract infection 2.7%, urinary retention 9%, haematuria 5.2%, urinary tract irritation 11.4%, urinary fistula 1.5% and dysuria 5.1%. Compared with “cold knife” DVIU in that review, urinary retention was 9 vs. 0.4% (p < 0.0001) and haematuria was 5.2 vs. 2% (p=0.034), respectively.

toxicities.event: False passage, urethral perforation and bleeding during dilatation
toxicities.incidence: In the cited comparison of DVIU and dilatation, false passage occurred in 0.96 and 0.94%, respectively. In the retrospective comparison by Yu et al., urethral bleeding occurred in 6.5 with balloon dilatation vs. 32% with DVIU (p=0.017).
recognition: Blind dilatation with rigid sounds can cause false passage, spongiosal perforation or urethral bleeding.
prevention: Prefer visually controlled to blind dilatation.

toxicities.event: Increasing stricture complexity after repeated urethral manipulation
recognition: Repeated manipulation may increase stricture length and complexity and delay urethroplasty.
prevention: Do not perform repetitive (> 2) DVIU or dilatations if urethroplasty is viable.

toxicities.event: Bleeding, infection, pain and impaired quality of life during intermittent self-dilatation
toxicities.incidence: Reported urethral bleeding was 7.1% and UTI/epididymitis 4.7-18.1%. In a prospective study of n=85, 35% and 26% reported moderate and severe catheterisation difficulty, respectively; 32% and 17% reported moderate and severe pain, respectively. Quality of life was rated moderate by 32% and poor by 55%. In a study of 286 patients, 33% had at least one infection annually.
recognition: Catheterisation difficulty, pain and reduced quality of life are reported drawbacks; poorer quality of life was associated with younger age and proximal stricture location.

toxicities.event: Complications after intralesional platelet rich plasma or saline injection with DVIU
toxicities.incidence: In the RCT by Rezaei et al., complications occurred in 70% with DVIU + PRP and 79% with DVIU + saline; the difference was not significant.
recognition: Reported events were urethral bleeding, haematuria, urethral pain, pelvic pain, urinary leakage and genitoperineal swelling.
prevention: Intralesional injections should be used only within a clinical trial; further validation of PRP is needed before general clinical use.

toxicities.event: Severe complications after intralesional Mitomycin C for posterior stenosis
toxicities.incidence: In the multi-institutional study reported by Redshaw et al., grade 3 complications occurred in 4/55 (7%): osteitis pubis (n=2), bladder neck necrosis (n=1) and rectourethral fistula (n=1).
recognition: Osteitis pubis, bladder neck necrosis and rectourethral fistula were the severe events described.

management.actions: In the cited study, three affected patients ultimately required urinary diversion; one also required faecal diversion.

prevention: Do not use MMC outside a clinical trial.

toxicities.event: Failure and complications of urethral stents
toxicities.incidence: Failure requiring re-intervention was reported in 30-53%. For posterior urethral stents, reported urinary incontinence was 19-82%; the document also describes a high risk of 82-100% in the posterior urethra, particularly after irradiation or when the stricture extends into the membranous or bulbar urethra.
recognition: Reported causes of failure include recurrent stricture, encrustation, migration and urethral hyperplasia. Other events include recurrent UTI, haematuria and genito-perineal pain. In the bulbar urethra, incontinence risk increases when a stent is placed next to the external sphincter.

management.actions: Subsequent urethroplasty, usually with stent removal, is possible but is likely to be more complex than initial urethroplasty; the technique depends on stricture length and local tissue quality.

prevention: Do not use permanent urethral stents or stents for penile strictures.
Do not use stents for posterior urethral strictures.
Avoid stenting when subsequent urethroplasty is being considered.

toxicities.event: Haematuria and dysuria after drug-coated balloon dilatation
toxicities.incidence: In ROBUST-3, haematuria and dysuria were reported more often after DCBD than after standard dilatation/DVIU (11.4% versus 2.1%). No serious adverse events related to DCBD were reported.
recognition: Haematuria and dysuria.
prevention: If DCBD is used, careful clinical review and prospective data collection, ideally within a post-marketing registry or clinical trial, are advised.

toxicities.event: Paclitaxel detected in semen after drug-coated balloon dilatation
recognition: Paclitaxel was detected in semen up to six months after treatment.
prevention: Use contraception if the partner has child-bearing potential.

toxicities.event: Penile and sexual complications after transecting excision and primary anastomosis
toxicities.incidence: In the RCT by Nilsen et al., at three months worse ejaculation (26%), reduced glans filling (26%), penile shortening (16%) and chordee (10%) were significantly more frequent with tEPA than FGU. At 12 months, reduced glans filling (19%) and shortening (26%) remained significantly more frequent. Scrotoperineal haematoma occurred in 24 with tEPA versus 4% with FGU. In the comparison reported by Chapman et al., erectile dysfunction assessed at six months occurred in 14.3% with tEPA versus 4.3% with ntEPA.
recognition: Changes in ejaculation, glans filling or penile length; chordee, erectile dysfunction and scrotoperineal haematoma.
prevention: For short bulbar strictures unrelated to straddle injury, use non-transecting excision and primary anastomosis or free graft urethroplasty instead of tEPA.

toxicities.event: Penile chordee after penile anastomotic urethroplasty
recognition: Post-operative penile curvature is the concern underlying restriction of this operation for penile strictures.
prevention: Do not offer anastomotic urethroplasty for penile strictures > 1 cm because of the risk of post-operative chordee.

toxicities.event: Oral donor-site morbidity after mucosal graft harvesting
toxicities.incidence: After LMG harvesting, speaking problems persisted beyond six months in 13.8-20% in the cited comparative studies. Oral tightness after BMG harvesting was present in up to 24% beyond six months. Chauhan et al. reported numbness (61%), chewing difficulty (54%), swelling (48%) and articulation problems (40%) during the first week in their comparison of donor-site outcomes.
recognition: LMG harvesting was associated with more difficulty eating or drinking, speaking and protruding the tongue, and with dysgeusia; BMG harvesting caused more oral tightness. Lower lip mucosa harvesting may cause persistent discomfort, neurosensory deficits, altered salivation and aesthetic changes.
prevention: Inform patients offered an oral graft about the differing potential complications of buccal, lingual and lower lip harvesting.
The document does not establish whether closing the buccal harvest site is preferable to leaving it open.
Chamomile or chlorhexidine rinses have been suggested for the first post-operative days, without evidence that they reduce pain or other oral complications.

toxicities.event: Complications after staged bulbar urethroplasty
toxicities.incidence: After 2nd stage Johanson urethroplasty, urethrocutaneous fistula was reported in 3-15%. Revision after the 1st stage was required in up to 19%, including recurrence of LS in grafts (8.8%), graft contracture (6.6%) and stomal stenosis (3.3%). Late outcomes after the 2nd stage included post-micturition dribble in 14-18%, stress urinary incontinence in up to 16%, penile curvature in up to 9%, erectile dysfunction in up to 4% and diverticulum in 1%.
recognition: Early events include wound dehiscence, UTI, epididymitis, scrotal abscess and penile numbness; late events also include cold glans.

toxicities.event: Complications after perineal urethrostomy
toxicities.incidence: Reported complications occurred in 2.5-11.4%; Clavien-Dindo grade 1 events occurred in 2.9-18.8%, grade 2 in 0-2.9% and grade 3 in 5.7-6.2%. At medium-term follow-up, post-micturition dribble was reported by 22.2-30.8%. For the midline incision used in “7-flap” PU, superficial wound infection was 1.9% versus 18.6% and superficial wound dehiscence was 11.9% versus 23.3% with inverted U or lambda incisions.
recognition: Superficial wound dehiscence, scrotal abscess, UTI, urosepsis, bleeding, and transient scrotal pain or numbness.

management.actions: Surgical revision with V-Y plasty, augmentation or complete ReDo is most common; periodic dilatation or urinary diversion are also described.

toxicities.event: Rectal injury or urosymphyseal fistulation during posterior endoscopic incision
recognition: Deep incision at the six o’clock position risks rectal injury; at twelve o’clock it risks urosymphyseal fistulation, especially after radiotherapy.
prevention: Do not make deep incisions at the six or twelve o’clock positions during DVIU for VUAS or radiation-induced BMS.

toxicities.event: Urinary incontinence after endoluminal treatment of non-traumatic posterior stenosis
toxicities.incidence: The evidence summary reports de novo UI in up to 25% and worsening of existing UI in up to 15% after endoluminal treatment. In the comparison by Kranz et al., de novo incontinence after TUR occurred in 13.8 for VUAS versus 1.7% for BNS (p=0.011).
recognition: New or worsened urinary incontinence following treatment.

management.actions: The document advises waiting three to four months after DVIU before proceeding with incontinence surgery, if needed, and excluding recurrence by cystoscopy first; other authors wait twelve months.

prevention: Warn patients about possible new or aggravated urinary incontinence before endoluminal treatment.

toxicities.event: Incontinence and other morbidity after ReDo vesico-urethral anastomosis
toxicities.incidence: Incontinence is described as inevitable with a transperineal approach. The evidence summary reports de novo incontinence of 0-58% with retropubic ReDo VUA.
recognition: Urinary incontinence following reconstruction.

management.actions: Subsequent anti-incontinence surgery may be required. AUS implantation should be deferred until anastomotic patency is stable; most cited authors advise waiting at least three to six months.

prevention: Warn patients that incontinence is inevitable after transperineal ReDo VUA and that later anti-incontinence surgery may be needed.
Offer a retropubic approach when the patient is continent before ReDo VUA.

toxicities.event: Incontinence after reconstruction for bladder neck or bulbomembranous stenosis following benign prostatic obstruction surgery
toxicities.incidence: Incontinence was reported in up to 14% after bladder neck reconstruction and up to 25% after BMS reconstruction in patients previously operated on for BPO.
recognition: New urinary incontinence after reconstruction.
prevention: Warn patients about the risk of de novo urinary incontinence.

toxicities.event: Incontinence and erectile dysfunction after urethroplasty for radiation-induced bulbomembranous stricture
toxicities.incidence: For radiation-induced BMS, the evidence summary reports de novo incontinence in 19-26% and new erectile dysfunction in 0-35%. In the comparison by Rourke et al., de novo UI was 26 vs. 25% (p=1) and new ED was 35 vs. 0% (p=0.06) after EPA versus augmentation urethroplasty, respectively.
recognition: New urinary leakage or erectile dysfunction following surgery.
prevention: Warn patients of both risks before urethroplasty for radiation-induced BMS.

toxicities.event: Rectal injury and incontinence after deferred excision and primary anastomosis for traumatic posterior stenosis
toxicities.incidence: Rectal injury was reported in 0-10.2% and urinary incontinence in 6.8-8.5% after deferred EPA.
recognition: Rectal injury is an uncommon but severe complication; incontinence is usually attributed to bladder-neck incompetence. Rectal injury tends to be more frequent in complicated cases or after prior urethral manipulations.
prevention: Use a midline perineal incision to access the posterior urethra; the document associates it with less local nerve and vessel damage, fewer surgical-site infections and shorter hospitalisation than an inverted U incision.
Do not perform total pubectomy during abdomino-perineal reconstruction because it increases complications without improving exposure.

toxicities.event: New stress urinary incontinence after female urethral dilatation
toxicities.incidence: New onset SUI was reported in 1.4%.
recognition: Stress urinary leakage following dilatation.

toxicities.event: New urinary incontinence and acute complications after vaginal flap urethroplasty
toxicities.incidence: Among the 150 women described, 14 (9.3%) developed new UI and 14 (9.3%) developed other acute complications.
recognition: Other reported acute events included UTI and an intravaginal urinary stream.

toxicities.event: Urinary extravasation after urethroplasty
toxicities.incidence: After three weeks of catheterisation following different urethroplasties, extravasation on urethrography was reported in 2.2-11.5%. In the study by Grossgold et al., high-grade leakage was defined by length > 1.03 cm and width > 0.32 cm; length > 1.03 cm alone independently predicted restricture.
recognition: Leakage on pcRUG, RUG or VCUG before catheter removal; significant leakage can lead to peri-urethral inflammation, abscess or fistulation.

management.actions: Maintain or reinsert the catheter and repeat the examination after one week.
The catheter can be removed without another urethrogram because this degree of leakage does not appear to affect long-term restricture rates.
Keep the catheter for an additional week and reassess.

prevention: Assess for extravasation with validated urethrography before removing the catheter after urethroplasty.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Advise safer sexual practices, recognition of STI symptoms, and prompt access to investigation and treatment.
Avoid unnecessary urethral catheterisation and provide catheterisation training for physicians and nurses.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients considered for urethral catheterisation; physicians and nurses performing the procedure

prophylaxis.recommendation: Do not use a catheter larger than 18 Fr when its only purpose is urinary drainage; avoid non-coated latex catheters.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients requiring urinary drainage by urethral catheter
Patients with bacteriuria undergoing urethral surgery

prophylaxis.recommendation: Give an intra-operative prophylactic antibiotic regimen according to local resistance profiles.

Obtain a pre-operative urine culture and give a therapeutic antibiotic course when infection or colonisation is present; with an indwelling catheter, at least attempt pre-operative suppression of colonisation.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients undergoing urethral reconstruction with infection, urinary colonisation or an indwelling catheter

prophylaxis.type: Prevention of recurrence after dilatation or DVIU
prophylaxis.recommendation: Use ISD to stabilise the stricture when urethroplasty is not viable; intra-urethral corticosteroids may be added to ISD for stabilisation.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients after dilatation or DVIU for whom urethroplasty is not a viable option

prophylaxis.recommendation: After urethroplasty, assess leakage by a validated form of urethrography before catheter removal.
Use contraception if the partner has child-bearing potential because paclitaxel was detected in semen after treatment.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients treated with DCBD whose partner has child-bearing potential
prophylaxis.duration: Paclitaxel was detectable in semen up to six months after treatment

infection_management.prevention: Promote safer sexual practices and recognition of STI symptoms, with access to prompt assessment and treatment for men with urethritis.
infection_management.management: Provide timely investigation and antimicrobial treatment.

infection_management.prevention: Screen for and treat asymptomatic bacteriuria before urological procedures that breach the mucosa; treat catheter-associated asymptomatic bacteriuria before traumatic urinary tract interventions.
infection_management.management: If infection is suspected, obtain a urine culture to confirm it and identify the organism and antibiotic susceptibility. Treat bacteriuria before surgery.

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: Urinary infection or colonisation before urethral reconstruction
infection_management.prevention: Use pre-operative urine culture; in patients with an indwelling catheter, at least attempt to suppress colonisation before surgery.
infection_management.management: Give a pre-operative therapeutic antibiotic course when infection or colonisation is present.

infection_management.prevention: Administer intra-operative antibiotic prophylaxis according to local resistance profiles. The document states that prolonged post-operative antibiotics have not been shown to lower infectious complication rates and that antibiotic prophylaxis is not routinely recommended solely to prevent clinical UTI after urethral catheter removal.

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: UTI and epididymitis associated with ISD
Recurrent UTI associated with urethral stents
infection_management.prevention: Do not use permanent stents or stents for penile or posterior urethral strictures.

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: Peri-urethral abscess or fistulation associated with urinary extravasation
infection_management.prevention: Check for leakage by urethrography before catheter removal after urethroplasty.
infection_management.management: For persistent significant extravasation, maintain or reinsert the catheter and repeat the examination after one week.

therapies_index.name: Observation
approved_indications: Incidentally detected, asymptomatic strictures with a calibre > 16 Fr.
Asymptomatic recurrence may be left untreated with regular follow-up.
therapies_index.administration: Follow the stricture without immediate intervention.
monitoring: Regular follow-up is an option for asymptomatic recurrence.
Assess symptoms carefully because patients may conceal their effects on daily life.

therapies_index.name: Suprapubic catheter
approved_indications: Long-term management may be considered for radiation-induced bulbomembranous strictures and/or poor performance status.
An option for frail patients unable to undergo surgery or patients declining further urethral surgery.
Bladder drainage during urethral rest when obstruction becomes incapacitating or retention develops.
First-line drainage for severe obstruction, recurrent UTI or retention early after neophallic reconstruction.
therapies_index.administration: Suprapubic urinary drainage; use may be temporary or long-term according to the clinical situation.
key_toxicities: Catheter-related complications occurred in 27% of patients retaining a suprapubic catheter in the cited radiation-induced stricture series.

therapies_index.name: Direct vision internal urethrotomy (DVIU)
therapies_index.mechanism: Incises the stricture so that mucosal healing can restore patency before wound contraction.
approved_indications: A primary, single, non-obliterative bulbar stricture < 2 cm.
A short, veil-like recurrence after bulbar urethroplasty.
Non-obliterative VUAS or radiation-induced BMS as an initial endoluminal treatment.
One attempt for short, non-obliterative post-traumatic posterior stenosis.
therapies_index.administration: An endoscopic incision, usually under general or spinal anaesthesia; local anaesthesia with or without sedation has also been reported. Do not use for penile strictures, as sole treatment of segments > 2 cm, or for completely obliterative posterior stenosis.
key_toxicities: Bleeding, urinary extravasation, urinary retention, infection, false passage and erectile dysfunction have been reported.
Repeated urethral manipulation may increase stricture length and complexity.
Endoluminal treatment of posterior stenosis may cause new urinary incontinence or worsen existing incontinence.
monitoring: Assess patency or recurrence and the need for another intervention.
Remove the catheter within 72 hours after an uncomplicated procedure.

therapies_index.name: “cold knife” DVIU
therapies_index.mechanism: Cuts the stricture to permit mucosal healing.
approved_indications: A DVIU technique selected according to operator experience and available resources.
therapies_index.administration: Endoscopic cold-knife incision.
key_toxicities: The cited systematic review reported an overall complication rate of 6.5% and erectile dysfunction in 5.3% of cases.

therapies_index.name: Laser urethrotomy
approved_indications: A hot-knife alternative for DVIU, with technique chosen according to experience and resources.
therapies_index.administration: Endoscopic laser incision; lasers reported include Neodymium:YAG, Argon, Holmium:YAG, Potassium titanyl phosphate (KTP) and Tm:Yag.
key_toxicities: Urinary retention and haematuria were more frequent with laser than with cold-knife DVIU in the cited review of retrospective series.

therapies_index.name: Plasmakinetic (bipolar) urethrotomy
approved_indications: A hot-knife DVIU technique that may be selected according to operator experience and resources.
therapies_index.administration: Endoscopic bipolar urethrotomy.

therapies_index.name: Urethral dilatation
therapies_index.mechanism: Stretches the narrowed segment and disrupts scar tissue, allowing mucosal healing to precede wound contraction.
approved_indications: The same indications as a single DVIU in men.
Initial treatment of FUS, dilating to 24-41 Fr.
Non-obliterative VUAS or radiation-induced BMS as initial endoluminal treatment.
An initial option for a short, non-obliterative stricture in trans women.
therapies_index.administration: May be performed in an office under local anaesthesia. Visually controlled dilatation is preferred to blind dilatation; do not use repeated procedures with curative intent when urethroplasty is viable.
key_toxicities: False passage, spongiosal perforation, bleeding and UTI are reported risks.
Repeated manipulation can increase stricture complexity.
New SUI after female dilatation was reported in 1.4%.
monitoring: Assess recurrence and the need for further treatment.
Remove the catheter within 72 hours after uncomplicated dilatation.

therapies_index.name: Visually controlled dilatation
therapies_index.mechanism: Disrupts the narrowed segment by stretching it.
approved_indications: Preferred over blind dilatation.
An initial option for non-obliterative VUAS or radiation-induced BMS.
therapies_index.administration: Perform dilatation under visual control after endoscopic or fluoroscopic guidewire placement.
key_toxicities: Haematuria, false passage, procedural failure and UTI were recorded in the cited series.

therapies_index.name: Balloon dilatation
therapies_index.mechanism: Expands the stricture by dilatation.
approved_indications: An evaluated modality of urethral dilatation.
key_toxicities: Urethral bleeding and UTI were reported.

therapies_index.name: Intermittent self-dilatation (ISD)
therapies_index.mechanism: Helps stabilise narrowing after endoluminal treatment rather than curing the stricture.
approved_indications: Stabilisation after male dilatation or DVIU when urethroplasty is not viable.
Weekly use with a 16-18 Fr catheter after repeat dilatation for a 1st recurrence of FUS.
Palliative management of recurrent posterior stenosis, particularly when surgery is unsuitable or declined.
Palliative treatment of low-grade meatal stenosis in trans men.
therapies_index.administration: Performed by the patient; the female 1st-recurrence recommendation specifies planned weekly use of a 16-18 Fr catheter.
key_toxicities: Urethral bleeding, UTI or epididymitis, catheterisation difficulty and pain have been reported.
It can substantially impair quality of life, and adherence may be poor.
Repeated dilatation may increase stricture complexity and delay urethroplasty.
monitoring: Assess recurrence, ability to perform catheterisation and effects on quality of life.

therapies_index.name: triamcinolone
therapies_index.mechanism: Intra-urethral corticosteroid use is intended to delay wound contraction at the stricture.
approved_indications: Studied as an ointment added to ISD to stabilise urethral strictures.
therapies_index.administration: Applied locally as a catheter lubricant during ISD; one cited trial used it for six weeks.
key_toxicities: The two cited additional trials reported no ointment-related complications.
monitoring: Assess stricture recurrence and time to recurrence.

therapies_index.name: clobetasol
approved_indications: An intra-urethral steroid regimen studied for LS-related strictures; its reported effect should be understood as stabilisation rather than cure.
therapies_index.administration: clobetasol cream 0.05% was used as lubricant on a 10-16 Fr catheter or dilator twice a day for a minimum of two months in the cited cohort.
monitoring: Assess whether treatment escalation is needed and whether the instillation interval can be extended.

therapies_index.name: Intralesional injections
therapies_index.mechanism: Adjuvant injection aims to limit fibroblast proliferation and excessive urethral scarring.
approved_indications: Use after DVIU is restricted to a clinical trial.
therapies_index.administration: Inject into the stricture region as an adjunct to endoluminal treatment; drug, dose, volume and technique remain uncertain.
monitoring: Careful clinical review and prospective collection of treatment data are advised.

therapies_index.name: Mitomycin C
therapies_index.mechanism: Investigated as an antifibrotic adjunct intended to limit luminal fibrosis.
approved_indications: Studied as an intralesional or intraluminal adjunct to endoluminal stricture treatment; intralesional injection should be confined to a clinical trial.
For posterior stenosis, MMC should not be used outside a clinical trial.
therapies_index.administration: Intralesional or intraluminal administration has been studied; no standard dose, volume or technique is established in the guide.
key_toxicities: A cited posterior-stenosis study reported grade 3 osteitis pubis, bladder neck necrosis and rectourethral fistula after adjunctive MMC.
monitoring: Careful clinical review and prospective data collection are advised.

therapies_index.name: Platelet rich plasma
approved_indications: Investigated as an injection added to DVIU for primary bulbar strictures < 1.5 cm; further validation is required before general clinical use.
therapies_index.administration: Injected as an adjunct to DVIU in the cited trial.
key_toxicities: Grade 1 urethral bleeding, haematuria, urethral pain, pelvic pain, urinary leakage and genitoperineal swelling were reported in the trial's complication assessment.

therapies_index.name: Urethral stents
therapies_index.mechanism: Oppose wound contraction following dilatation or DVIU.
approved_indications: A temporary stent may be used after DVIU for recurrent bulbar strictures only when urethroplasty is not viable.
Permanent stents and stents for penile or posterior strictures are discouraged.
therapies_index.administration: Insertion can be performed under local or spinal anaesthesia; temporary stents can be removed after six to twelve months.
key_toxicities: Recurrence, encrustation, migration, urethral hyperplasia, recurrent UTI, haematuria and genitoperineal pain were reported.
Posterior placement carries a high risk of urinary incontinence.
A failed stent can make later urethroplasty more complex.
monitoring: Assess patency, migration, encrustation and need for re-intervention.

therapies_index.name: Temporary stent
therapies_index.mechanism: Temporarily resists contraction of the treated urethral segment.
approved_indications: May prolong time to another recurrence after DVIU for a recurrent bulbar stricture when urethroplasty is not viable.
therapies_index.administration: Placed after endoluminal treatment and removed after six to twelve months; the cited Wong et al. series used a three months stent.
key_toxicities: Failure or re-intervention may follow recurrence, migration or encrustation.
monitoring: Assess recurrence and stent-related complications.

therapies_index.name: Permanent urethral stents
therapies_index.mechanism: Provide ongoing resistance to wound contraction.
therapies_index.administration: Do not use permanent urethral stents.
key_toxicities: High complication and failure rates; subsequent urethroplasty becomes more challenging if a stent fails.

therapies_index.name: Drug (paclitaxel)-coated balloon dilatation
therapies_index.mechanism: Balloon delivery of paclitaxel aims to reduce scar formation through its antimitotic action.
approved_indications: Offer for a recurrent bulbar stricture < 3 cm after at least two failed endoscopic treatments, only when urethroplasty is not an option.
therapies_index.administration: Performed after standard dilatation or DVIU.
key_toxicities: Haematuria and dysuria were more frequent in the coated-balloon arm than in controls in ROBUST-3.
paclitaxel was detected in semen for up to six months after treatment.
monitoring: Careful clinical review and prospective data collection, ideally through a post-marketing registry or trial, are advised.
Contraception is urged if the partner has child-bearing potential.

therapies_index.name: paclitaxel
therapies_index.mechanism: Its antimitotic action is used to reduce scar formation.
approved_indications: Coating for a balloon used in selected recurrent bulbar strictures.
therapies_index.administration: Delivered by drug-coated balloon dilatation.
key_toxicities: Detected in semen for up to six months after treatment.
monitoring: Contraception is urged when the partner has child-bearing potential.

therapies_index.name: Urethroplasty
therapies_index.mechanism: Reconstructs the narrowed urethral segment.
approved_indications: Definitive reconstruction for selected anterior strictures and posterior stenoses.
Recommended for a 2nd recurrence of FUS when ISD cannot be performed or definitive treatment is desired.
therapies_index.administration: Technique depends on stricture anatomy, aetiology, tissue quality, patient factors and surgical expertise. Do not perform within three months of urethral manipulation.
key_toxicities: Recurrence, urinary extravasation, infection and functional or sexual complications vary by technique.
monitoring: Use urethrography to assess extravasation before catheter removal.
Offer follow-up to every patient after urethroplasty, routinely for at least one year, using a risk-adjusted protocol.
Assess anatomy, patient-reported outcomes and sexual function as indicated.

therapies_index.name: Staged augmentation urethroplasty
therapies_index.mechanism: Reconstructs the urethra in stages, potentially including graft placement followed by tubularisation.
approved_indications: Complex penile or anterior strictures unsuitable for single-stage repair in patients fit for reconstruction.
An option for complex bulbar disease and selected strictures related to failed hypospadias repair.
therapies_index.administration: Allow at least four to six months before a second stage if the first stage has healed satisfactorily; additional revisions may make the reconstruction multistage.
key_toxicities: Graft contraction, wound dehiscence, fistula, infection and later urinary or sexual complications were reported.
monitoring: Assess first-stage healing before tubularisation.
Warn that more than two stages may be required.

therapies_index.name: Single-stage augmentation urethroplasty
therapies_index.mechanism: Augments the narrowed urethra in one reconstructive operation.
approved_indications: An option for selected penile strictures, taking previous interventions and stricture features into account.
An option for LS-related strictures when local conditions are favourable.
therapies_index.administration: Patient selection may depend on operative findings; an intended single-stage repair may need conversion to staged repair.
key_toxicities: Recurrence remains possible, particularly if diseased tissue is augmented rather than removed.
monitoring: Counsel before surgery about possible conversion to a staged procedure.

therapies_index.name: Anastomotic urethroplasty
therapies_index.mechanism: Joins urethral ends after treatment of a short narrowed segment.
approved_indications: May be offered in selected, very short penile strictures, usually < 1 cm.
Reported in two women with very short mid-urethral strictures.
therapies_index.administration: Do not offer for penile strictures > 1 cm.
key_toxicities: Penile chordee is a concern after penile anastomotic repair.

therapies_index.name: Excision and primary anastomosis (EPA)
therapies_index.mechanism: Excises the scarred segment and reconnects healthy urethral ends without tension.
approved_indications: Short bulbar strictures suitable for tension-free anastomosis.
Selected bulbomembranous strictures after surgery for benign prostatic obstruction.
Selected radiation-induced BMS and post-traumatic posterior stenoses.
therapies_index.administration: Perform a tension-free anastomosis; selection depends on stricture length and tissue characteristics.
key_toxicities: Complications depend on the site and whether the corpus spongiosum is transected.
monitoring: Assess extravasation before catheter removal and follow for recurrence.

therapies_index.name: Transecting EPA (tEPA)
therapies_index.mechanism: Removes the full thickness of the strictured bulbar segment and surrounding spongiofibrosis, then performs a tension-free anastomosis.
approved_indications: Short post-traumatic bulbar strictures with nearly or completely obliterated lumen and full-thickness spongiofibrosis.
therapies_index.administration: Transect the corpus spongiosum and perform a spatulated, tension-free anastomosis.
key_toxicities: Penile shortening, reduced glans filling, chordee, ejaculatory changes, erectile dysfunction and scrotoperineal haematoma were reported.
monitoring: Assess patency and penile or sexual outcomes.

therapies_index.name: Non-transecting excision and primary anastomosis
therapies_index.mechanism: Repairs the short bulbar stricture while avoiding complete corpus spongiosum transection.
approved_indications: Preferred over tEPA, alongside free graft urethroplasty, for short bulbar strictures unrelated to straddle injury.
therapies_index.administration: Use a non-transecting repair when operative findings permit it.
key_toxicities: Erectile dysfunction and other complications remain possible, although erectile complications were lower than with tEPA in cited comparisons.
monitoring: Assess patency and erectile function.

therapies_index.name: Free graft urethroplasty
therapies_index.mechanism: Augments the urethra with a graft placed against a vascularised recipient bed.
approved_indications: Bulbar strictures unsuitable for EPA.
An alternative to tEPA for short bulbar strictures unrelated to straddle injury.
A long stricture requiring ReDo urethroplasty may be treated with an oral mucosa free graft.
therapies_index.administration: Place the graft with close contact against a well-vascularised bed; dorsal, dorsal-lateral or ventral positioning can be selected according to expertise and operative findings.
key_toxicities: Donor-site morbidity depends on graft source.
Recurrence and post-void dribbling have been reported.
monitoring: Assess graft healing, urethral patency and donor-site effects.

therapies_index.name: Augmented anastomotic repair
therapies_index.mechanism: Excises a short nearly obliterative portion, joins the remaining urethral plate and augments the repair with an onlay graft.
approved_indications: A bulbar stricture unsuitable for EPA that contains a short, nearly obliterative segment.
therapies_index.administration: Combine limited excision and anastomosis with graft augmentation.
key_toxicities: Recurrence is possible; one cited comparison reported greater recurrence than with dorsal free graft urethroplasty.
monitoring: Assess long-term patency.

therapies_index.name: augmented non-transecting anastomotic bulbar urethroplasty [ANTABU]
therapies_index.mechanism: Provides an augmented anastomotic repair without spongiosal transection.
approved_indications: Described as a non-transecting alternative for bulbar strictures requiring augmented anastomotic repair.
key_toxicities: Permanent ED occurred in one patient (6.7%) in the cited series.

therapies_index.name: Perineal urethrostomy (PU)
therapies_index.mechanism: Creates a perineal urinary outlet to restore voiding.
approved_indications: A management option for complex anterior urethral strictures.
An option when formal reconstruction is unsuitable or declined.
An option when further restoration of urethral patency is not feasible.
therapies_index.administration: May be temporary or permanent; choose the technique according to patient characteristics and surgical experience.
key_toxicities: Wound dehiscence, scrotal abscess, UTI or urosepsis, bleeding, transient scrotal pain or numbness and post-micturition dribble have been reported.
Stomal failure or recurrent narrowing can require revision.
monitoring: Assess outlet patency, voiding symptoms and patient satisfaction.

therapies_index.name: augmented Gil-Vernet-Blandy perineal urethrostomy
therapies_index.mechanism: Augments a perineal outlet with a free oral mucosa graft.
approved_indications: Consider when stricture disease reaches the proximal bulbar or membranous urethra.
therapies_index.administration: A Gil-Vernet-Blandy PU with dorsal and/or ventral graft augmentation.

therapies_index.name: “7-flap” PU
therapies_index.mechanism: Creates a perineal outlet using a unilateral, posteriorly based scrotal flap.
approved_indications: Consider for proximal bulbar or membranous disease and in obese men.
therapies_index.administration: Uses a midline incision and a unilateral scrotal flap.
key_toxicities: Superficial wound infection and dehiscence remain possible.

therapies_index.name: loop PU
therapies_index.mechanism: Forms a perineal outlet while avoiding transection of the mobilised bulbar urethra.
approved_indications: Reported as a modification of the “7-flap” PU.
therapies_index.administration: Mobilise the bulbar urethra as a loop without transection.

therapies_index.name: Malone meatoplasty
therapies_index.mechanism: Widens a short distal meatal narrowing.
approved_indications: Short distal meatal strictures in men.
therapies_index.administration: Combine dorsal and ventral meatotomy.
monitoring: Assess patency and cosmetic satisfaction.

therapies_index.name: skin flap meatoplasty
therapies_index.mechanism: Uses a skin flap to widen the distal urethral outlet.
approved_indications: An open repair option for distal urethral strictures.
key_toxicities: Urinary spraying was the main functional complaint in the cited studies.

therapies_index.name: Meatotomy/meatoplasty
therapies_index.mechanism: Enlarges a narrowed urethral meatus.
approved_indications: Treatment of female meatal strictures.
Simple meatotomy is an option for high-grade meatal stenosis in trans men, refusal of ISD or preference for a durable solution.
therapies_index.administration: An open meatal procedure; after meatotomy in trans men, the meatus will occupy a hypospadiac position.
monitoring: Assess outlet patency and voiding symptoms.

therapies_index.name: Y-V meatoplasty
therapies_index.mechanism: Reconstructs the narrowed neomeatus.
approved_indications: Short meatal stenosis < 1 cm in trans women when open reconstruction is indicated.
monitoring: Assess recurrence.

therapies_index.name: neovaginal advancement flap
therapies_index.mechanism: Advances neovaginal tissue to reconstruct the meatus.
approved_indications: An option for meatal strictures of 1-2 cm in trans women.
therapies_index.administration: An inverted U or “7-flap” advancement was described.
monitoring: Assess recurrence.

therapies_index.name: ReDo vesico-urethral anastomosis (ReDo VUA)
therapies_index.mechanism: Excises the stenosis and reconstructs a tension-free bladder-to-urethra anastomosis.
approved_indications: Obliterative or endoluminal-treatment-refractory VUAS in non-irradiated patients or irradiated patients with adequate bladder function.
therapies_index.administration: Retropubic, perineal, combined abdominoperineal and robot-assisted approaches are described; offer a retropubic approach if the patient is continent before surgery.
key_toxicities: Urinary incontinence is inevitable with the transperineal approach; anastomotic dehiscence and other operative morbidity have been reported.
monitoring: Confirm stable anastomotic patency before later artificial urinary sphincter placement; the cited guidance generally advises at least three to six months.
Reconstruction is advised in experienced high-volume centres.

therapies_index.name: Artificial urinary sphincter (AUS)
approved_indications: An option for urinary incontinence after posterior reconstruction once anastomotic patency is stable.
therapies_index.administration: Following ReDo VUA, placement is generally deferred for at least three to six months to establish stable patency.
key_toxicities: Cuff erosion and a need for revision were reported after the cited pull-through reconstruction.
monitoring: Ensure stable patency before implantation.

therapies_index.name: Transurethral resection (TUR)
therapies_index.mechanism: Resects obstructing tissue or a stenotic segment.
approved_indications: An initial option for non-obliterative BNS after surgery for benign prostatic obstruction.
Can remove obstructive sloughed tissue after HIFU or cryoablation; its role for necrotic debris after radiotherapy is limited.
therapies_index.administration: Transurethral endoscopic resection.
key_toxicities: New urinary incontinence and recurrence have been reported.
monitoring: Assess patency and continence.

therapies_index.name: “hot-knife” DVIU
therapies_index.mechanism: Incises a narrowed urethral segment using an energy-based technique.
approved_indications: An initial option for non-obliterative BNS after surgery for benign prostatic obstruction.
An available DVIU technique selected according to operator experience and resources.
therapies_index.administration: Endoscopic incision; avoid deep incisions at the six and twelve o’clock positions for VUAS or radiation-induced BMS.
key_toxicities: Deep posterior incisions can injure the rectum or cause a urosymphyseal fistula.
The cited review of laser DVIU reported an overall complication rate of 11.8% (39/330).

therapies_index.name: bladder neck reconstruction with Y-V or T-plasty
therapies_index.mechanism: Augments the bladder neck by advancing local bladder flaps.
approved_indications: BNS refractory to endoscopic treatment.
therapies_index.administration: Advance local bladder tissue with or without scar resection; minimally invasive approaches were described.
key_toxicities: De novo incontinence was reported.
monitoring: Assess patency and continence.

therapies_index.name: salvage prostatectomy
therapies_index.mechanism: Removes the obstructed prostate after prior treatment.
approved_indications: May be offered to fit, motivated patients with adequate bladder function and a prostatic stricture caused by irradiation or high-energy treatment.
key_toxicities: Rectal injury, VUAS and incontinence are described concerns.

therapies_index.name: Urinary diversion
therapies_index.mechanism: Redirects urinary drainage away from an unusable urethral outlet.
approved_indications: Recurrent or complex cases with loss of bladder capacity and/or incapacitating local symptoms.
A possible final option for a devastated posterior urethra.
therapies_index.administration: Continent or incontinent diversion, with or without cystectomy, according to bladder function, symptoms and patient status.

therapies_index.name: cystectomy
therapies_index.mechanism: Removes the bladder to palliate severe local symptoms.
approved_indications: Perform during urinary diversion for intractable bladder pain, spasms and/or haematuria.
therapies_index.administration: Performed with urinary diversion.

therapies_index.name: progressive perineal excision and primary anastomosis (EPA)
therapies_index.mechanism: Excises posterior scar and restores urethral continuity with a tension-free anastomosis.
approved_indications: Obliterative post-traumatic posterior stenosis.
Non-obliterative post-traumatic posterior stenosis after failed endoluminal treatment.
therapies_index.administration: Perform through a midline perineal incision; reconstruction is advised in a high-volume centre.
key_toxicities: Incontinence and rectal injury have been reported.
monitoring: Assess anastomotic patency and functional outcomes.

therapies_index.name: ReDo-urethroplasty
therapies_index.mechanism: Reconstructs the urethra after failure of a previous urethroplasty.
approved_indications: An option after a 1st failed reconstruction for motivated patients unwilling to accept palliative endoluminal treatment or diversion.
therapies_index.administration: The technique depends on the recurrent defect and whether another tension-free anastomosis is feasible.
monitoring: Assess patency and the need for further treatment.

therapies_index.name: Badenoch pull-through technique
therapies_index.mechanism: Reconstructs continuity when the proximal urethral end lies too deeply for conventional anastomotic suturing.
approved_indications: An option in primary or repeat posterior reconstruction when adequate mucosa-to-mucosa suturing is not feasible.

therapies_index.name: abdomino-perineal reconstruction
therapies_index.mechanism: Combines abdominal and perineal access for complex posterior reconstruction.
approved_indications: Reserve for very long distraction defects or complicated situations including para-urethral bladder base fistula, trauma-related recto-urethral fistula and bladder neck injury.
therapies_index.administration: Avoid total pubectomy; partial pubectomy may be used when required.
key_toxicities: Total pubectomy increases bleeding, pelvic instability and dead space without improving exposure compared with partial pubectomy.

therapies_index.name: Heineke-Mikulicz urethroplasty
approved_indications: An option for very short, low-grade strictures < 1.5 cm at the junction of the neophallic urethra and fixed urethra.
monitoring: Assess patency.

therapies_index.name: staged urethroplasty
therapies_index.mechanism: Reconstructs a narrowed segment over successive operations.
approved_indications: Use for neophallic urethral strictures in trans men when open reconstruction is indicated.
An alternative for selected complex or recurrent strictures elsewhere in the reconstructed urethra.
therapies_index.administration: Do not perform urethroplasty within six months after neophalloplasty.
monitoring: Assess tissue healing and subsequent urethral patency.

therapies_index.name: perineostomy
therapies_index.mechanism: Provides an alternative perineal route for voiding.
approved_indications: An alternative to suprapubic drainage for severe early obstruction after neophallic reconstruction.
A definitive option for refractory strictures in trans men or those who do not want complex reconstruction.
therapies_index.administration: Early perineostomy is a specialist procedure; it may be closed during later formal reconstruction.

therapies_index.name: vaginal graft augmentation urethroplasty
therapies_index.mechanism: Augments a female urethral stricture using a vaginal graft.
approved_indications: A described reconstructive option for FUS.
therapies_index.administration: The reported procedures used a dorsal approach.
monitoring: Assess recurrence, flow rate and PVR.

therapies_index.name: vaginal flap augmentation urethroplasty
therapies_index.mechanism: Augments the female urethra using a vaginal tissue flap.
approved_indications: A described reconstructive option for FUS.
therapies_index.administration: The reported procedures used a ventral approach.
key_toxicities: New urinary incontinence, UTI and an intravaginal direction of urinary flow were reported.
monitoring: Assess patency and continence.

therapies_index.name: labial/vestibular graft augmentation urethroplasty
therapies_index.mechanism: Augments the female urethra with labial or vestibular graft tissue.
approved_indications: A described reconstructive option for FUS.
therapies_index.administration: Ventral and dorsal graft placement were reported.
key_toxicities: One postoperative UTI was reported in a ventral graft patient.
monitoring: Assess patency and PVR.

therapies_index.name: labial/vestibular flap urethroplasty
therapies_index.mechanism: Uses labial or vestibular tissue as a flap for female urethral reconstruction.
approved_indications: A described reconstructive option for FUS.
monitoring: Assess patency.

therapies_index.name: buccal mucosa graft (BMG) urethroplasty
therapies_index.mechanism: Uses buccal mucosa to augment the reconstructed urethra.
approved_indications: A graft option for bulbar, penile, female and reconstructed urethral strictures, selected according to the clinical situation.
therapies_index.administration: Graft positioning and whether repair is single-stage or staged depend on stricture and tissue characteristics.
key_toxicities: Harvest-site pain, numbness, chewing difficulty and oral tightness have been reported.
monitoring: Assess urethral patency and oral donor-site morbidity.

therapies_index.name: lingual mucosa graft (LMG)
therapies_index.mechanism: Provides oral mucosa for graft-based urethral reconstruction.
approved_indications: Use as an available oral graft when graft reconstruction is needed.
therapies_index.administration: Harvest from the tongue for urethral grafting.
key_toxicities: Eating or drinking difficulty, speech problems, impaired tongue protrusion, altered taste and donor-site numbness have been reported.
monitoring: Discuss potential oral complications before grafting and assess donor-site effects afterward.

therapies_index.name: penile skin graft
therapies_index.mechanism: Provides skin for graft-based urethral augmentation.
approved_indications: An option when buccal or lingual mucosa is unavailable, unsuitable or declined.
Do not use genital skin graft in LS-related strictures.
therapies_index.administration: Skin may be harvested from the penis or foreskin.
key_toxicities: Recurrence is a particular concern when genital skin is used in LS-related disease.
monitoring: Assess patency and graft-related morbidity.

therapies_index.name: penile skin flap
therapies_index.mechanism: Transfers vascularised penile skin for urethral reconstruction.
approved_indications: A flap option for selected anterior strictures or a poorly vascularised urethral bed.
Avoid penile skin flaps in failed hypospadias repair with LS or scarred skin.
therapies_index.administration: May be used as a patch or, when complete one-stage tubular reconstruction is needed, as a tube.
key_toxicities: Superficial skin necrosis, fistula, penile deformity, post-void dribbling and sacculation have been reported.
monitoring: Assess flap viability, patency and urogenital morbidity.

therapies_index.name: cell-free tissue engineered grafts
therapies_index.mechanism: A cell-free matrix provides a scaffold for host-cell ingrowth.
approved_indications: Do not use with extensive spongiofibrosis, after failed urethroplasty or for stricture length > 4 cm.
therapies_index.administration: Graft materials described include porcine small intestine submucosa, acellular bladder matrix and acellular dermal matrix.
monitoring: Assess patency; outcomes were poorer with an unhealthy urethral bed or longer strictures.

therapies_index.name: autologous tissue-engineered oral mucosa grafts
therapies_index.mechanism: A matrix seeded with the patient's oral mucosal cells forms a graft.
approved_indications: Do not use outside a clinical trial.
therapies_index.administration: Production requires an oral mucosa biopsy of 0.5 cm² followed by laboratory manufacture before implantation.
key_toxicities: Oral adverse events were minimal in the cited prospective study.
monitoring: Safety, patency and cost-effectiveness remain under investigation.

therapies_index.name: Antibiotics
approved_indications: Treat infection or colonisation before urethral surgery.
Give intra-operative prophylaxis at urethral surgery.
Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria before urological procedures that breach the mucosa, including relevant traumatic interventions.
therapies_index.administration: Select intra-operative prophylaxis according to local resistance profiles. Prolonged postoperative use through or beyond catheter removal has not been shown to reduce infective complications.
monitoring: Obtain a pre-operative urine culture; most reconstructive urologists do so one to two weeks before surgery.

therapies_index.name: rofecoxib
approved_indications: Investigated for stricture prevention after TURP; further RCTs are needed to confirm efficacy and safety.

therapies_index.name: hyaluronic acid (HA)
approved_indications: Investigated with carboxymethylcellulose for prevention of urethral stricture after transurethral prostate surgery; further RCTs are needed.
therapies_index.administration: Studied by urethral instillation together with carboxymethylcellulose.

therapies_index.name: carboxymethylcellulose (CMC)
approved_indications: Investigated with hyaluronic acid for prevention of urethral stricture after transurethral prostate surgery; further RCTs are needed.
therapies_index.administration: Studied by urethral instillation together with hyaluronic acid.

therapies_index.name: anticholinergic drugs
therapies_index.administration: Systematic use during postoperative catheterisation did not significantly reduce involuntary pericatheter voiding.

therapies_index.name: chamomile
approved_indications: Suggested for oral rinsing soon after buccal mucosa harvesting, without evidence that it reduces pain or other oral complications.
therapies_index.administration: Oral rinse during the first postoperative days.

therapies_index.name: chlorhexidine
approved_indications: Suggested for oral rinsing soon after buccal mucosa harvesting, without evidence that it reduces pain or other oral complications.
therapies_index.administration: Oral rinse during the first postoperative days.

conditions.name: urethral stricture disease
conditions.description: The guideline covers urethral narrowing in male, female and transgender patients. In males, an anterior urethral stricture involves fibrosis of the mucosa and surrounding corpus spongiosum; narrowing in the posterior urethra is preferably called stenosis. Narrowing of a reconstructed urethra is also termed a stricture despite the absence of surrounding spongiosal tissue.
conditions.epidemiology: In males, estimated incidence is 229-627 per 100,000, mean age is 45.1, and incidence rises sharply after 55 years. The anterior urethra is involved in 92.2% of cases, particularly the bulbar urethra (46.9%). Aetiology varies significantly between regions.
conditions.clinical_presentation: In a retrospective series of 611 patients with endoscopically confirmed strictures, presentations included LUTS (54.3%), acute urinary retention (22.3%), UTI (6.1%) and difficult catheterisation (4.8%). Genitourinary pain affected 22.9-71% across cited studies. Other reported complaints included spraying (9%), visible haematuria (3.1-5%), urethral abscess or necrotising fasciitis (2.3%), urgency (14%) and incontinence (1-4%). Sexual-function problems may coexist.

subtypes.name: anterior urethral strictures in males
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Involve the spongiosum-surrounded urethra between the meatus and urogenital diaphragm.

subtypes.name: posterior urethral stenosis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Involves the membranous urethra, prostatic urethra or bladder neck, where there is no corpus spongiosum.

subtypes.name: female urethral stricture (FUS)
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Most authors describe a persistent anatomical reduction in urethral calibre.

subtypes.name: strictures in trans men
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Can occur in distinct segments of the reconstructed urethra.

subtypes.name: strictures in trans women
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Usually occur at the neomeatus.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish symptom severity and duration, possible cause, previous treatment, associated problems, sexual function and factors affecting surgery.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Suspected urethral stricture disease.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Ask specifically about pelvic, genital or perineal injury, instrumentation, surgery, irradiation, focal therapy and urethritis; record the most recent intervention.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the bladder, genitalia, urethra, prostate, potential graft donor site and suitability for operative positioning.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Suspected urethral stricture disease.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Assess the meatus, scars suggestive of LS, fistulae, urethral induration and any mass; examine the oral cavity, measure BMI and assess hip mobility.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify infection and, when indicated, its organism and antibiotic sensitivity.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Urinalysis during assessment of LUTS; culture if infection is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Treat bacteriuria before surgical intervention.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess flow obstruction and identify retention; measurements can also monitor treatment response.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Suspected urethral stricture disease.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A reduced maximum flow with a prolonged plateau is characteristic, but visual interpretation of the curve alone is not a reliable screening method.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess bladder function or whether impaired flow and raised PVR reflect detrusor underactivity.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Selected patients with suspected bladder dysfunction; not indicated for the vast majority.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: May help estimate the likelihood of needing post-operative ISC.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Determine the presence, site and length of a stricture and assess associated abnormalities.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Particularly in men being considered for reconstructive surgery.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Reported diagnostic sensitivity and specificity are 91% and 72%; RUG may underestimate stricture length.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Show urethra proximal to narrowing and improve assessment of length or an injury gap.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Combine with RUG for nearly or completely obliterative strictures, stenoses and PFUI.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm or rule out a narrowing and assess other urethral or bladder pathology.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: An adjunct to imaging when additional information is required.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Usually cannot establish stricture length when the instrument cannot traverse the narrowing.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess injury-gap length, bladder-neck competence, scarring and associated fistulae, false passages, stones or bony abnormalities.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Additional assessment of PFUI when imaging does not provide sufficient information.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess anterior stricture location, length and spongiofibrosis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Additional assessment of anterior urethral strictures.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: In a cited comparison, correlation of measured length with operative findings was 94% for SUG versus 59% for RUG (p < 0.001); the pre-operative clinical significance of measuring spongiofibrosis remains uncertain.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide anatomical detail and identify associated pathology.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider as an ancillary investigation for posterior urethral stenosis.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: May estimate posterior stenosis length more accurately than RUG and VCUG.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure symptom burden, quality-of-life effects and patient-perceived outcomes.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Men undergoing surgery and subsequent follow-up.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A patent urethra does not necessarily mean that the patient regards treatment as successful.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Document erectile and ejaculatory function and subsequent change.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before and after urethral stricture surgery.

staging.system: EAU classification according to the degree of urethral narrowing

definitions.description: Imaging shows a normal urethra; lumen and degree are recorded as -.
Subclinical narrowing with a lumen > 16 Fr; degree Low.
Low-grade narrowing with a lumen of 11-15 Fr.
High-grade or flow-significant narrowing with a lumen of 4-10 Fr; degree High.
Almost obliterative narrowing with a lumen of 1-3 Fr.
Complete obliteration with no lumen (0 Fr).

staging.additional_rules: The Panel proposed this consensus classification for male patients with normally functioning bladders. A urethral plate < 3 mm is considered tight or high-grade; with normal bladder function, flow generally does not fall until luminal diameter is below 10 Fr.

prognostic_tools.name: Risk-stratified proposals during follow-up after urethral surgery

risk_groups.criteria: Anastomotic repair in the bulbar or (bulbo)membranous segment without prior radiotherapy, hypospadias or BXO/LS features.
Bulbar anastomotic repair with prior radiotherapy, hypospadias or BXO/LS features; penile or non-traumatic posterior urethroplasty; or graft or flap substitution urethroplasty.

prognostic_tools.interpretation: The groups determine the proposed intensity and duration of post-urethroplasty surveillance.

follow_up.schedule: Offer follow-up after urethroplasty for at least one year. For low-risk repairs, the proposed assessments are at 3 months, 12 months and 24 months; follow-up may end after two years with advice to return if symptoms worsen. For standard-risk repairs, assess at 3 months, 12 months, 24 months and 5 years; follow-up may end after five years, although longer surveillance should be considered after penile or substitution urethroplasty.
recommended_tests: Uroflowmetry and PROM, including sexual function, at each scheduled low- or standard-risk visit.
For low-risk repairs, anatomic assessment by urethrocystoscopy or RUG-VCUG at 3 months as suggested by the Panel, and subsequently when indicated.
For standard-risk repairs, anatomic assessment at 3 months, 12 months and 24 months, and at 5 years when indicated.
Investigate deterioration suggesting recurrence with anatomic testing.
long_term_effects: Recurrent narrowing can occur after initially patent reconstruction.
Late recurrence later than five years was reported in up to 15% of cases.
Persistent voiding symptoms, pain, sexual dysfunction, penile shortening and curvature may adversely affect patient satisfaction despite anatomical patency.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Follow-up should capture both anatomical findings and patient-reported function. Patients should seek urological assessment if symptoms recur after scheduled surveillance ends.

conditions.name: penile urethral strictures
conditions.description: These affect the penile urethra between the fossa navicularis and bulbar urethra. The segment has a thin surrounding layer of corpus spongiosum.
conditions.epidemiology: Idiopathic disease accounts for 34% of penile strictures in a cited series.

subtypes.name: failed hypospadias repair-related strictures
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Prior reconstruction may leave inadequate urethral plate and local tissue.

subtypes.name: lichen sclerosus-related penile urethral strictures
subtypes.distinguishing_features: LS affects skin and may recur after reconstruction using genital skin.

subtypes.name: distal urethral strictures
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Include meatal stenosis and fossa navicularis narrowing.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Determine location and length before reconstruction.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Men being considered for reconstructive surgery.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Very distal narrowing can be difficult to assess.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess foreskin, meatus, scar, LS and tissue available for repair.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before selecting a reconstructive approach.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Unfavourable tissue findings may require a staged rather than single-stage procedure.

follow_up.schedule: Penile urethroplasty is included among operations with standard recurrence risk: proposed reviews at 3 months, 12 months, 24 months and 5 years. Consider a longer period after penile urethroplasty.
recommended_tests: Uroflowmetry and PROM, including sexual function, at each proposed visit.
Urethrocystoscopy or RUG-VCUG at 3 months, 12 months and 24 months, then when indicated.
long_term_effects: Recurrence can develop after reconstruction.
Penile curvature, shortening or altered sexual function can affect patient satisfaction.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Advise urological review if symptoms worsen after surveillance ends.

conditions.name: failed hypospadias repair-related strictures
conditions.description: Stricture after failed hypospadias repair is a distinct, potentially complex condition. Earlier operations may leave absent spongiosal tissue at parts of the penile urethra and insufficient local tissue for reconstruction. Other associated abnormalities can include glans deformity, dehiscence, urethrocutaneous fistula and chordee.
conditions.epidemiology: After hypospadias repair, meatal stenosis or urethral stricture is reported in 1.3-20% of cases, depending on the original condition and operative technique.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Patients may have recurrent narrowing alongside cosmetic, urinary or sexual difficulties. Multiple previous procedures, extensive scarring and concurrent LS can complicate reconstruction; affected men may report reduced self-esteem.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish original meatal position and the number and type of previous operations.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Assessment of FHR.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Previous interventions influence reconstructive planning.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess urethral plate, skin quality, scarring, LS, fistulae and chordee.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before reconstruction.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An inadequate urethral plate or other adverse local findings may favour staged reconstruction.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Define the location and length of narrowing.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When reconstructive surgery is contemplated.

follow_up.schedule: Repairs in patients with a history of hypospadias fall within the proposed standard-risk schedule of 3 months, 12 months, 24 months and 5 years.
recommended_tests: Uroflowmetry and PROM, including sexual function, at proposed visits.
Anatomic assessment at 3 months, 12 months and 24 months, and subsequently when indicated.
long_term_effects: Further revision may be necessary after a staged repair.
Long-term outcomes can include recurrent narrowing and persisting functional or cosmetic concerns.

conditions.name: lichen sclerosus-related penile urethral strictures
conditions.description: LS-related penile narrowing occurs in the setting of a scarring skin condition. Recurrence after augmentation with genital skin grafts or flaps is reported to be high.
conditions.epidemiology: Lichen sclerosus involves the urethra in 20% of cases and accounts for 48.6% of panurethral stricture disease in a cited series. Reported recurrence after genital-skin graft or flap augmentation is 50-100%.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Genital scarring and adverse local tissue quality may affect the choice of reconstruction.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess scarring suggestive of LS and the quality of local tissues.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before choosing reconstruction.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm LS if the result would change management; assess suspected malignancy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be performed when confirmation changes management and is essential if malignancy is suspected.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Determine stricture extent before reconstructive surgery.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When reconstruction is being considered.

follow_up.schedule: Repairs associated with LS are included in the proposed standard-risk schedule at 3 months, 12 months, 24 months and 5 years; longer surveillance can be considered after penile reconstruction.
recommended_tests: Uroflowmetry and PROM, including sexual function, at scheduled visits.
Anatomic assessment at 3 months, 12 months and 24 months, followed by testing when indicated.
long_term_effects: Recurrence after genital-skin reconstruction may occur late.
Recurrences associated with LS were reported most often during the first two to three post-operative years, although later events also occur.

conditions.name: distal urethral strictures
conditions.description: Distal narrowing encompasses meatal stenosis and strictures of the fossa navicularis. Meatal stenosis generally denotes a short narrowing at the external meatus without fossa navicularis involvement.
conditions.epidemiology: Up to 18% of urethral strictures reportedly involve the meatus or fossa navicularis. Reported causes include FHR, LS, trauma or instrumentation, and idiopathic disease. Meatal stenosis after neonatal circumcision was reported in less than 0.2% of children circumcised as neonates.

subtypes.name: meatal stenosis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Short narrowing confined to the meatus.

subtypes.name: fossa navicularis strictures
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Narrowing involves the fossa navicularis rather than being confined to the external meatus.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Determine meatal position and size and inspect for scarring.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Suspected distal stricture.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess stricture anatomy before reconstruction.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When reconstructive surgery is considered.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The most distal strictures can be difficult to evaluate with this technique.

conditions.name: bulbar strictures
conditions.description: Bulbar narrowing affects the segment between the penoscrotal junction and membranous urethra. The proximal bulbar segment lies within 5 cm of the membranous urethra; extension towards the membranous segment is termed BMS.
conditions.epidemiology: The bulbar urethra is affected in 46.9% of male strictures in a cited series. Idiopathic disease accounts for 63% of bulbar strictures in another cited series.
conditions.clinical_presentation: In a retrospective study of 214 anterior urethroplasty patients, weak stream was reported by 49%, incomplete emptying by 27% and urinary frequency by 20%. In another retrospective series of 614 such patients, post-void dribble occurred in 73%. Blunt perineal trauma most frequently affects the bulbar urethra.

subtypes.name: “Short” bulbar strictures
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Generally short enough for excision followed by a tension-free anastomosis; the usual limit is around 2 cm.

subtypes.name: “Longer” bulbar strictures
subtypes.distinguishing_features: May not be amenable to tension-free excision and primary anastomosis.

subtypes.name: short post-traumatic bulbar strictures
subtypes.distinguishing_features: May be nearly or completely obliterated with full-thickness spongiofibrosis after straddle injury.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess obstructed flow and urinary retention.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Suspected stricture.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Locate and measure the stricture before reconstruction.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When reconstructive surgery is considered.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Can underestimate length.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm narrowing and assess its calibre.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When additional information beyond imaging is required.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess length, location and associated spongiofibrosis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Additional pre-operative assessment of anterior narrowing.

follow_up.schedule: After bulbar or (bulbo)membranous anastomotic repair without radiotherapy, hypospadias or BXO/LS features, the proposed low-risk visits are at 3 months, 12 months and 24 months. Graft or flap repairs, or anastomotic repairs with those risk features, follow the standard-risk visits at 3 months, 12 months, 24 months and 5 years.
recommended_tests: Uroflowmetry and PROM, including sexual function, at scheduled visits.
Anatomic evaluation at 3 months for low-risk repair, then when indicated.
Anatomic evaluation at 3 months, 12 months and 24 months for standard-risk repair, then when indicated.
long_term_effects: Late recurrence after bulbar urethroplasty is possible.
Post-void dribbling, changes in ejaculation and erectile function can follow reconstruction.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Patients should seek assessment if symptoms recur after scheduled follow-up.

conditions.name: penobulbar or panurethral strictures
conditions.description: Penobulbar narrowing extends continuously from the penile into the bulbar urethra. It differs from multifocal disease, in which two or more separate narrowed segments have healthy urethra between them. Panurethral disease involves a particularly extensive urethral segment.
conditions.epidemiology: LS was the most common cause of panurethral disease (48.6%) in a cited series.

subtypes.name: penobulbar strictures
