subtypes.distinguishing_features: Continuous involvement of penile and bulbar segments.

subtypes.name: panurethral strictures
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Extensive disease for which reconstruction may require multiple techniques or tissue sources.

subtypes.name: multifocal strictures
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Two or more narrowed areas separated by healthy lengths of urethra.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Map the location and extent of narrowing before reconstruction.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When reconstructive surgery is considered.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess local scarring, LS and potential sources of reconstructive tissue.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before reconstructive planning.

follow_up.schedule: Graft or flap substitution reconstruction falls within the proposed standard-risk schedule at 3 months, 12 months, 24 months and 5 years; consider longer surveillance after substitution urethroplasty.
recommended_tests: Uroflowmetry and PROM, including sexual function, at scheduled visits.
Anatomic evaluation at 3 months, 12 months and 24 months, and later when indicated.
long_term_effects: Longer strictures have a higher risk of recurrence after urethroplasty than shorter strictures.

conditions.name: non-traumatic posterior urethral stenosis
conditions.description: Non-traumatic narrowing of the posterior urethra can involve the vesico-urethral anastomosis, bladder neck, bulbomembranous segment or prostatic urethra. Aetiology, continence and bladder function influence management.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Obstructive symptoms may coexist with urinary incontinence or impaired bladder function, particularly after previous prostate treatment or irradiation.

subtypes.name: vesico-urethral anastomosis stricture (VUAS)
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Narrowing at the vesico-urethral anastomosis after RP.

subtypes.name: bladder neck stenosis (BNS)
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Bladder-neck narrowing when the prostate remains in situ, including after TURP or simple prostatectomy.

subtypes.name: radiation-induced bulbomembranous strictures (BMS)
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Bulbomembranous narrowing after irradiation, with potential damage to surrounding tissues.

subtypes.name: prostatic strictures secondary to radiation/high energy sources
subtypes.distinguishing_features: May coexist with prostatic necrosis and tissue sloughing.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess stenosis and the proximal urethra.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Especially when stenosis is nearly or completely obliterative.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: RUG alone cannot define the extent of an obliterative stenosis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess posterior stenosis length and associated fistulae or other pathology.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider as an ancillary investigation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm narrowing and assess associated pathology.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When further detail beyond imaging is required; also before incontinence surgery after endoluminal treatment to rule out recurrence.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Inform decisions about reconstruction.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When bladder dysfunction is suspected or reconstruction is contemplated.

staging.additional_rules: The guideline distinguishes non-obliterative from completely obliterated posterior stenosis because this changes the suitability of endoluminal treatment.

follow_up.schedule: Non-traumatic posterior urethroplasty is included in the proposed standard-risk assessments at 3 months, 12 months, 24 months and 5 years.
recommended_tests: Uroflowmetry and PROM, including sexual function, at scheduled visits.
Anatomic evaluation at 3 months, 12 months and 24 months, then when indicated.
long_term_effects: Urinary incontinence can arise or worsen after treatment.
Recurrent stenosis can require further assessment.

conditions.name: vesico-urethral anastomosis stricture (VUAS)
conditions.description: This denotes narrowing or obliteration at the bladder-neck level after RP, rather than bladder neck stenosis in a patient whose prostate remains in situ.
conditions.epidemiology: VUAS after radical prostatectomy was reported in 0.5-30% of patients; most modern series report 1-3%. After salvage RP, reported risk is 22-40%. Most cases develop within the first two years.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Obstruction may occur alongside pre-existing or subsequent urinary incontinence.

subtypes.name: non-obliterative VUAS
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A residual lumen remains.

subtypes.name: obliterative VUAS
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The anastomotic lumen is completely closed.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the location and extent of narrowing.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Particularly for near-obliteration or complete obliteration.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate the lumen and rule out recurrence.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When additional assessment is needed or before subsequent incontinence surgery.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Determine whether bladder function is adequate when reconstruction is contemplated.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before ReDo VUA, particularly after irradiation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Reduced capacity, poor compliance or other severe radiation-related pathology may make reconstruction unsuitable.

follow_up.schedule: After posterior reconstruction, the proposed standard-risk reviews are at 3 months, 12 months, 24 months and 5 years. Following endoluminal treatment, recurrence should be excluded before incontinence surgery.
recommended_tests: Uroflowmetry and PROM, including sexual function, after urethroplasty.
Anatomic evaluation at 3 months, 12 months and 24 months after urethroplasty, then when indicated.
Cystoscopy before incontinence surgery following endoluminal treatment.
long_term_effects: Urinary incontinence after transperineal ReDo VUA is described as inevitable.
Recurrence may affect the timing of subsequent incontinence surgery.

conditions.name: bladder neck stenosis (BNS)
conditions.description: Bladder-neck narrowing or contracture is termed BNS when the prostate remains in situ, including after transurethral surgery or simple prostatectomy.
conditions.epidemiology: BNS after transurethral prostate surgery occurs in 0.3-9.7% of patients in cited reports. It occurs more frequently in smaller prostate glands after monopolar and bipolar TURP.
conditions.clinical_presentation: May cause posterior urinary outflow obstruction.

subtypes.name: non-obliterative bladder neck stenosis (BNS)
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A lumen remains at the narrowed bladder neck.

subtypes.name: BNS with complete obliteration
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The bladder-neck lumen is fully closed.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate bladder-neck narrowing and establish whether the lumen is obliterated.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Assessment of suspected stenosis or recurrence.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess posterior narrowing, particularly if nearly or completely obliterated.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When anatomical delineation is required.

follow_up.schedule: Following non-traumatic posterior urethral reconstruction, the proposed standard-risk reviews are at 3 months, 12 months, 24 months and 5 years.
recommended_tests: Uroflowmetry and PROM, including sexual function, at proposed visits.
Anatomic evaluation at 3 months, 12 months and 24 months, then when indicated.
long_term_effects: New urinary incontinence can occur after bladder-neck reconstruction.

conditions.name: radiation-induced bulbomembranous strictures (BMS)
conditions.description: These strictures affect the bulbomembranous urethra after irradiation. Injury and reduced healing capacity can extend beyond the visibly narrowed segment; proximity to the external sphincter adds complexity.
conditions.epidemiology: Urethral strictures were reported at around four years in 1.5% after EBRT, 1.9% after BT and 4.9% after combined EBRT-BT. Unlike strictures after RP, incidence after irradiation increases over time.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Posterior obstruction may coexist with stress urinary incontinence, bladder pain, spasms or other radiation-related tissue injury.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Define the stenosis and proximal urethra.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Particularly for near-obliterative or obliterative disease.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess posterior anatomy and associated pathology, including fistulation.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: As an ancillary test when additional anatomical information is needed.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Inform the feasibility of reconstruction.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When reconstruction is being considered in a patient with suspected radiation-related bladder dysfunction.

follow_up.schedule: After urethroplasty in a patient with prior radiotherapy, the proposed standard-risk assessments are at 3 months, 12 months, 24 months and 5 years.
recommended_tests: Uroflowmetry and PROM, including sexual function, at scheduled visits.
Anatomic evaluation at 3 months, 12 months and 24 months, then when indicated.
long_term_effects: After surgery for radiation-induced BMS, de novo incontinence was reported in 19-26% and new erectile dysfunction in 0-35% of cases.
Radiation-related bladder dysfunction can affect reconstructive outcomes.

conditions.name: prostatic strictures secondary to radiation/high energy sources
conditions.description: Irradiation or high-energy prostate treatments can cause prostatic tissue necrosis, sloughing and urethral obstruction.
conditions.epidemiology: After cryotherapy and HIFU, reported stricture incidence is 1.1-3.3% and 10.3%, respectively. In salvage settings, reported incidence is 3-10% after EBRT, 5-12% after cryotherapy and 15-30% after HIFU.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Obstruction can coexist with necrotic tissue, impaired bladder function or severe local symptoms.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess prostatic obstruction and associated urethral pathology.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Suspected prostatic stricture.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Determine bladder capacity and function when further reconstruction or diversion is considered.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: After failure of endoluminal treatment or with suspected bladder dysfunction.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess associated pathology, including fistulation.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When associated pathology may alter management.

long_term_effects: Persistent or recurrent obstruction and radiation-related bladder symptoms may affect longer-term management.

conditions.name: post-traumatic posterior stenosis
conditions.description: Following PFUI, partial injury or unsuccessful early realignment can leave a non-obliterative membranous stenosis. Complete disruption can leave an obliterative distraction defect in which dense fibrosis separates the urethral ends.
conditions.epidemiology: Motor vehicle accidents are described as the main cause of blunt posterior urethral injury associated with pelvic fracture.
conditions.clinical_presentation: The resulting posterior obstruction may occur alongside sexual dysfunction or urinary incontinence attributable to the original injury.

subtypes.name: non-obliterative stenosis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A residual lumen remains after partial injury or unsuccessful early realignment.

subtypes.name: obliterative stenosis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A complete injury leaves separated urethral ends with intervening fibrotic tissue.

subtypes.name: pelvic fracture urethral injury (PFUI)
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Pelvic-fracture-associated posterior urethral injury that can result in a distraction defect.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Delineate the distal and proximal urethra and estimate the injury gap.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Evaluation of PFUI and posterior stenosis before reconstruction.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess gap length, bladder-neck competence, scarring and associated fistulae, false passages, calculi or bony abnormalities.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When additional information is required beyond imaging.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess anatomy and features relevant to operative planning.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Ancillary assessment of PFUI.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: In a cited study, the MRI-measured pubo-urethral stump angle predicted the need for a more elaborate approach.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Document function after injury and during recovery.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Assessment before and after reconstructive surgery.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Normal erectile function may return during the first two years after trauma.

staging.additional_rules: The distinction between non-obliterative and obliterative disease determines whether an endoluminal approach can be considered.

follow_up.schedule: Following urethroplasty, offer at least one year of follow-up; the proposed schedule for low-risk bulbar or (bulbo)membranous anastomotic repair is 3 months, 12 months and 24 months when the specified additional risk features are absent.
recommended_tests: Uroflowmetry and PROM, including sexual function, at proposed visits.
Anatomic assessment at 3 months, with later anatomic testing when indicated.
long_term_effects: Recurrent posterior narrowing is possible.
Erectile and ejaculatory changes and urinary incontinence may occur after the injury or reconstruction.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Interpret post-operative sexual-function changes in the context of the initial trauma.

conditions.name: female urethral stricture (FUS)
conditions.description: Most authors describe FUS as persistent anatomical narrowing that reduces urethral calibre. Definitions of reduced calibre vary from < 10 Fr to < 20 Fr; most series use < 14 Fr, compared with a reported normal calibre of 18-30 Fr.
conditions.epidemiology: Among women with refractory LUTS, 2-29% have BOO; of those with BOO, 4-20% have a urethral stricture. Estimated FUS prevalence among women with refractory LUTS is 0.08-5.4%, with a marked rise after 64 years of age. Reported causes were idiopathic in 48.5%, iatrogenic in 24.1% and traumatic in 16.4%. The mid or mid-to-distal segment was affected most often (58%); panurethral disease was uncommon (4%).
conditions.clinical_presentation: Symptoms are prolonged and non-specific. Reported frequencies were frequency 63%, urgency 55%, incomplete emptying 36%, poor flow 32%, urinary incontinence 31%, strain void 21.5%, UTI 20.5%, nocturia 20.5% and dysuria 20%. Less frequent presentations were urethral pain 2.7%, terminal dribble 2%, haematuria 1.6% and renal failure 0.5%. Reported mean diagnostic delays were 4.3-12 years (range 1-30 years).

subtypes.name: meatal strictures
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Short narrowing confined to the external meatus.

subtypes.name: panurethral strictures
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Rare extensive involvement, reported in 4%.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess symptoms and identify prolapse, masses, scars, LS, lichen planus or vulvo-vaginal atrophy.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Women with refractory LUTS.

diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Preliminary dilation is necessary in many cases before an instrument can pass.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When additional functional assessment is required.

Assess for recurrence after treatment when clinically indicated.

New urinary incontinence is reported after some interventions.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: A patent urethra during continuing ISD or planned repeat dilatation should not be equated with freedom from stricture.

conditions.name: strictures in trans men
conditions.description: After FtM reconstruction, narrowing may involve the preserved native urethra, reconstructed fixed part (pars fixa), anastomosis with the neophallus or phallic urethra. Reconstructed segments lack the usual surrounding spongiosal tissue.
conditions.epidemiology: Urethral stricture was reported in 2-56% of FtM transgender patients.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Early after neophallic reconstruction, obstruction can severely affect quality of life or occur with recurrent UTI or retention. Symptoms and management depend on stricture site, length and local tissue quality.

subtypes.name: meatal stenosis in trans men
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Narrowing at the reconstructed meatus; the guideline distinguishes low-grade from high-grade disease.

subtypes.name: strictures at the neophallic urethra
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Narrowing in the segment within the neophallus or metoidioplasty.

subtypes.name: strictures at the anastomosis neophallic urethra-fixed part of the urethra
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Narrowing where the phallic urethra joins the pars fixa.

subtypes.name: strictures at the fixed part of the urethra
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Narrowing in the reconstructed perineal segment.

diagnostic_workup.test: Assessment of reconstruction history and stricture anatomy
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish elapsed time since reconstruction, location, length and local tissue quality.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Suspected stricture after neophallic reconstruction.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: These features determine the available treatment approaches.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess for urinary extravasation.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before catheter removal after treatment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Reinsertion of a urethral catheter can be difficult if extravasation is detected after removal.

staging.additional_rules: The anatomical classification after FtM surgery distinguishes native urethra, fixed part (pars fixa), anastomotic part and phallic urethra.

follow_up.schedule: After endoscopic incision or urethroplasty, the urethral catheter was anecdotally maintained for two to three weeks. A cited study advised three-week catheterisation after trans-male urethroplasty.
recommended_tests: Peri-catheter urethrography before catheter removal.
long_term_effects: Recurrent narrowing may require further intervention.

conditions.name: strictures in trans women
conditions.description: Following MtF surgery, narrowing usually occurs at the neomeatus, formed at the junction of the distal bulbar urethra and neovagina. The remaining bulbar and posterior segments correspond to those in a biological man.
conditions.epidemiology: Reported neomeatal stricture incidence in MtF transgender patients is 4-40%.

subtypes.name: meatal strictures
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Can be short (< 1 cm) or somewhat longer (1-2 cm); site and length affect reconstructive choices.

special_populations.population: Women with refractory lower urinary tract symptoms
special_populations.considerations: Female urethral stricture symptoms are non-specific and may persist for a long time before diagnosis. Pelvic examination assesses possible alternative or coexisting conditions.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Assess flow rate, post-void residual and voiding cystourethrogram or video-urodynamics. For female urethral stricture, initial urethral dilatation is to 24-41 Fr. At the 1st recurrence, repeat dilatation with planned weekly intermittent self-dilatation using a 16-18 Fr catheter, or plan repeat dilatation. At the 2nd recurrence, perform urethroplasty if the patient cannot perform intermittent self-dilatation or wants definitive treatment. Treat a short meatal stricture with meatotomy/meatoplasty.

special_populations.considerations: Treatment depends on time since reconstruction, stricture site and length, and local tissue quality. Tissue healing usually stabilises after six months.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Do not perform endoscopic incision or urethroplasty within six months after neophalloplasty. For severe obstruction, recurrent urinary tract infection or retention during early healing, use a suprapubic catheter initially; specialist perineostomy is an alternative. Do not perform more than two endoscopic incisions unless the intent is palliative. If open reconstruction is indicated for a neophallic urethral stricture, perform staged urethroplasty. Definitive perineostomy is an option for refractory strictures or when complex reconstruction is unwanted.

special_populations.population: Trans women after gender confirming surgery
special_populations.considerations: Strictures occur almost exclusively at the neomeatus. Long-term effectiveness data for initial dilatation are unavailable.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Initial dilatation is acceptable for a short, non-obliterative stricture. If open reconstruction is indicated for short (< 1 cm) meatal stenosis, perform Y-V meatoplasty; a neovaginal advancement flap is described for longer (1-2 cm) meatal strictures.

special_populations.considerations: Previous operations can leave deficient urethral and surrounding tissues, making reconstruction complex. Unsatisfactory appearance and urinary or sexual dysfunction may affect self-esteem.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Refer these patients to specialist centres and propose psychological and/or psychosexual counselling when indicated. The choice between single-stage and staged repair may depend on intra-operative findings; an inadequate urethral plate favours staged repair. Do not use penile skin grafts or flaps when lichen sclerosus or scarred skin is present.

special_populations.considerations: Skin involvement and scarring increase concern about recurrence when genital skin is used for reconstruction. Evidence comparing single-stage with staged oral mucosa graft urethroplasty is of very poor quality.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Do not use genital skin for augmentation penile urethroplasty. Perform single-stage oral mucosa graft urethroplasty for penile strictures when local conditions are favourable. Do not perform staged bulbar urethroplasty if single-stage repair is possible. Intra-urethral clobetasol cream 0.05% on a 10-16 Fr calibration device, twice a day for a minimum of two months, was studied as stricture stabilisation rather than cure.

special_populations.considerations: Radiation-related tissue injury impairs healing, and associated bladder dysfunction or peri-urethral pathology may make reconstruction unsuitable.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Consider a long-term suprapubic catheter for radiation-induced bulbomembranous strictures and/or poor performance status. For non-obliterative stenosis, visually controlled dilatation or direct vision internal urethrotomy is a 1st-line treatment. For refractory short (< 2.5 cm) radiation-induced bulbomembranous strictures, use excision and primary anastomosis or augmentation urethroplasty according to surgeon experience; use augmentation urethroplasty for long (> 2.5 cm) strictures. Warn about new incontinence and erectile dysfunction. ReDo vesico-urethral anastomosis requires adequate bladder function; consider urinary diversion when bladder function or local tissue conditions preclude reconstruction.

special_populations.population: Frail patients or patients with poor performance status
special_populations.considerations: Fitness for surgery and willingness to accept catheter-related complications influence the choice between reconstruction and longer-term urinary drainage.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Consider a long-term suprapubic catheter, particularly for radiation-induced bulbomembranous strictures. Offer perineal urethrostomy to men with anterior urethral stricture disease who are unfit or unwilling to undergo formal reconstruction.

special_populations.considerations: Prolonged lithotomy positioning increases the risk of leg compartment syndrome. Obesity was also identified as a possible adverse prognostic factor in some urethroplasty series, although evidence on its effect is not consistent.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Assess positioning and hip mobility before prolonged or exaggerated lithotomy. Consider “7-flap” urethroplasty in obese men when perineal urethrostomy is appropriate.

special_populations.population: Patients after surgery for benign prostatic obstruction
special_populations.considerations: Bladder neck stenosis and bulbomembranous strictures may follow prostate surgery. Reconstruction near the external sphincter carries a risk of new urinary incontinence.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: For non-obliterative bladder neck stenosis, use transurethral resection or “hot-knife” direct vision internal urethrotomy as 1st-line treatment. Perform Y-V or T-plasty bladder neck reconstruction for stenosis refractory to treatment. Bulbomembranous strictures can be managed with excision and primary anastomosis or graft augmentation according to length and tightness. Warn patients about new urinary incontinence after reconstruction.

special_populations.population: Patients with pelvic fracture urethral injury
special_populations.considerations: Posterior stenosis may be non-obliterative after a partial injury or obliterative after complete urethral disruption. Complex reconstruction has its best results at the first attempt.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Do not treat an obliterative stenosis endoscopically. One endoluminal attempt may be performed for a short, non-obliterative stenosis. Perform progressive perineal excision and primary anastomosis for an obliterative stenosis or after failed endoluminal treatment of a non-obliterative stenosis. Undertake open reconstruction only in high-volume centres.

special_populations.population: Patients with limited suitability of oral mucosa for graft harvesting
special_populations.considerations: Oral tobacco use, chewing betel leaves or previous oral mucosa harvesting may increase donor-site morbidity or limit usable graft tissue.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Assess the oral cavity and previous graft harvest when planning reconstruction. If buccal or lingual mucosa is unavailable, unsuitable or unacceptable to the patient, penile skin may be used for reconstruction, except where genital skin is contraindicated by lichen sclerosus.
