document_sections.heading: 1.1 Aims and scope
document_sections.content: The European Association of Urology (EAU) guideline addresses urethral strictures in male, female and transgender patients while recognising geographical differences in healthcare provision. Its recommendations reflect the evidence available to the panel, but adherence cannot guarantee the best individual outcome. Clinical expertise, patient preferences and individual circumstances remain essential; the guideline is neither a mandate nor a legal standard of care.

document_sections.heading: 1.2 Panel composition
document_sections.content: An international, multidisciplinary group of clinicians with expertise in urethral strictures developed the guideline.

document_sections.heading: 1.4 Publication history
document_sections.content: The guideline first appeared in 2021.

document_sections.heading: 2.1 Methods
document_sections.content: For the 2021 guideline, the panel systematically identified and evaluated relevant literature across all sections. Searches of Medline, EMBASE and the Cochrane Libraries covered 2008 to 2019 and were limited to English-language publications; the panel agreed topic-specific eligibility criteria beforehand. An online form accompanies each recommendation and assesses evidence, effects, uncertainty, benefits and harms, and patient preferences. It draws on GRADE principles without claiming to be GRADE. References use a classification modified from the Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine Levels of Evidence. Recommendation strength is expressed as ‘strong’ or ‘weak’, according to the balance of desirable and undesirable consequences. The panel considers treatment ‘success’ subjective and poorly defined: an anatomically patent urethra may coexist with post-void dribbling, erectile or ejaculatory dysfunction, or altered genital appearance that the patient finds unacceptable. Accordingly, the guideline generally reports patency or recurrence rather than ‘success’. Durable surgery depends on tension-free approximation of healthy urethral ends, a well-vascularised graft bed with close graft contact, epithelial coverage before wound contraction and fibrosis cease, and recognition that completely destroyed circumferential urethral mucosa will not regenerate spontaneously. The panel published two systematic reviews in 2021, concerning single-stage oral mucosa graft urethroplasty for male Lichen Sclerosus-related strictures and free graft augmentation for bulbar strictures; their findings informed the 2023 guideline.

document_sections.heading: 2.2 Review
document_sections.content: The guideline underwent peer review before its initial 2021 publication.

document_sections.heading: 3.1 Definitions
document_sections.content: In males, an anterior urethral stricture is narrowing caused by fibrosis of the mucosa and surrounding corpus spongiosum (‘spongiofibrosis’). Because the posterior male urethra lacks spongiosal tissue, ‘stenosis’ is preferred there. Meatal stenosis generally denotes a short narrowing at the meatus that does not involve the fossa navicularis. Female urethral stricture (FUS) has no universal definition; most authors require fixed anatomical narrowing with reduced calibre. Proposed thresholds range from < 10 Fr to < 20 Fr, most commonly < 14 Fr, against a reported normal calibre of 18-30 Fr. In transgender patients, ‘stricture’ also describes narrowing of a reconstructed urethra despite the absence of surrounding spongiosal tissue.

document_sections.heading: 3.2 Epidemiology
document_sections.content: Among males, incidence rises sharply after 55 years of age; mean age is 45.1, and estimated overall incidence is 229-627 per 100,000 males. The anterior urethra accounts for 92.2% of affected sites, particularly the bulbar urethra (46.9%). Among females with refractory lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS), 2-29% have bladder outflow obstruction (BOO), of whom 4-20% have a urethral stricture; true FUS therefore affects 0.08-5.4% of women with refractory LUTS. Incidence increases markedly after 64 years of age. Following hypospadias repair, meatal stenosis or stricture is reported in 1.3-20% of cases, varying with severity and technique; incidence is significantly higher in well-resourced countries, where repair is more frequent. Up to 18% of all strictures involve the meatus or fossa navicularis, commonly following failed hypospadias repair (FHR), lichen sclerosus (LS), trauma or instrumentation, or without identified cause. Meatal stenosis after neonatal circumcision is reported in less than 0.2% of children. Strictures affect 2-56% of female-to-male (FtM) transgender patients (‘transmen’) and 4-40% of male-to-female (MtF) transgender patients (‘transwomen’); in transwomen, they arise almost exclusively at the neomeatus.

document_sections.heading: 3.3 Aetiology and prevention
document_sections.content: Causes differ substantially between regions because of differences in healthcare quality, environment and clinical practice. Regardless of location, stricture disease harms physical health and quality of life (QoL) and generates costs from primary and recurrent treatment. Prevention aims to reduce infection, trauma and iatrogenic injury, or mitigate their effects when avoidance is not possible.

document_sections.heading: 3.3.1 Aetiology and prevention in males
document_sections.content: This section considers sexually transmitted infection, inflammation, external trauma, iatrogenic injury, failed hypospadias repair, congenital strictures and strictures without an identified cause.

document_sections.heading: a. Sexually transmitted infection
document_sections.content: Sexually transmitted infection (STI)-related urethritis, particularly gonorrhoea, previously accounted for 40% of strictures in well-resourced countries. Safer sex practices and more accessible, timely antimicrobial treatment are thought to explain its decline. Infective urethritis now accounts for 0.9% to 4.6% of cases in contemporary well-resourced settings but remains the leading cause in low-resourced countries, comprising 41.6% of strictures. Evidence level 3 links access to STI investigation and treatment with declining infective-urethritis-related strictures. The guideline recommends counselling men with urethritis about safer sex and STI symptoms and ensuring prompt assessment and treatment (Strong).

document_sections.heading: b. Inflammation
document_sections.content: LS affects the urethra in 20% of cases and is the leading reported cause of panurethral disease (48.6%). Its cause is unresolved, although an autoimmune origin is suspected; environmental factors and non-autoimmune comorbidities may contribute. Compared with circumcised men, uncircumcised men have an age-adjusted odds ratio [OR] of 53.55; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 7.24-395.88 for LS. Reported associations also include higher mean body mass index (BMI), diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, tobacco use, hyperlipidaemia and hypertension.

document_sections.heading: c. External urethral trauma
document_sections.content: External urethral trauma is the second most frequent cause of strictures in adults. Potential settings include sport, driving, intercourse and combat. Blunt straddle injuries or perineal kicks most often affect the bulbar urethra. Urethral injury accompanies 15% of penile fractures. Motor vehicle accidents are the principal cause of blunt posterior injuries associated with pelvic fractures; penetrating injuries are uncommon outside combat.

document_sections.heading: d. Iatrogenic urethral injury
document_sections.content: Iatrogenic injury is among the leading causes in well-resourced countries, accounting for 32-79% of strictures. Avoiding such injury is the principal preventive opportunity for urologists. Frequent sources are catheterisation or cystoscopy, surgery for benign prostatic obstruction (BPO) or prostate cancer, and radiotherapy.

document_sections.heading: d.1 Urethral catheterisation
document_sections.content: Catheterisation accounts for 11.2-16.3% of strictures. In Hollingsworth et al.’s meta-analysis, stricture or erosion followed short-term catheterisation (< 3 weeks) in a pooled 3.4% (CI: 1-7%) of patients in higher-quality studies; studies mainly involving men with spinal cord injury and indwelling catheters gave 8.7% (CI: 0.0-18.7%). Injury can occur during insertion or while a catheter remains in place. Among insertion injuries, false passage accounted for 29.7% and inflation of the balloon within the urethra for 70.3%; catheter-related urethral injury occurred at 3.2 per 1,000 inpatients. In a six-month prospective multicentre study of 37 referred patients with catheter trauma, 24% subsequently performed ISD weekly and 11% required at least one dilation. Another follow-up study of 37 such patients found strictures in 78%. Bulbar and posterior sites were most often injured. Studies estimated that around 25% of hospital indwelling catheterisations were unnecessary or inappropriate; institutional guidance and criteria reduced catheter use. Deficient catheterisation knowledge among resident doctors has been proposed as a contributor to trauma, while a prospective single-institution study found targeted nurse training reduced iatrogenic injuries. A balloon-pressure-valve safety catheter has not undergone comparative assessment. In Bugeja et al.’s observational cohort of 174 patients, adverse events occurred in 7% with standard Foley catheterisation versus 0% with a guidewire-containing urethral catheterisation device (UCD), without statistical testing. Another prospective observational study found non-urology doctors could use Seldinger technique catheterisation successfully. These technologies require prospective raondomised controlled trials (RCTs) and cost-benefit assessment. Catheter calibre is proposed as a pressure-related contributor: reducing size from 22 Fr to 18 Fr significantly reduced fossa navicularis strictures after radical prostatectomy (RP), from 6.9% to 0.9% (p=0.02). Older cardiac-surgery comparisons associated uncoated latex, versus silicone, with more urethritis and strictures, although other studies found no difference. Modern latex catheters have polymer coatings because of stricture, hypersensitivity and demonstrated in vitro latex-toxicity concerns. Prolonged catheterisation has also been implicated. Evidence levels were 2b for unnecessary inpatient catheterisation, 2a for training, 3 for larger calibre and 1a for uncoated latex. Recommendations: avoid unnecessary catheterisation (Strong); train physicians and nurses who catheterise (Strong); do not exceed 18 Fr when drainage is the sole aim (Weak); and avoid uncoated latex catheters (Strong).

document_sections.heading: d.2 Transurethral prostate surgery
document_sections.content: Following transurethral prostate surgery, urethral stricture occurs in 4.5-13% and bladder neck stenosis (BNS) in 0.3-9.7%. This surgery accounts for 41% of iatrogenic stricture causes. The bulbomembranous urethra is most often affected, followed by the fossa navicularis and penile urethra. Proposed mechanisms include penoscrotal friction, inadequate lubrication, repeated resectoscope movement, mucosal disruption and urinary extravasation, or current leakage from poor insulation. Excessive or circumferential resection and large loops generating heat in small intraurethral adenomas may contribute to BNS; prolonged postoperative inability to void may contribute to posterior stenosis.

document_sections.heading: d.2.1 Risk factors for development of urethral stricture and bladder neck stenosis
document_sections.content: After monopolar transurethral resection of prostate (TURP), prostatic inflammation (OR: 4.31) and operation duration > 60 min (OR: 4.27) independently predicted stricture. Following bipolar TURP, slower resection rate (OR: 0.003), intraoperative mucosal rupture (OR: 2.44) and postoperative infection (OR: 1.49) were independent predictors. A 26 Fr rather than 24 Fr sheath was associated with more bulbar strictures after monopolar TURP (11.4% vs. 2.9%, p=0.018). With combined transurethral resection and vaporisation, room-temperature versus body-temperature irrigation was associated with higher stricture risk (21.3% vs. 6.3%, p=0.002). BNS is more frequent in smaller glands after monopolar and bipolar TURP. Lee et al. identified adenoma weight as an independent predictor after monopolar TURP; Tao et al. identified total prostate volume (< 46.2 g) (OR: 1.5), but not resected gland weight.

document_sections.heading: d.2.2 Incidence of urethral stricture and bladder neck stenosis with different energy modalities
document_sections.content: Cornu et al.’s systematic review and meta-analysis found no significant difference in stricture or BNS rates among monopolar, bipolar, holmium laser enucleation and photoselective vaporisation. Another meta-analysis found no difference between thulium (Tm:Yag) laser and bipolar TURP. Sheath size, energy setting, operating duration and follow-up may confound cross-study comparisons; there is no strong evidence that one modality causes a clinically meaningful excess risk. Modality selection should consider overall safety and efficacy. Table 3.1 compares incidence by modality. Another systematic review found the lowest stricture incidence with enucleation, followed by B-TURP and ablation, then M-TURP, but no significant difference remained after twelve months of follow-up.

document_sections.heading: d.2.3 Interventions to prevent urethral stricture and bladder neck stenosis
document_sections.content: In Sciarra et al.’s single-blind RCT (n=96), strictures at twelve months occurred in 17% with placebo versus 0% with rofecoxib after TURP (p=0.0039). In Chung et al.’s single-blind RCT (n=180), urethrographic stricture occurred in 1.25% after urethral hyaluronic acid (HA) and carboxymethylcellulose (CMC) versus 8.64% with placebo (p=0.031). Further RCTs must confirm effectiveness and safety. Of earlier studies of routine preliminary Otis urethrotomy, only one reported at least twelve months’ follow-up and found no significant stricture difference between TURP alone and urethrotomy followed by TURP (21% vs. 14%). Others proposed internal urethrotomy for pre-existing meatal or urethral strictures. In Lee et al.’s retrospective comparison of 1,135 patients, 667 received TURP and 468 TURP plus transurethral incision of the prostate (TUIP); at median 38 months, BNS occurred in 12.3% versus 6.0% (p < 0.001), respectively. For glands < 30 g, rates were 19.3% versus 7.7% (p < 0.05). Larger prospective RCTs are needed before additional preventive surgery can be recommended. An RCT with more than twelve months’ follow-up did not show a significant reduction from routine pre-TURP urethrotomy (evidence level 1b). Do not routinely undertake urethrotomy without a pre-existing stricture (Strong).

document_sections.heading: d.3 Radical prostatectomy
document_sections.content: Vesico-urethral anastomosis stricture (VUAS) is reported after RP in 0.5-30% of patients, although most recent series report 1-3%; salvage RP has a higher reported risk of 22-40%. Most cases develop within the first two years. Tewari et al.’s 2012 meta-analysis found no significant difference among open, laparoscopic and robotic RP. A later UK national cohort reported significantly lower VUAS after robotic RP (3.3%) than after laparoscopic (5.7%) or open RP (6.9%), consistent with an earlier US study. Surgeon volume, experience and a potentially shorter robotic learning curve may explain differences between population cohorts and clinical-study meta-analysis.

document_sections.heading: d.3.1 Risk factors for development of vesicourethral anastomosis strictures
document_sections.content: Reported patient or disease factors include higher cancer grade and stage, larger prostate, coronary artery disease, obesity, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, earlier bladder-outlet surgery and older age. Surgical factors include non-nerve-sparing surgery, anastomotic urine leakage, longer operation and greater estimated blood loss. Reported VUAS rates were 27.7% for surgeons performing < 40/year versus 22% for those performing > 40/year.

document_sections.heading: d.3.2 Interventions to prevent vesicourethral anastomosis strictures
document_sections.content: Srougi et al.’s prospective RCT of 95 patients found no significant twelve-month VUAS difference after bladder-neck mucosal eversion. Kowelewski et al.’s meta-analysis found no VUAS-rate difference between interrupted and continuous anastomotic suturing. Bai et al.’s systematic review could not meta-analyse barbed versus conventional sutures because of heterogeneity, but reported no VUAS with either method.

document_sections.heading: d.4 Prostate radiation and ablative treatments
document_sections.content: At around four years, strictures occurred in 1.5% after external beam radiation therapy (EBRT), 1.9% after brachytherapy (BT) and 4.9% after combined EBRT-BT, usually in the bulbomembranous urethra. Unlike after RP, incidence rises over time after irradiation. Reported incidence is 1.1-3.3% after cryotherapy and 10.3% after high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU). In salvage settings, reported risks rise to 3-10% after EBRT, 5-12% after cryotherapy and 15-30% after HIFU. Increasing use of irradiation and ablation is expected to increase treatment-induced strictures.

document_sections.heading: d.4.1 Risk factors for the development of radiation strictures
document_sections.content: Awad et al.’s meta-regression of 46 studies identified combined ERBT + BT and longer follow-up as significant predictors after prostate radiation; biochemical equivalent dose, age and androgen deprivation therapy were not shown to predict stricture. Previous TURP was omitted from that analysis but independently predicted stricture in an earlier single-institution analysis (HR: 2.81), as did PSA level < 10 ng/ml (HR: 0.47).

document_sections.heading: d.4.2 Interventions to prevent radiation induced urethral strictures
document_sections.content: Delaying adjuvant or salvage EBRT by nine months was associated with fewer strictures (HR: 0.6), but must be weighed against cancer-control risks. BT applicator needles may move downward between fractions, potentially contributing to strictures below the prostatic apex at the ‘hot spot’. Reduced dose there, more careful needle positioning, avoidance of midline insertion and plastic rather than steel needles are collectively thought to have reduced BT-related strictures.

document_sections.heading: e. Failed hypospadias repair
document_sections.content: Although sometimes grouped with iatrogenic disease, post-repair strictures merit separate consideration because penile spongiosal tissue may be absent at several levels and good local reconstructive tissue may be scarce.

document_sections.heading: f. Congenital
document_sections.content: A congenital diagnosis requires exclusion of iatrogenic, inflammatory and traumatic causes. Incomplete or incorrect joining of urethral segments formed from the urogenital sinus and urethral folds is proposed as the origin. These strictures are generally short, deep in the bulbar urethra and diagnosed young; examples are Moorman’s ring and Cobb’s collar.

document_sections.heading: g. Idiopathic
document_sections.content: An unidentified cause is reported for 34% of penile and 63% of bulbar strictures. Unrecognised trauma is considered a possible explanation.

document_sections.heading: 3.3.2 Aetiology in females
document_sections.content: Reported FUS causes were idiopathic in 48.5%, iatrogenic in 24.1% and traumatic in 16.4%. Iatrogenic sources include earlier dilation, difficult or traumatic catheterisation followed by fibrosis, and urethral operations, chiefly diverticulum surgery, fistula repair and anti-incontinence procedures; trauma mainly follows pelvic fracture. Radiation and infection are uncommon causes. Mid or mid-to-distal urethra is involved most often (58%), whereas panurethral disease is uncommon (4%).

document_sections.heading: 4.1 According to stricture location
document_sections.content: Anatomical location matters because it influences subsequent management.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.1.1 Anterior urethra
document_sections.content: In males, the anterior urethra extends from the meatus to the urogenital diaphragm and remains surrounded by corpus spongiosum. Meatal strictures occur at the external opening and may extend into the fossa navicularis. Penile strictures occupy the region between fossa navicularis and bulbar urethra; externally it runs approximately from the balanopreputial sulcus to the penoscrotal junction, ventral to the corpora cavernosa within a thin spongiosal layer. The bulbar urethra runs from the penoscrotal junction to the membranous urethra at the urogenital diaphragm and is surrounded by bulbospongiosus muscle. Its proximal segment lies within 5 cm of the membranous urethra, with eccentric urethral position and abundant ventral spongiosum; its distal segment extends towards the penoscrotal junction. Extension into the membranous region is termed bulbomembranous strictures (BMS). Penobulbar strictures span penile and bulbar segments. Multifocal strictures instead comprise two or more separate narrowings with healthy intervening urethra, potentially within the same or different subdivisions.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.1.2 Posterior urethra
document_sections.content: The male posterior urethra is approximately 5 cm long. Its membranous segment traverses the urogenital diaphragm between proximal bulbar urethra and distal verumontanum; the prostatic segment extends through the gland to the bladder neck. The bladder neck, surrounded by the internal urinary sphincter, joins prostate and bladder. ‘Bladder neck stenosis’ or contracture implies a prostate remains in situ, whereas narrowing at this site after RP is termed VUAS.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.2 In females
document_sections.content: The female urethra measures approximately 4 cm and is conventionally divided into upper, middle and lower parts.

document_sections.heading: 4.2 According to stricture tightness
document_sections.content: Definitions distinguishing low- and high-grade strictures remain disputed. A urethral plate < 3 mm is considered tight or high grade. With normal bladder function, urinary flow reportedly does not decline until lumen diameter falls below 10 Fr. The panel’s consensus-based Table 4.1 proposes male narrowing categories for patients with normally functioning bladders, ranging from imaging-normal to obliterative disease.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.1 Trans women
document_sections.content: Following MtF gender-confirming surgery, the penile urethra is removed. Neomeatal stricture occurs where distal bulbar urethra joins the neovagina; remaining bulbar and posterior segments correspond to those in biological males.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.2 Trans men
document_sections.content: After FtM gender-confirming surgery, four urethral regions are recognised: preserved native female urethra from bladder neck to original meatus; a reconstructed fixed or perineal part (‘pars fixa’), usually made from local vestibular or anterior vaginal mucosa and lacking spongiosal cover; the junction between pars fixa and neophallus; and a phallic urethra within the neophallus or metoidioplasty, usually a skin tube without spongiosal cover.

document_sections.heading: 5. DIAGNOSTIC EVALUATION
document_sections.content: Comprehensive assessment encompasses history, examination, urinalysis with or without culture, uroflowmetry, post-void residual (PVR), radiography and endoscopy.

document_sections.heading: 5.1 Patient history
document_sections.content: History should establish symptom severity and duration, possible cause, prior interventions, complications, associated conditions and factors influencing surgical outcomes. In a retrospective series of 611 endoscopically confirmed cases, initial presentations were LUTS in 54.3%, acute retention in 22.3%, urinary tract infection (UTI) in 6.1% and difficult catheterisation in 4.8%. Among 214 anterior-urethroplasty patients, weak stream occurred in 49%, incomplete emptying in 27% and frequency in 20%; another series of 614 found post-void dribble in 73%. Genitourinary pain affects 22.9-71%, may involve bladder or urethra, accompanies more severe LUTS, is more likely in younger men and resolves after reconstruction in most. Other reported complaints include spraying (9%), visible haematuria (3.1-5%), urethral abscess or necrotising fasciitis (2.3%), urgency (14%) and incontinence (1-4%). Establish trauma, instrumentation, surgery, irradiation or focal therapy, and urethritis history. Record prior approaches and the latest intervention date because they may affect imaging or operative timing. Document baseline erectile and ejaculatory function with validated tools: sexual problems are common and surgery may affect function. Functional status can influence curative versus palliative treatment. Assess diabetes, immunosuppression and smoking as potential healing factors; oral tobacco or betel leaves may impair oral graft quality or donor-site outcomes. Earlier oral mucosa harvest may require another donor tissue or an alternative such as perineal urethrostomy (PU).

document_sections.heading: 5.2 Physical examination
document_sections.content: Examine for a palpable bladder and note suprapubic tube position if antegrade access or a repair-facilitating sound might be needed. Record foreskin, meatal size and position, LS-suggestive scarring, fistulae and urethral induration; a rare mass may indicate urethral carcinoma. LS biopsy may be undertaken if it changes care and is essential when malignancy is suspected. Rectal examination should assess possible prostatic causes of symptoms and, with posterior stenosis, prostatic rectal adherence and surrounding-tissue mobility. Examine oral donor tissue, measure BMI to identify obesity-related risk of leg compartment syndrome during prolonged lithotomy, and assess hip mobility before exaggerated lithotomy.

document_sections.heading: 5.2.1.1 Patient reported outcome measure (PROM)
document_sections.content: The urethral stricture surgery PROM (USS-PROM), first validated in 2011, incorporates six LUTS questions derived from ICIQMLUTS, a LUTS-related QoL question, the Peeling voiding chart and EQ-5D; the postoperative form adds two satisfaction questions. It has been validated in German, Spanish, Italian, Dutch, Turkish, Polish and Japanese. Another North American PROM remains under development and needs validation. Evidence level 2a supports the psychometric validity of a stricture-surgery PROM; evidence level 3 addresses sexual dysfunction and possible surgical effects. For men undergoing stricture surgery, use a validated PROM for symptoms and QoL (Strong), and a validated sexual-function tool (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 5.2.1.2 Urinalysis and urine culture
document_sections.content: Urinalysis is essential when assessing LUTS. If infection is suspected, obtain culture to confirm it, identify the organism and determine antibiotic susceptibility. Treat bacteriuria before surgery to reduce peri-operative sepsis risk.

document_sections.heading: 5.2.1.3 Uroflowmetry and post-void residual estimation
document_sections.content: A reduced maximum flow rate with a prolonged plateau suggests constrictive obstruction, but visual interpretation alone is subjective and unreliable for stricture screening. A statistical uroflowmetry model predicted stricture with sensitivity of 80–81% and specificity of 77–78%. Combine flow assessment with ultrasound PVR to identify retention potentially requiring urgent drainage; flow measures also assist monitoring and response assessment. Urodynamics is unnecessary for the vast majority. It may aid decisions and counselling with suspected bladder dysfunction, including severe storage LUTS, irradiation or neurological disease, or distinguish detrusor underactivity and an acontractile detrusor when postoperative intermittent self-catheterisation (ISC) is a concern. Of assessed urodynamic measures, only urethral closure pressure distinguished stricture from BPO: 22.07 vs. 28.4 cm H2O, p=0.0039, r=0.61, BPO vs. stricture. Statistical flow-pattern prediction carries evidence level 3. Obtain uroflowmetry and PVR when stricture is suspected (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 5.2.1.4 Urethrography
document_sections.content: Retrograde urethrography (RUG) evaluates whether a stricture exists, its position and length, and associated false passages or diverticula. Reported diagnostic sensitivity is 91%, specificity 72%, positive predictive value 89% and negative predictive value 76%. Most reports find that it underestimates length; specialist urological interpretation outperformed independent physician interpretation for site and length. RUG poorly depicts very distal disease or proximal extent when contrast cannot traverse a tight narrowing. Adding voiding cystourethrography (VCUG) improves proximal and length assessment for (nearly) obliterative strictures, stenoses and pelvic fracture urethral injury (PFUI). Results are two-dimensional and affected by penile stretch, pelvic rotation and body habitus. Risks include infection, discomfort, contrast reaction following intravasation and radiation. Brodny or Knutson clamps were less painful than a Foley catheter technique. Evidence levels are 2a for RUG’s utility and length limitations, its inability alone to assess obliterative disease, and less painful clamps. Obtain RUG to determine site and length before considering male reconstruction (Strong); add VCUG for (nearly) obliterative strictures, stenoses or PFUI (Strong); prefer a clamp over a Foley catheter during urethrography to lessen pain (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 5.2.1.5 Cystourethroscopy
document_sections.content: Cystourethroscopy can identify or rule out a suspected stricture, including narrowing preceding symptom or flow change, and detect LS or other pathology. Ordinary scopes usually cannot establish length because their calibre exceeds that of symptomatic strictures; 6.5 Fr and 4.5 Fr ureteroscopes have been used to address this and permit bladder assessment, including stones. Endoscopy is particularly useful for proximal BMS missed on RUG. Combined retrograde urethroscopy and antegrade suprapubic cystoscopy can inform PFUI repair by assessing defect length, bladder-neck competence and scarring, bony spicules, fistulae and stones. Compared with combined contrast studies, it gave similar length estimates but detected fistulae, false passages and calculi more often. The corresponding evidence levels are 3. Add cystourethroscopy to imaging when additional information is necessary (Weak); for PFUI, consider combined retrograde and antegrade endoscopy as an imaging adjunct when further detail is needed (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 5.2.1.6 Ultrasound
document_sections.content: Sonourethrography (SUG) provides a non-invasive three-dimensional assessment of anterior stricture site, length and spongiofibrosis. Comparative studies found more accurate stricture diagnosis than RUG and closer agreement with operative length: 94% for SUG versus 59% for RUG (p < 0.001), with the closest reported correlation in penile strictures. Intraoperative SUG changed a preoperatively planned reconstructive approach in 19% of men. Real-time elastography can quantify and characterise spongiofibrosis, but the clinical value of preoperative grading remains unestablished; three-dimensional sonographic reconstruction remains investigational. SUG can be performed as an outpatient procedure at relatively low cost and assesses fibrosis. Limitations include reduced bulbar sensitivity, operator dependence, specialised training, limited availability and urethral distension requiring intraurethral anaesthesia. Table 5.1 compares diagnostic accuracy across studies.

document_sections.heading: 5.2.1.7 Magnetic resonance imaging
document_sections.content: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has been studied for PFUI and anterior and posterior narrowing. In anterior strictures, one study found MRI urethrography comparable with RUG for site and operative length, while another found closer MRI agreement for length. In mixed anterior and posterior disease, MRI and combined RUG/SUG each achieved sensitivity = 100%, specificity = 91.7%, without a significant length difference. Another posterior-stenosis study found MRI length closer to operative findings than RUG. For PFUI, MRI pubo-urethral stump angle predicted the need for an elaborated approach on multivariate analysis. MRI also identified diverticula, tumours, fistulae and stones more accurately in one study. After prostate irradiation, it may show a urinary–pubic symphysis fistula missed by other imaging and otherwise mistaken for isolated pubic osteomyelitis. Greater anatomical detail is offset by cost and interpretive complexity, so MRI is not routine but may reveal management-changing associated disease. Table 5.2 compares studies. Evidence level 2a supports MRI’s greater accuracy for posterior-stenosis length and detection of associated pathology. Consider MRI urethrography as an additional test in posterior stenosis (Strong). Figure 5.1 presents a diagnostic flowchart; its visible note specifies VCUG for (nearly-) obliterative strictures or stenosis.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.1 Observation
document_sections.content: Urinary flow generally declines once calibre is < 10 Fr; wider asymptomatic strictures may be found incidentally. Purohit et al. observed 42 incidental strictures > 16 Fr with repeat cystoscopy: at median 23 months, five (12%) progressed to 11-15 Fr, without symptoms or surgery. Observation is an option, although long-term evolution is unknown. After urethroplasty, only 65% of patients with anatomical recurrence < 16 Fr in one series had symptoms. In a multicentre study, recurrence > 16 Fr led to intervention in 4% at one year and 12% at two years, versus 41% and 49% for recurrence < 16 Fr. Those needing treatment had worse PROMs; long-term outcomes without intervention are unknown. Asymptomatic recurrence may be observed with regular follow-up, but apparent absence of symptoms warrants caution: some patients restrict drinking or social activity and seek care only when these adaptations fail.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.2 Suprapubic catheter
document_sections.content: Radiation-associated strictures have lower reconstructive stricture-free rates than non-irradiated disease. Among Fuchs et al.’s 75 patients initially diverted suprapubically for isolated radiation-induced BMS, 51% elected urethroplasty after mean 25 months. Overall performance status did not differ significantly between chronic-catheter and urethroplasty groups, but every patient with poor performance remained catheterised. Patients with stress urinary incontinence (SUI) more often retained the catheter; SUI improved in 61%. Catheter complications affected 27% of those retaining it. Ileal-conduit diversion occurred in 30% of those who kept a suprapubic catheter versus 8% after urethroplasty. Long-term catheterisation is also an option for frail patients unable to undergo surgery or those declining further urethral surgery and accepting catheter complications. Evidence level 3 describes low progression risk for incidental asymptomatic strictures > 16 Fr and the observation that only about half of suprapubically diverted radiation-induced BMS patients proceed to reconstruction. Do not intervene for incidental asymptomatic strictures > 16 Fr (Weak); consider a long-term suprapubic catheter for radiation-induced BMS and/or poor performance status (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 6.2 Endoluminal treatment of anterior urethral strictures in males
document_sections.content: Less invasive, faster procedures may benefit patients when specialist reconstruction is unavailable or an immediately accessible approach is preferred.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.1 Direct vision internal urethrotomy
document_sections.content: Direct vision internal urethrotomy (DVIU) is commonly used first-line. It is generally performed under general or spinal anaesthesia in well-resourced settings, but has also been tolerated under local anaesthesia with or without sedation.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.1.1.1 Direct vision internal urethrotomy for primary stricture treatment
document_sections.content: Steenkamp et al. randomised 210 patients with apparently comparable non-obliterative strictures at various locations to outpatient filiform dilation or DVIU under local anaesthesia; RUG was performed at 3, 6, 9, 12, 24, 36 and 48 months. Effectiveness was similar, and both approaches became less effective as stricture length increased. A retrospective iatrogenic-stricture cohort found significantly lower patency with DVIU than urethroplasty (32.2 versus 82.4-83.5%). Retrospective DVIU cohorts with at least one year of follow-up reported patency from 8% to 77%, with median recurrence before twelve months in most; heterogeneous lesions and varying definitions partly explain the range. Selection depends on prognostic stricture characteristics. Table 6.1 presents individual series.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.1.1.2 Direct vision internal urethrotomy for recurrent strictures and as salvage treatment after failed urethroplasty
document_sections.content: The OPEN trial defined recurrence as at least one previous failed urethrotomy, dilation or urethroplasty, predominantly DVIU. Despite poor recruitment, 108 patients were randomised to urethroplasty and 112 to DVIU in a 24-month protocol. Voiding-symptom improvement was similar. Urethroplasty recipients had 2.6 higher odds of maximum-flow improvement > 10 ml/s (p=0.001). Re-intervention occurred in 13.8% after urethroplasty versus 25.9% after DVIU, a reported 48% lower risk with urethroplasty (HR: 0.52; 95% CI: 0.31-0.89; p=0.017); self-dilation did not count as re-intervention. QoL gains were similar, although urethroplasty cost more; follow-up was limited to two years. As salvage after prior EPA, BMG or penile-skin graft urethroplasty, Brown et al. reported patency after one DVIU in thirteen of 37 cases (35%) with mean recurrent length 4 cm; range: 1.5-7 cm. Rosenbaum et al. selected 43 short (< 1 cm), veil-like BMG graft-end recurrences and reported 51% patency at mean twelve months.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.1.1.3 Predictors of failure of “cold knife” direct vision internal urethrotomy
document_sections.content: Adequately powered multicentre trials are lacking, limiting confidence in individual predictors. The most favourable candidates appear to have a previously untreated, single, bulbar stricture of max. 2 cm. Barbagli et al. reported five-year patency of 71% for untreated 1-2 cm bulbar strictures. Table 6.2 details study-specific prognostic findings and shows that results vary by site, length, calibre, multiplicity and prior DVIU.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.1.2.1 Laser urethrotomy
document_sections.content: Neodymium:YAG, Argon, Holmium:YAG, Potassium titanyl phosphate (KTP) and Tm:Yag have been used. A systematic review found four RCTs comparing laser and ‘cold knife’ urethrotomy; follow-up was short and none reported outcomes by location. Meta-analysis of two reporting recurrence gave relative risks favouring laser of 0.55 (95% CI: 0.18-1.66; p=0.29) at three months, 0.39 (95% CI: 0.19-0.81; p=0.01) at six months and 0.44 (95% CI: 0.26-0.75; p=0.003) at twelve months. Jin et al.’s review of 44 case series, comprising nineteen laser and 25 ‘cold knife’ reports, found weighted overall stricture-free rates of 74.9% (371/495) and 68.5% (1874/2735), respectively (p=0.004); heterogeneity and unreported follow-up duration limit interpretation. At first DVIU, rates were 58.6% versus 42.7% (p=0.09); in bulbar disease, 52.9% versus 60% (p=0.66). In Yenice et al.’s RCT of primary bulbar disease, ‘cold knife’ (n=29) and holmium:YAG laser (n=34) produced twelve-month patency of 79% and 68% (p=0.3). Chen et al.’s RCT found one-year patency of 88% with laser (n=24) versus 18% with ‘cold knife’ (n=22) (p < 0.05); the laser advantage disappeared by two years, and at five years rates were 12% versus 9% (p > 0.05). Gamal et al. randomised n=40 per technique and found equivalent maximum-flow improvement at one year.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.1.2.2 Plasmakinetic (bipolar) urethrotomy
document_sections.content: In Cecen et al.’s RCT (n=136), plasmakinetic versus ‘cold knife’ patency was 86% versus 70% at nine months (p=0.025), but 63% versus 67% at eighteen months (p=0.643). A prospective cohort of primary strictures < 2 cm reported twelve-month patency of 23/30 (77%) versus 19/30 (63%) (p=0.04). A retrospective series (n=27) reported 74% patency for 1-2.5 cm strictures after mean fourteen months, negligible operative blood loss and no postoperative incontinence. Conflicting, heterogeneous and short-term evidence does not establish superiority of any DVIU technique; complication rates are similar, so the panel does not favour one technique.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.1.3.1 Complications of “cold knife” direct vision internal urethrotomy
document_sections.content: Jin et al.’s review of twelve reports involving 1,940 patients found an overall complication rate of 6.5%, including erectile dysfunction (ED) in 5.3%. Graversen et al. reported ED in eleven of 104 (10.6%). Risk appears higher for penile strictures; together with poor patency, this supports discouraging penile DVIU.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.1.3.2 Complications of “hot knife” direct vision internal urethrotomy
document_sections.content: Jin et al.’s review reported complications in 11.8% (39/330) after ‘hot knife’ DVIU; Table 6.3 details reported events.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.1.3.3 Complications of “cold knife” vs. “hot knife” direct vision internal urethrotomy
document_sections.content: Only 1/4 RCT series in a systematic review reported complications: 8.9% with laser, involving perineal contrast extravasation or recurrence, versus 15.5% with ‘cold knife’, involving bleeding. Two later RCTs found similar urinary extravasation rates, and one found similar urinary incontinence (UI). Jin et al.’s retrospective-series review found no significant laser–‘cold knife’ differences in UI, urinary extravasation or UTI, but more retention and haematuria with laser. Conversely, Yenice et al. reported haematuria only after ‘cold knife’, without a significant difference (p=0.6). Table 6.3 compares individual adverse events and p-values.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.1.3.4 Complications of direct vision internal urethrotomy vs. dilatation
document_sections.content: A Cochrane review found no significant overall intraoperative complication difference between single dilation and DVIU (14% vs. 11%; RR: 0.75; 95 CI: 0.36-1.55), nor differences in difficulty voiding, haematuria, false passage, pain or filiform-leader problems. False passages occurred in 0.94% after dilation and 0.96% after DVIU; routine filiform guidance may explain their low frequency. In a small retrospective study, balloon dilation (n=31) caused less urethral bleeding than DVIU (n=25), 6.5 vs. 32% (p=0.017), and less UTI, 3.2 vs. 24% (p=0.037). Reports also describe increasing lesion length and number after DVIU; repeated DVIU or dilation may increase complexity and postpone urethroplasty.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.1.3.5 Complications of “cold knife” direct vision internal urethrotomy vs. urethroplasty
document_sections.content: In the OPEN trial, any adverse event occurred in 61% after urethroplasty and 26.1% after DVIU. After urethroplasty, oral mucosa graft (OMG) donor-site mouth pain affected 14.6% and wound infection 4.9%. ED affected 4.9% after urethroplasty versus 2.6% after DVIU; serious adverse events occurred in 8.5% versus 8.7%. Evidence levels accompanying the DVIU section are 1b for poor penile outcomes and length-related failure, 3 for selected short primary bulbar lesions and short veil-like postoperative recurrences, and 1a for conflicting evidence about ‘hot knife’ superiority beyond one year. Do not use DVIU for penile strictures (Strong) or DVIU/dilation alone for long segments > 2 cm (Strong). Perform DVIU/dilation for a primary, single, non-obliterative bulbar lesion < 2 cm (Weak), or a short veil-like recurrence after bulbar urethroplasty (Weak). Either ‘hot’ or ‘cold knife’ may be selected according to expertise and resources (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 6.2.2.1 Modalities of dilatation and results
document_sections.content: Dilation can be performed in an office under local anaesthesia without complex equipment. It disrupts scar through stretching rather than incision; both dilation and DVIU seek re-epithelialisation faster than wound contraction after mucosal disruption. Dilating a bulbar lesion with rigid instruments requires experience to avoid perforation. Guidewire-based, visually controlled methods seek to reduce false passage, spongiosal perforation and bleeding associated with blind dilation. Direct blind-versus-controlled comparisons are unavailable; studies of controlled methods report low complications and recurrence ranging from 23.5-64.5%. Table 6.4 presents techniques, recurrence definitions and complications.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.2.2 Effectiveness of dilatation compared with direct vision internal urethrotomy
document_sections.content: A systematic review found only one prospective RCT comparing dilation with DVIU and detected no difference. A retrospective cohort (n=56) estimated three-year recurrence-free survival at 35.5% after balloon dilation versus 28% after DVIU (p=0.21). Evidence does not establish either procedure as superior; indications for a single dilation match DVIU indications. Avoid repeated dilation or DVIU with curative intent: durable freedom from recurrence is not expected, and repeated manipulation can significantly increase stricture length and complexity while delaying urethroplasty. Evidence levels are 3 for low complications with guided dilation and 1b for the poor long-term outcomes and added complexity of repetition. Prefer visually controlled to blind dilation (Weak). Do not perform repetitive (> 2) DVIU/dilations when urethroplasty is viable (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 6.2.3 Post-dilatation/direct vision internal urethrotomy strategies
document_sections.content: Adjunctive approaches after dilatation or DVIU seek to limit wound contraction, increase the interval without recurrence and improve reported stricture-free outcomes. They generally stabilise a stricture rather than eliminate it; their results should be interpreted accordingly.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.3.1 Intermittent self-dilatation
document_sections.content: Intermittent self-dilatation (ISD) is assessed as a means of maintaining urethral calibre after endoluminal treatment.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.3.1.1 Results
document_sections.content: A systematic review of six randomised or quasi-randomised trials, with eight to 24 months of follow-up, reported recurrence in 85/197 (43%) men using ISD and 128/207 (62%) not using it (RR: 0.70; 95% CI: 0.48-1.00; p=0.05). Because heterogeneity was significant and study quality very low, the review authors considered the estimate uncertain. Adverse events did not differ significantly (RR: 0.60; 95% CI: 0.11-3.26; p=0.56). Trials found no significant difference between six and twelve months of ISD in 48 patients (RR: 0.67; 95% CI: 0.12-3.64), or between low-friction hydrophylic and polyvinyl chloride catheters in 59 patients (RR: 0.32; 95% CI: 0.07-1.40). After dilatation, Chhabra et al. reported re-intervention in 12.3% of patients adhering to ISD versus 20.5% of those not adhering (p=0.2). At a mean 25 months, Greenwell et al. reported further intervention in 13/31 (42%) men using ISD versus 47/95 (49%) not using it (p=0.46); among those requiring intervention, the respective numbers of repeat operations were 2.6 and 3.4. Neither group had major complications.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.3.1.2 Complications
document_sections.content: Potential stricture stabilisation must be weighed against ISD-related burdens. Reported urethral bleeding was 7.1%, and UTI/epididymitis was 4.7-18.1%. In a prospective multicentre study (n=85), moderate and severe catheterisation difficulty affected 35% and 26%, respectively; moderate and severe pain affected 32% and 17%, respectively. Quality of life was rated moderate by 32% and poor by 55%; younger age predicted poorer quality of life, and impairment was greater with proximal posterior or bulbar strictures. Among 286 ISD users, mainly > 60 years old, 20% reported ISD problems, 33% had at least one infection annually, and 67% still used ISD after a mean 58 months. Khan et al. reported eight withdrawals among 30 (26.7%) men assigned ISD: two could not perform it and one stopped because of pain. Repeated dilatation, including ISD, can increase stricture complexity and defer urethroplasty.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.3.1.3 Intermittent self-dilatation combined with intra-urethral corticosteroids
document_sections.content: Intra-urethral corticosteroid ointment used as catheter lubricant is intended to delay contraction. A 2014 review of three prospective RCTs comparing ISD with or without triamcinolone included 67 steroid-treated and 68 control patients followed for twelve to 36 months. Recurrence occurred in fifteen (22.4%) versus 25 (36.7%) patients (OR: 0.51; 95% CI: 0.24-1.10; p=0.09); time to recurrence was longer with steroid (weighted mean difference = 0.29; 95% CI: 0.08-1.00; p=0.05), without an adverse-event difference. Subsequently, Ergun et al. studied six weeks of ISD (n=30) versus ISD plus triamcinolone (n=30) after DVIU for primary short (< 2 cm) strictures, bulbar in 82% and posterior in 18%. At 24 months, recurrence was not significantly different: 33.3 and 30%, respectively. Regmi et al. found recurrence of 22% with ISD plus triamcinolone (n=27) versus 46% with ISD alone (n=28; p=0.04); median time to recurrence was 11.9 ± 3 months versus 7.4 ± 4.5 months, respectively (p=0.16). Neither trial reported ointment-related complications. In a cohort of n=28 with LS-related strictures, clobetasol cream 0.05% applied to a 10-16 Fr calibration catheter or dilator twice a day for a minimum of two months avoided treatment escalation in 25 (89%) after a mean 25 months. Since most continued steroid-assisted calibration, this represents stabilisation rather than cure. Twelve (42.8%) reduced treatment frequency, and three (10.7%) eventually stopped. Evidence summaries assign LE 1a to reduced recurrence with ISD and to delayed recurrence with added intra-urethral corticosteroids. Recommendations are to use ISD after dilatation or DVIU to stabilise a stricture when urethroplasty is not viable (Weak), and to add intra-urethral corticosteroids for stabilisation (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 6.2.3.2 Intralesional injections
document_sections.content: Adjuvant injection into the lesion is intended to limit fibroblast proliferation and excessive urethral scarring.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.3.2.1 Steroids
document_sections.content: A 2014 systematic review found five comparisons of submucosal steroid injection versus no injection after DVIU, including two RCTs. Meta-analysis of those RCTs, with 57 steroid-treated and 58 control patients, found no statistically significant recurrence difference (OR: 0.53; 95% CI: 0.25-1.13; p=0.10). Recurrence occurred significantly later with steroid (weighted mean difference = 4.43; 95% CI: 2.77–6.09, p < 0.00001). Adverse events, including infection, bleeding and extravasation, did not differ significantly (weighted mean difference = 1.59; 95% CI: 0.71–3.58, p=0.26).

document_sections.heading: 6.2.3.2.2 Mitomycin C
document_sections.content: A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of adjuncts to minimally invasive treatment in men associated mitomycin C (MMC) with the lowest recurrence rate: intralesional injection OR 0.23, 95% CI 0.11-0.48; P<0.001, and intraluminal injection OR 0.11, 95% CI 0.02-0.61; P=0.01. Another 2021 review by Xu et al. found a significant effect of MMC added to DVIU for short (< 2cm) anterior strictures in the longer (>12 months) follow-up group. Because adequately powered, well-conducted RCTs and standardised dose, technique and volume are lacking, careful clinical review and prospective collection of trial data are advised.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.3.2.3 Platelet rich plasma
document_sections.content: In an RCT of primary bulbar strictures < 1.5 cm, Rezaei et al. compared DVIU plus platelet rich plasma (PRP; n=44) with DVIU plus saline (n=43). At two years, the respective stricture-free rates were 78% and 56% (p=0.034). Complications affected 70% with PRP and 79% with saline, without a significant difference. Bleeding, haematuria, urethral or pelvic pain, urinary leakage and genitoperineal swelling were all Clavien-Dindo grade 1. Validation is required before routine implementation. The evidence summary states that intralesional agents might improve short-term stricture-free rates versus DVIU alone, but experience is limited, use is off-label and the drug, dose, volume and technique remain substantially uncertain (LE 1a). Restrict intralesional injections to clinical trials (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 6.2.3.3 Urethral stents
document_sections.content: Stents are intended to counter contraction after dilatation or DVIU. Placement takes < 60 minutes, can use local or spinal anaesthesia and can be performed as day surgery. Stents may be permanent or temporary, with the latter removable after six to twelve months.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.3.3.1 Results
document_sections.content: Permanent stainless-steel mesh stents are no longer sold. An RCT in bulbar strictures found longer median stricture-free survival with temporary stenting after dilatation/DVIU than with dilatation/DVIU alone: 292 versus 84 days (p < 0.001); recurrence within one year affected 20.6% versus 82.8%. Wong et al. reported median stricture-free survival of 23 months after DVIU plus a temporary three-month stent versus two months after DVIU alone. Failure requiring another intervention is common (30-53%), usually through recurrence, encrustation, migration or urethral hyperplasia; further complications include recurrent UTI, haematuria and genito-perineal pain. Posterior stents carry a 82-100% risk of UI, particularly after irradiation or when narrowing reaches the membranous or bulbar urethra. Bulbar placement near the external sphincter increases UI risk. Penile use is anecdotal: Jung et al. observed failure in 4/7 (57%) after a mean eight months; none of those with failed distal or pan-penile treatment became stricture-free, and recurrence was significantly greater than for bulbar placement. Temporary stents appear to have fewer, less serious complications than permanent devices, although they have not been compared directly.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.3.4 Drug-coated balloon dilatation
document_sections.content: Drug (paclitaxel)-coated balloon dilatation (DCBD) following ordinary dilatation or DVIU aims to reduce scar formation through paclitaxel's antimitotic action. ROBUST-3 randomised patients with predominantly bulbar strictures < 3cm and at least two failed endoscopic treatments to DCBD (n=79) or standard dilatation/DVIU (n=48). Cystoscopic anatomic patency at six months was 75% versus 27% (p<0.001); estimated survival without retreatment at one year was 83% versus 22% (p<0.001). No serious DCBD-related adverse events occurred, although haematuria and dysuria were more frequent with DCBD than in controls (11.4% versus 2.1%). Paclitaxel remained detectable in semen up to six months, prompting contraception when a partner could bear children. If DCBD is used, careful review and prospective data collection, ideally through a post-marketing registry or trial, are advised. The comparative finding is graded LE 1b. Offer DCBD for a recurrent short (< 3 cm) bulbar stricture after at least two endoscopic treatments only when urethroplasty is not an option (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 6.2.3.4.1 Treatment of stent failure
document_sections.content: Urethroplasty after stent failure, usually with stent removal, remains possible but is likely more complex than initial reconstruction. Embedded steel wires can severely damage the spongiosum. Horiguchi et al. associated previous stenting independently with greater stricture complexity (OR: 13.7; 95% CI: 1.7-318.3; p=0.01) and more complex urethroplasty (OR: 6.9; 95% CI: 1.1-64.5; p=0.04). Permanent stents accounted for 62% in that study and can become epithelialised, usually within six months, making removal difficult. Reconstruction depends on stricture length and local tissue quality; most cases allow preservation of the urethral plate and one-stage substitution. Reported patency ranges from 16.7-100%, probably reflecting differences in stricture complexity rather than established superiority of any repair. Avoid stents if later urethroplasty is contemplated. They are not first-line treatment but may be considered after recurrent narrowing following DVIU/dilatation in patients unable or unwilling to undergo complex urethroplasty. Evidence summaries assign LE 3 to the high failure and complication rates of permanent stents and their effect on later repair, LE 3 to greater penile failure, and LE 1b to delayed bulbar recurrence with temporary stents. Do not use permanent stents (Strong) or stents for penile strictures (Strong). Use a temporary stent after DVIU for recurrent bulbar narrowing to delay recurrence only if urethroplasty is not viable (Weak).
