document_sections.heading: 6.3 Open repairs (urethroplasty): site and aetiology (clinical scenario) treatment options
document_sections.content: Open reconstruction is considered according to stricture location, cause and clinical circumstances.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.1 The role of urethroplasty in the management of penile urethral strictures
document_sections.content: Failed hypospadias repair, LS and distal penile strictures merit separate consideration because their causes, associated problems or location differ, although published penile-stricture series often mix these aetiologies.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.1.1 Staged augmentation urethroplasty
document_sections.content: A nominally two-stage repair can require further stages: revision after the initial stage, usually for graft contracture, is reported in 0-20%, and the pre-second-stage revision range is 0-20%. Reconstruction specialists generally favour staging for complex disease with repeated previous procedures, marked spongiofibrosis, scarring requiring removal or a poor urethral plate. Tubularisation has been proposed at least four to six months after the first stage if healing is satisfactory. Mangera et al.'s review reported average patency of 90.5% across staged penile graft techniques at average follow-up of 22.2 months. For staged OMG repair, site-specific patency was 73.3 to 100%. Ekerhult et al. and Joshi et al. reported UCF in 17.2% and 2.6%, respectively; other studies did not report it clearly.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.1.2 Single-stage augmentation urethroplasty
document_sections.content: Single-stage repair avoids additional operations and the procedural, cosmetic and functional consequences of a first stage. Some studies suggest 50% or more never return for the second stage, particularly older men or those with multiple failed procedures who are satisfied after the first, or patients reluctant to undergo another operation. Mangera et al. reported 75.7% overall patency for single-stage graft repairs at average follow-up of 32.8 months. Individual reports give dorsal OMG (n=320), 63-100%; ventral OMG (n=54), 55-92.6%; double dorsal-plus-ventral penile/scrotal skin graft/OMG onlay (n=14/8/4), 88.5%; dorsal penile skin graft (n=44), 62-78%; and penile skin flap (n=367), 67-100%. High-level evidence does not establish a superior technique. Dorsal positioning appears more commonly used. Mangera et al. found better patency with OMG than with other grafts, mainly penile skin. Jiang et al. reported significantly greater penoscrotal patency with double BMG onlay than single onlay (88.9% versus 60.9%), but double-onlay follow-up was significantly shorter. Limited sexual-function reports did not identify significant postoperative impairment. Long, complex strictures may be unsuitable for a single stage; intra-operative findings can necessitate conversion. Single-stage LS repair enlarges rather than removes diseased urethra, leaving future recurrence possible. The influence of earlier procedures is uncertain because reports omit or exclude such patients, and study findings conflict. Previous urethral surgery and high BMI have been identified as poor prognostic factors in some single-stage series.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.1.3 Anastomotic urethroplasty in men with penile urethral strictures
document_sections.content: Penile anastomotic repair has traditionally been discouraged because of postoperative chordee. Selected very short strictures, usually < 1 cm, have nonetheless been repaired with 80-93% patency, satisfactory quality of life and sexual function, and no reported chordee in the cited series. Evidence summaries report single-stage augmentation stricture-free ranges of 70%-100% for dorsal OMG, 67-100% for PSF, 55-92.6% for ventral OMG and 62-78% for dorsal SG; staged OMG ranges are 70-100% (LE 2b). The proposed interstage interval has LE 4; selective anastomotic repair and conversion for adverse operative findings have LE 3. Offer penile augmentation by a single-stage or staged route according to earlier interventions and stricture features (Strong). Allow at least four to six months before a satisfactory first stage is followed by the second (Weak). Do not offer anastomotic repair for penile strictures > 1 cm because of chordee risk (Strong). Explain that adverse operative findings may require conversion to staging (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 6.3.1.4 Specific considerations for failed hypospadias repair-related strictures
document_sections.content: Failed hypospadias repair (FHR) encompasses recurrent narrowing, glans deformity or dehiscence, urethral dehiscence, UCF and chordee. Reconstruction is difficult because the urethral plate, penile skin and dartos fascia may be deficient or absent; incomplete records can obscure the original meatus and previous operations. Several procedures may be needed, so specialist high-volume management is advised. The stigmatizing expression historically applied to multiply operated patients should be avoided. Men with FHR may have reduced confidence and self-esteem, problematic appearance, urinary or sexual function, disappointment after failed repair and a sense that further repair is unavailable. Single-stage and staged approaches are available. Staging is generally advised when the urethral plate is inadequate; consent should address both approaches because scarring, LS, UCF, chordee or poor plate quality can change the operative plan. Avoid skin grafts or flaps in scarred skin or concurrent LS: Depasquale et al. reported 90% recurrence at long-term follow-up. Reported patency ranges are 71-95% for mainly BMG staged repair and 80-100% for single-stage repair, but published FHR 'success' can include outcomes other than urethral patency. Previous-operation counts are often unavailable for individual approaches. In a five-year comparison of 345 patients, Barbagli et al. reported 48% overall failure-free survival and significantly lower failure-free survival after staged than single-stage surgery; baseline comparability is unclear and selection differences could explain the result. Kozinn et al. reported revisions after the first and second stages in 16% and 14%, respectively, more often than in non-FHR penile cases. Whether FHR itself predicts poorer repair outcomes remains disputed. Concurrent UCF can be repaired with urethroplasty. Saavendra et al. reported 89.3% stricture-free among 56 patients at median 21 months, chiefly after staged repair or perineal urethrostomy. Verla et al. reported outcomes in 76 patients at median 89 months ranging from 29% after anastomotic repair to 90% after the first stage alone of multistage repair. Evidence summaries grade complex tissue and treatment needs LE 4, psychosocial effects LE 2b, and unsatisfactory skin-graft or flap outcomes LE 3. Regard FHR patients as complex and refer them to specialist centres (Weak); propose psychological and/or psychosexual counselling for appearance-related, sexual or urinary difficulties (Weak); and do not use penile skin grafts or flaps when FHR coexists with LS or scarred skin (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 6.3.1.5 Specific considerations for lichen sclerosus-related penile urethral strictures
document_sections.content: Because LS affects skin, genital skin grafts and flaps are discouraged: reported disease recurrence is 50-100%, usually within the first two to three postoperative years but sometimes later. Principal approaches use single-stage or staged OMG. A Panel systematic review included fifteen studies and 649 patients: 366 from five non-randomised comparative studies and 283 from ten single-arm retrospective studies. Single-stage OMG reported success of 65-100% after twelve to 67 months of mean or median follow-up, while staged OMG results were 60-79%. Selection bias and other methodological problems might explain the difference. Complications were uncommon (0-12%), mainly Grade 1-3. Evidence quality was very poor, so the review could not establish single-stage superiority; in carefully selected patients without unfavourable local tissues, it may produce high success and improve voiding and QoL. Evidence summaries grade skin-associated recurrence LE 4 and single-stage OMG patency of 65 to 100% without inferiority to staged OMG LE 3. Do not use genital skin for augmentation of LS-related penile strictures (Strong). Perform single-stage oral mucosa graft urethroplasty if local conditions are not adverse (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 6.3.1.6 Distal urethral strictures (meatal stenosis, fossa navicularis strictures)
document_sections.content: Open options include Malone meatoplasty, a skin-flap meatoplasty, and SG or OMG graft reconstruction. For short meatal narrowing, Malone dorsal-plus-ventral meatotomy has reported patency up to 100% and cosmetic satisfaction of 83%. Hofer et al.'s ventral scar excision and mucosal eversion achieved 81% freedom from stricture at mean 41 months. Across three studies of 67 patients, skin-flap meatoplasty achieved 90-96% patency, high satisfaction and minimal functional complaints, chiefly spraying, with no ED cases. Graft repairs using OMG or SG in 106 patients achieved 69-91% patency; reported cosmetic satisfaction was favourable, and mild spraying resolved spontaneously. Although routine single-stage tubularised grafting is not recommended, a selected distal-penile series reported 89.9% patency with a 'two-in one approach'. Daneshvar et al. reported 96% stricture-free after transurethral ventral inlay OMG at median 16 months, a short follow-up. The evidence summary gives an overall post-meatoplasty or urethroplasty patency range of 57-100%, dependent on procedure, with high satisfaction and few complications (LE 3). Offer open meatoplasty or distal urethroplasty for meatal, fossa navicularis or distal strictures (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 6.3.2 Urethroplasty for bulbar strictures
document_sections.content: Bulbar reconstruction is considered in relation to whether excision permits a tension-free repair, stricture aetiology and length.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.2.1 “Short” bulbar strictures
document_sections.content: A 'short' bulbar stricture lacks a precise length definition: it generally permits excision and tension-free anastomosis, usually around 2 cm. In fit patients, options are transecting or non-transecting EPA and FGU.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.2.1.1 Excision and primary anastomosis
document_sections.content: EPA removes a narrowed segment and reconnects the remaining urethra; transecting and non-transecting variants are considered separately.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.2.1.1.1 Excision and primary anastomosis with transection of corpus spongiosum (transecting EPA)
document_sections.content: Transecting EPA (tEPA) removes the full thickness of the affected bulbar urethra and surrounding spongiofibrosis before a spatulated, tension-free anastomosis.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.2.1.1.1.1 Patency rates
document_sections.content: An ICUD review reported composite tEPA patency of 93.8% and endorsed it for short bulbar narrowing when another method's anticipated patency is below 90%; that advice did not account for penile complications. Prospective data give 88% patency at twelve months. Studies defining anatomic failure as inability to pass a 16 Fr endoscope report 85.5-97% patency. Median recurrence time is 3.5 to thirteen months. Several authors favour tEPA for short traumatic bulbar obliteration with full-thickness spongiofibrosis, often following a straddle injury. Horiguchi et al. reported 98.5% patency and improved erectile function at one year in such patients. Other tEPA reports frequently include straddle or perineal injuries but seldom present separate aetiology-specific outcomes.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.2.1.1.1.2 Complications
document_sections.content: In Nilsen et al.'s RCT of strictures < 2 cm, penile adverse effects occurred more often with tEPA than FGU. At three months, tEPA patients significantly more often reported worse ejaculation (26%), reduced glans filling (26%), shortening (16%) and chordee (10%). Reduced filling (19%) and shortening (26%) remained significantly more frequent at 12 months. Scrotoperineal haematoma was also significantly more frequent with tEPA, 24 versus 4%. IIEF-5 did not differ significantly at three or twelve months. Transection may disrupt antegrade spongiosal and urethral blood flow, potentially contributing to these problems and ED; ntEPA was developed to spare it.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.2.1.1.2 Non-transecting excision and primary anastomosis
document_sections.content: Non-transecting EPA (ntEPA) aims to avoid complete division of the corpus spongiosum.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.2.1.1.2.1 Patency rates
document_sections.content: Except for straddle injuries typically associated with obliteration and full-thickness spongiosal scarring, ntEPA is an alternative for short bulbar strictures of other causes. Reported patency without further intervention is 93.2-99% at median follow-up of 17.6 to 37.1 months; anatomic assessment with a 16 Fr cystoscope yielded 97.9% at twelve months. Waterloos et al. reported 88.4% patency with tEPA versus 93.2% with ntEPA (p=0.33), but follow-up was significantly longer with tEPA (118 versus 32 months; p < 0.001); 11.1% scheduled for ntEPA required conversion. Chapman et al. found anatomic patency of 93.8% versus 97.9%; follow-up was 74.1 (SD: 45.4) versus 37.1 (SD: 20.5) months, respectively (p < 0.001).

document_sections.heading: 6.3.2.1.1.2.2 Complications
document_sections.content: At six months, ED defined by a SHIM reduction of > 5 points was significantly less frequent after ntEPA than tEPA (4.3 versus 14.3%); transection was the sole multivariable factor associated with sexual dysfunction. Other studies reported ED lasting more than six months in 2-6% after ntEPA. Grade > 2 Clavian-Dindo complication ranges were 3.6-8.1% after tEPA and 4.3-6.8% after ntEPA, without a significant difference. No published trial compares ntEPA directly with FGU for patency and complications.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.2.1.2 Free graft urethroplasty
document_sections.content: FGU is also used for short bulbar strictures, partly because ED has been reported after EPA. A meta-analysis of ten cohort papers reported higher patency with tEPA than BMG FGU (91.5% versus 70%) but fewer erectile complications with BMG FGU (9% versus 25%). Its methodology is disputed because it omitted risk-of-bias assessment and the timing of ED measurement. An RCT found no significant patency difference between tEPA and BMG FGU (88% versus 87%) or erectile-function difference, although penile complications were more frequent with tEPA. Dogra et al. prospectively assessed 87 patients undergoing EPA or penile/bulbar substitution: sexual function fell by 20% across groups and recovered after six months. Evidence summaries grade traumatic short-stricture tEPA patency LE 3; for non-straddle short bulbar strictures, comparable patency with tEPA, ntEPA and FGU but fewer erectile or penile effects with ntEPA and FGU is graded 1b-3*, with LE1b for tEPA versus FGU and LE3 for the broader comparison. Use tEPA for a short traumatic bulbar stricture with (nearly) complete obliteration and full-thickness spongiofibrosis (Strong). Prefer ntEPA or FGU over tEPA for short bulbar strictures unrelated to straddle injury (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 6.3.2.2 “Longer” bulbar strictures
document_sections.content: Bulbar strictures that cannot undergo tension-free EPA require consideration of graft augmentation or selected augmented anastomotic approaches.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.2.2.1 Free graft urethroplasty
document_sections.content: FGU is the preferred approach when EPA is unsuitable; buccal mucosa is currently the most commonly used graft, although other grafts and flaps are possible. Reported bulbar FGU patency is 88-91% over twelve to 40 months, with a suggestion of deterioration over time. Conventional midline separation of bulbospongiosus can injure muscle and perineal nerves, potentially causing post-void dribbling or ejaculatory problems. A muscle- and nerve-sparing approach has therefore been introduced for graft repair and can also be used for EPA. In an RCT of 50 patients, Elkady et al. found similar operating times (100 versus 105 min), significantly less dribbling (4% versus 36%, p=0.01), and fewer ejaculatory changes (8% versus 40%, p=0.02) with sparing. A separate multicentre comparison of 50 patients by Fredrick et al. found no statistically significant difference in these functional outcomes. Limited, conflicting evidence prevents a recommendation for routine sparing.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.2.2.2 Augmented anastomotic repair
document_sections.content: Augmented anastomotic repair (AAR) has mainly been used when a stricture of +/- 2-4 cm is too long for tension-free EPA, or when a longer stricture contains a shorter nearly obliterated portion. The most narrowed part is excised, the plate reconnected and the remaining segment augmented with an onlay graft. Reported AAR patency is 91.1 - 91.9% at twelve to 28 months; Redmond et al. found a 4.8 higher recurrence risk than with dorsal FGU. A non-transecting variant, ANTABU, achieved 100% patency in sixteen patients after median thirteen months in Bugeja et al.'s series; one patient (6.7%) had permanent ED. Evidence summaries give FGU patency of 88-91% at short-to-medium follow-up LE 1b and AAR patency of 88-92% for a nearly obliterative bulbar component, with possible decline over time, LE 3. Use FGU if EPA is unsuitable (Strong). Use AAR when a short, nearly obliterative component exists within a bulbar stricture unsuitable for EPA (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 6.3.2.2.3 Location of the graft during urethroplasty for bulbar strictures
document_sections.content: Optimal bulbar graft placement has not been established. Described placements are ventral, lateral, dorsolateral and dorsal, as onlay from outside or inlay from inside the opened urethra. A Panel review of studies published from 1996, each including at least 20 patients and twelve months of follow-up, found one RCT, four non-randomised comparisons and 36 case series covering 3,683 patients. In the RCT, ventral (n=40) and dorsal (n=40) BMG onlay achieved 90 - 92.5% patency at twelve months (p=0.51). Non-randomised comparisons found no significant patency differences across the evaluated graft positions. Case-series patency ranges were 62.1-98.3% for dorsal onlay, 74.3-94.4% for ventral onlay and 78.4-92% for dorsal inlay. No evidence suggests greater ED risk with one of the four techniques. Post-void dribbling was 0-28.1% for dorsal and 20-21% for ventral onlay. Other adverse events were similarly frequent, though UCF and diverticulum appeared only with ventral onlay, in two and one cases, respectively. Double ventral-dorsal onlay for high-grade or nearly obliterative strictures achieved 90-91% patency over 22-33 months. Graft position did not affect patency in the evidence summary (LE 1b). Select a dorsal, dorsal-lateral or ventral approach according to operative findings and surgical experience or practice (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 6.3.2.3 Staged urethroplasty for bulbar urethral strictures
document_sections.content: Staged reconstruction is considered for selected complex bulbar disease.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.2.3.1 Indications
document_sections.content: Possible indications include fistula, false passage, abscess or cancer; failed complex previous urethroplasty, including FHR; uncertainty about the best repair; radiation injury; severe spongiofibrosis; or LS. LS is disputed as an indication, and some groups consider it a contraindication. Kozinn et al. recommend at least ten months between the 1st and 2nd stages in LS to allow graft complications to become apparent.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.2.3.2 Outcomes
document_sections.content: Series including bulbar disease report staged-repair patency of 33.3-94.6% at mean follow-up of 11.2-50 months. Mesh, preputial and oral grafts or marsupialisation have been used. One comparison in LS reported 52.2% patency after staging versus 86% after single-stage buccal mucosa repair (p < 0.01), but differing patient and stricture characteristics likely influence this contrast. Between 19-45.5% of patients planned for staging declined 2nd-stage tubularisation. Early effects include dehiscence, UTI, epididymitis, scrotal abscess and penile numbness. UCF following 2nd-stage Johanson repair is reported in 3-15% and may be undercounted when small fistulae close conservatively. Up to 19% need revision after stage 1: LS recurrence in grafts 8.8%, contraction 6.6% and stomal stenosis 3.3%. Reported later stage-2 problems include post-void dribbling 14-18%, SUI up to 16%, curvature up to 9%, ED up to 4%, diverticulum 1% and cold glans. Mesh-graft staging appears particularly associated with SUI, curvature and ED. Satisfaction was 86% after mesh-graft staging and 96.6% after buccal-graft staging, but samples were too small to detect significant differences. All series are retrospective and heterogeneous in indications, sites, lengths and populations, limiting conclusions. Evidence summaries report 33.3-90% patency and high satisfaction (LE 3), identify LS as a relative contraindication with long-term patency of 52.2% versus 64.3% without LS (LE 3), and note that up to 45.5% forgo stage 2 and up to 19% need stage-1 revision (each LE 3). Offer staging to fit men with complex anterior disease unsuitable for a single stage (Weak). Do not stage bulbar LS if single-stage repair is possible (Weak). Consider staging when a patient is undecided between perineal urethrostomy and reconstruction (Weak), and warn that more than two stages may be required (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 6.3.2.3.3 Risk factors
document_sections.content: Evidence concerning age, obesity, cause, prior irradiation and earlier surgery as predictors of urethroplasty outcome is unclear. The clearly identified multivariable predictors are length and site: shorter or bulbar strictures fare better than longer or penile strictures. Patients should be informed about the greater risk with long or penile disease.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.2.3.4 Risk factors for adverse outcomes
document_sections.content: Four multivariable series conflict on whether aetiology, comorbidity, length or previous treatment predict failure. Most do not implicate advanced age, although a retrospective series of 184 diverse repairs by Viers et al. found significantly greater recurrence beyond age 60, with reported outcomes of 94% at < 50 yrs and 74% at > 70 yrs. That series and Ahyai's 2015 series also identified prior radiotherapy as a risk; the latter reported 71% patency after median 29 months in previously irradiated patients. These findings do not permit a clear evidence-based recommendation.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.2.4 Management of recurrence after bulbar urethroplasty
document_sections.content: Kahokehr et al. followed nearly 400 patients and found recurrence in 6% (n=25); DVIU successfully treated 92% of failures, whereas 8% required another open repair. Recurrence features and follow-up length were not specified. Rosenbaum et al. and Javali et al. reported 82-86% patency with contralateral-cheek BMG FGU for repeat repair in 51 and 21 patients, within the range of primary outcomes. Among 534 patients, Vetterlein et al. found comparable patency of 87% for primary repair and repeat repair after prior BMG, versus 71% for secondary repair after prior surgery without BMG. A series of n=37 assessed revision EPA for strictures averaging 2.1 (range 1-3.5) cm. At mean 30 months, patency was 95% after failed primary EPA, which accounted for 51% of patients, and 94% after other failed urethroplasties, which accounted for 49%. The evidence summary grades comparable primary and repeat buccal-graft patency LE 3. Use oral mucosa FGU for ReDo urethroplasty of a long stricture (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 6.3.3 Urethroplasty for penobulbar or panurethral strictures
document_sections.content: Extensive reconstruction may combine techniques or use grafts other than OMG; patency is generally lower than for shorter repairs. In an RCT of mean 15 cm strictures, Hussein et al. found no difference between skin grafts and flaps in patency (72% versus 79%) or complications. Warner et al.'s multi-institutional review included 466 patients with lengths > 8 cm and reported 77.5% overall patency. A staged-repair cohort described by Kozinn et al. included 54.9% panurethral cases. Kulkarni et al. reported 83.7% overall patency after 59 months in 117 men with mean 14 cm strictures treated by a one-stage perineal approach with penile invagination and unilateral dissection. PU is an option for patients declining or unfit for complex repair. The evidence summary notes that panurethral reports generally originate from high-volume centres (LE 4) and that multiple materials or approaches may be necessary (LE 3). Offer panurethral urethroplasty at specialised centres (Weak), combining techniques when one cannot address the entire length (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 6.3.4 Perineal urethrostomy
document_sections.content: Perineal urethrostomy (PU) may provide a temporary or permanent urinary outlet for complex male strictures.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.4.1 Indications
document_sections.content: PU can restore voiding when previous urethroplasties have failed repeatedly, comorbidities rule out extensive repair after failed endoscopy, the surgeon is uncertain of the best reconstruction, or cancer treatment has required urethrectomy and/or penectomy.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.4.2 Types of perineal urethrostomy
document_sections.content: Johanson's anterior scrotal funnel, described in 1953, was modified by Gil-Vernet and Blandy into a posteriorly based flap; these approaches use an inverted U or lambda incision. Added dorsal and/or ventral OMG permits augmented Blandy PU in selected radiation- or LS-related disease, PU stenosis, or narrowing reaching the proximal bulbar or membranous urethra. The unilateral posteriorly based '7-flap' was developed for very obese men or proximal extension at any BMI; its later 'loop PU' variant mobilises the bulbar urethra without transection. A midline incision used for '7-flap' has been associated with less superficial infection (1.9% c.f. 18.6%) and dehiscence (11.9% c.f. 23.3%) than an inverted U or lambda incision; it may improve short-term outcomes (0% failure c.f. 6.2% at six months). Mean operative time across PU methods ranges from 97.2 minutes to 112 minutes. In a tertiary centre, PU represented 4.5% of 403 complex-stricture procedures in 2008 and 38.7% in 2017. PU recipients tend to be older: one series reported median 62.6 years versus 53.2 years for anterior urethroplasty recipients. Between 18.7% and 73.4% of men undergoing a successful first stage for complex anterior disease elect to continue voiding through its perineal opening instead of undergoing the 2nd stage.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.4.3 Outcomes
document_sections.content: Patency, complications, patient-reported outcomes and predictors of PU failure are assessed separately.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.4.3.1 Patency rates
document_sections.content: Retrospective, clinically heterogeneous series report PU patency of 70-95% at mean or median follow-up of 20–63 months; available data do not establish the best technique. McKibben et al. found 92.9% patency in 42 '7-flap' patients at median 53.6 months, and 100% in twenty loop-PU patients at median thirteen months. Lumen et al. reported 74.3% for Johanson versus 87.5% for Gil-Vernet-Blandy PU (p=0.248), with longer Johanson follow-up (median 36 versus nine months). In Barbagli et al.'s series of 173 men initially planned for staging, 127 (73.4%) did not pursue the 2nd stage; patency was 70% at median 62 months, illustrating declining patency over time.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.4.3.2 Complications
document_sections.content: Reported PU complications affect 2.5-11.4% and include superficial dehiscence, scrotal abscess, UTI or urosepsis, bleeding, and temporary scrotal pain or numbness. Most are Clavien-Dindo grade 1 (2.9-18.8%) or 2 (0-2.9%); grade 3 events are uncommon at 5.7-6.2%. At medium-term review, 22.2-30.8% report post-micturition dribbling.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.4.3.3 Patient reported outcomes
document_sections.content: At median 62 months, Barbagli et al. reported that 168/173 (97.1%) patients were satisfied or very satisfied with Gil-Vernet-Blandy PU and would repeat it; 166/173 (95.9%) judged the result excellent or good, 145/173 (85%) reported no personal problems, and 141/173 (82%) reported no partner problems. A small TURNS group showed significantly better urinary symptoms without a significant sexual-function change. Lumen et al. found satisfactory or acceptable IPSS in 26/32 (81.25%) patients after Johanson or Gil-Vernet-Blandy PU at respective median follow-ups of 32 and nine months. McKibben et al. reported mean PGI-I of 1.3 among nineteen loop-PU or '7-flap' patients at median 31 months.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.4.3.4 Risk factors for patency failure of the perineal urethrostomy
document_sections.content: PU outcomes are poorer with LS-, trauma- or infection-related strictures: reported failure is 36.7-67% at median 62 months. Previous failed urethroplasty and multiple earlier endoscopic or open procedures also predict worse outcomes. Barbagli et al. found an inverse relationship of patency with stricture length and patient age; the discussion contrasts this with Viers et al.'s age-related findings of 100% patency under age 50 versus 83% at ages 60-69. Lopez et al. linked ischaemic heart disease to greater failure risk. Failed PU can be revised by V-Y plasty, augmentation or complete ReDo, or managed by periodic dilatation or diversion. Evidence summaries rate favourable short- and long-term outcomes for complex disease LE 1a; outcomes in patients unable to tolerate major reconstruction LE 2b; equivalence among PU types LE 4; augmented Gil-Vernet-Blandy or '7-flap' for proximal bulbar or membranous extension LE 2; and '7-flap' in obesity LE 3. Offer PU for complex anterior disease (Strong), or for patients unfit or unwilling to undergo reconstruction (Weak). Choose the technique according to patient characteristics and experience (Weak). Consider augmented Gil-Vernet-Blandy or '7-flap' PU for proximal bulbar or membranous involvement (Weak), and consider '7-flap' urethroplasty in obese men (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 6.3.5 Posterior urethra
document_sections.content: Posterior disease is addressed separately for non-traumatic and post-traumatic stenosis.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.5.1 Non-traumatic posterior urethral stenosis
document_sections.content: Management depends on the stenosis and the patient's condition and goals.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.5.1.1 Treatment of non-traumatic posterior urethral stenosis
document_sections.content: Available choices include conservative care, endoluminal intervention and open or minimally invasive surgery, selected in light of health status and patient goals.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.5.1.2 Endoluminal management of non-traumatic posterior urethral stenosis
document_sections.content: Endoluminal options include dilatation, incision or resection, and selected strategies to stabilise recurrent narrowing.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.5.1.2.1 Dilatation of non-traumatic posterior urethral stenosis
document_sections.content: Dilatation can be performed under loco-regional anaesthesia for VUAS or radiation-induced BMS. Most reported patients had not previously received stricture treatment. Patency varies from 0-89%; de novo UI is reported in 0-11%, without other reported complications. Most non-obliterative VUAS series used visually controlled dilatation.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.5.1.2.2 Endoscopic incision/resection of non-traumatic posterior urethral stenosis (Table 6.8)
document_sections.content: Incision position depends on surgeon preference, but deep cuts at six and twelve o'clock should be avoided because of rectal injury and urosymphyseal fistulation, respectively; previous radiotherapy heightens fistula concern. VUAS bladder-neck incision performs less well after radiotherapy. DVIU studies chiefly concern initial or refractory VUAS, with some mixed VUAS/BNS or irradiated BMS cohorts. First 'cold/hot knife' DVIU patency is 25-80%; laser incision reports 69-100%. An unbalanced retrospective series by La Bossiere et al. favoured laser over dilatation, cold-knife DVIU and TUR. Redshaw et al. reported 50% patency after cold-knife incision versus 63% after hot-knife incision plus MMC for BNS (p=0.03). Reported UI ranges from 0 to 53%, but some studies lacked preprocedure continence assessment. Among studies with baseline data, reported de novo UI after DVIU was 0% to 10%. In Giannarini et al.'s series, eleven of 21 (52%) initially incontinent patients became continent and eight (38%) improved. Because recurrences usually arise early, waiting three to four months before necessary continence surgery is advised by some authors; others wait twelve months. Cystoscopy should first exclude recurrence. Popken et al. reported TUR patency of 47% in untreated VUAS without de novo SUI. Kranz et al. compared 87 post-RP VUAS and 60 post-TURP BNS patients: after median 27 (range: 1-98) months, patency was 40.2% versus 58.3% (p=0.031), and de novo incontinence was 13.8 versus 1.7% (p=0.011). Whether resection causes more incontinence than incision remains disputed. Brodak et al. found recurrence in two (9.1%) after bipolar TUR and four (23.5%) after holmium incision/vaporisation at mean 42 months (p=0.37); at six months Qmax was 13 versus 6.1 ml/s (p < 0.001). Bipolar vaporisation yielded 82% patency at mean 24 months among 28 previously treated VUAS patients. Cut-to-the-light treatment of complete obliteration is not advised because durable patency is very unlikely and a false rectal passage can form. Repeat DVIU can stabilise narrowing, although 6-10% ultimately require diversion or chronic suprapubic cystostomy. TUR can remove obstructing sloughed tissue after HIFU or cryoablation. For necrotic debris after radiotherapy, its role is limited: recurrence risk is 50% and de novo UI risk 15-25%.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.5.1.2.3 Post-dilatation/direct vision internal urethrotomy strategies for non-traumatic posterior urethral Stenosis
document_sections.content: After dilatation or DVIU, ISD, intralesional agents and stents have been investigated for recurrent non-traumatic posterior stenosis.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.5.1.2.3.1 Intermittent self-dilatation for non-traumatic posterior urethral stenosis
document_sections.content: ISD may be offered after dilatation/DVIU to stabilise recurrent posterior stenosis, particularly in patients unfit or unwilling to undergo surgery or with radiation-induced BMS. Its acceptability to some clinicians and patients must be balanced against reduced QoL and poor adherence.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.5.1.2.3.2 Intralesional injections for non-traumatic posterior urethral stenosis
document_sections.content: Antifibrotic injection during endoluminal treatment has been proposed to limit fibrosis and recurrence, principally in recurrent non-obliterative VUAS or BNS. Two series used corticosteroids and others MMC; respective patency ranges are 50-100% and 50-94%. No comparative trial of endoluminal treatment with versus without intralesional injection was identified. Most retrospective studies reported few complications, but Redshaw et al. described grade 3 events in four of 55 (7%): osteitis pubis (n=2), bladder-neck necrosis (n=1) and rectourethral fistula (n=1). Three ultimately needed urinary diversion, one also needing faecal diversion. In view of these potentially severe events, MMC should not be used outside a clinical trial.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.5.1.2.3.3 Urethral stent for non-traumatic posterior urethral stenosis
document_sections.content: Posterior stent use is anecdotal; reported patency is 47-60% and UI 19-82%. Evidence summaries for non-obliterative VUAS and radiation-induced BMS give visually controlled dilatation patency of 0-89% and DVIU patency of 25-100% with few complications and possible loco-regional anaesthesia (LE 3). They also describe six-o'clock rectal injury and twelve-o'clock urosymphyseal fistulation risks (LE 3); BNS patency of 58.3% with TUR and 72% with hot-knife incision (LE 3); possible stabilisation with repeat treatment (LE 3); de novo UI up to 25% or worsened existing UI up to 15% after endoluminal treatment (LE 3); unlikely success for completely obliterated VUAS, BMS or BNS (LE 3); and posterior-stent patency and incontinence concerns (LE 3). Use visually controlled dilatation or DVIU first for non-obliterative VUAS or radiation-induced BMS (Weak). Avoid deep six- or twelve-o'clock DVIU incisions in these conditions (Strong). Use TUR or hot-knife DVIU first for non-obliterative BNS after BPO surgery (Strong). Repeat endoluminal treatment may be used to stabilise non-obliterative VUAS or BNS (Weak). Warn about new or worsened UI (Weak). Do not use endoluminal treatment for completely obliterated VUAS, BMS or BNS (Strong), or posterior urethral stents (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 6.3.5.1.3 Lower urinary tract reconstruction for non-traumatic posterior urethral stenosis
document_sections.content: Fit, motivated patients may be considered for lower urinary tract reconstruction after repeated endoluminal failure or with complete posterior obliteration. Procedure selection depends on stenosis length, position, calibre and aetiology; continence and bladder function; previous radiotherapy; patient preference; and surgical expertise.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.5.1.3.1 Redo vesico-urethral anastomosis for vesico-urethral anastomotic stenosis after radical prostatectomy
document_sections.content: After removing the stenosis, ReDo VUA may use retropubic, perineal, combined abdominoperineal or robot-assisted access. Nikolavsky et al. propose retropubic access if VUAS involves the bladder neck, perineal access for short VUAS with an intact neck, and combined access for > 3 cm VUAS involving the neck. Bladder or bulbar-urethral mobilisation, corporal splitting and, if necessary, inferior pubectomy permit a tension-free anastomosis. Robot-assisted reports include combined repair of a 4.5 cm complete obliteration and a purely abdominal approach. Deep subpubic location and proximity to the external sphincter make surgery demanding and morbidity relevant, although many patients previously fit for RP remain candidates. In non-irradiated patients, reported patency is 60-91%; radiotherapy increases failure risk. Radiation-related poor bladder capacity or compliance, spasm, pain, necrosis, calcification or fistulation can make reconstruction futile. Undertake ReDo VUA only with adequate bladder function and without peri-urethral pathology; a gracilis or peritoneal flap may protect an irradiated anastomosis. Transperineal access inevitably causes UI through external-sphincter disruption. Pfalzgraf et al. reported new UI in four of eleven (36%) after retropubic surgery; other retropubic or predominantly retropubic series reported 58%, none among five, and one of four patients, respectively. Some authors therefore favour retropubic access when preoperative continence is good, although the approaches have not been directly compared for UI. Retropubic access also preserves perineal tissues for possible later AUS. Defer AUS until VUA patency is stable, since recurrence is difficult to treat around a cuff; timing lacks consensus, but most advise at least three to six months. The Panel advises reconstruction only in experienced high-volume centres, especially after radiation or energy ablation. Evidence summaries give ReDo VUA patency of 60-91% without radiation and 67% after radiation (LE 3), inevitable UI after transperineal access with possible AUS after three to six months (LE 3), and de novo UI of 0-58% after retropubic repair (LE 3). Perform ReDo VUA for obliterative or endoluminal-refractory VUAS in non-irradiated patients or irradiated patients with adequate bladder function (Weak). Warn of inevitable transperineal UI and potential later anti-UI surgery after at least three to six months (Strong). Offer retropubic ReDo VUA to a preoperatively continent patient (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 6.3.5.1.3.2 Posterior stenosis after surgery for benign prostatic obstruction
document_sections.content: Refractory bladder-neck stenosis and bulbomembranous narrowing after BPO surgery require different reconstructive approaches.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.5.1.3.2.1 Bladder neck reconstruction for bladder neck stenosis after surgery for benign prostatic obstruction
document_sections.content: For BNS refractory to endoscopy, local bladder flaps advance into the neck through Y-V or T-plasty, with or without scar resection. Reported patency is 83-100% at fourteen to 45 months. Minimally invasive laparoscopic and robot-assisted approaches are increasingly used. De novo UI occurs in 0-14%. Patient satisfaction was 88.5%, and QoL improved in 75%. A robot-assisted subtrigonal buccal-mucosa inlay has been reported in one case but needs further study.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.5.1.3.2.2 Bulbomembranous strictures after surgery for benign prostatic obstruction
document_sections.content: Post-TURP or post-simple-prostatectomy BMS can be managed as bulbar disease using EPA or graft augmentation according to stricture length and tightness. Kulkarni et al. reported similar patency after dorsal and ventral onlay, respectively 81.8% and 84.6% at mean 14 months. Reconstruction near the external sphincter after BPO surgery has injured the bladder neck carries UI risk up to 25%. Evidence summaries give bladder-neck Y-V/T-plasty patency of 83-100% (LE 3) and incontinence up to 14% after bladder-neck versus up to 25% after BMS reconstruction (LE 3). Perform Y-V or T-plasty for treatment-refractory BNS (Weak). Warn patients of possible new UI following either reconstruction in the setting of earlier BPO surgery (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 6.3.5.1.3.3 Radiation/high-energy induced posterior strictures
document_sections.content: Radiation and high-energy treatments can damage urethral and adjacent tissues, affecting reconstructive options.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.5.1.3.3.1 Bulbomembranous strictures secondary to radiation/high energy sources
document_sections.content: Radiation injury impairs healing within and beyond the narrowed segment; proximity to the external sphincter adds difficulty. Such patients were historically considered poor reconstructive candidates and diverted when endoscopy failed or was impossible. Most radiation-induced BMS are short enough for EPA, avoiding grafts or local flaps in poorly vascularised tissue; longer bulbar involvement requires augmentation despite those concerns. A systematic review found pooled patency of 80% without a significant EPA-versus-augmentation difference and reported SUI in 19%. Rourke et al. likewise found no significant differences between EPA and augmentation in new UI (26 versus 25%; p=1), new ED (35 versus 0%; p=0.06), or other adverse events (30% versus 33%; p=1).

document_sections.heading: 6.3.5.1.3.3.2 Prostatic strictures secondary to radiation/high energy sources
document_sections.content:
Radiotherapy, cryoablation and HIFU can cause prostatic necrosis, tissue sloughing and obstruction. When TUR fails and bladder capacity is adequate, salvage prostatectomy may be considered with attention to rectal injury, VUAS and incontinence. Mundy et al. reported patency in six of nine (67%) patients and AUS use for severe incontinence in one (11%). With poor bladder function, urethral necrosis or peri-urethral disease, consider supravesical diversion, particularly when bladder pain or spasms make a suprapubic catheter intolerable.

A report describes a “pull-through” alternative to cutaneous diversion for a severely damaged posterior urethra and non-functioning bladder after radiation. It combines salvage cystectomy, an ileal neobladder and urethral pull-through, followed by AUS implantation at a second stage. In that report, all eight patients had a patent posterior urethra after a median follow-up of 58 (range 16-84) months. Five had low-grade complications after the first stage; none had high-grade complications. Cuff erosion affected four out of eight (50%), requiring removal and later reimplantation. After a median of two revision surgeries (range 0 to 4), all achieved social continence and improved QoL. Further validation is needed before recommending this technique. The evidence summary assigns LE 3 to an 80% patency rate after urethroplasty for radiation-induced BMS, without a significant difference between EPA and augmentation; to the observation that BMS longer than 2-2.5 cm are rarely suitable for EPA; and to reported de novo incontinence of 19-26% and new ED of 0-35%. Salvage prostatectomy for prostatic strictures after radiation or high-energy treatment achieved 67% patency but substantial morbidity (LE 4). Recommendations are to choose EPA or augmentation for short (< 2.5 cm) radiation-induced BMS refractory to endoscopy according to surgeon experience (Weak), use augmentation for long (> 2.5 cm) radiation-induced BMS (Weak), warn about new incontinence and ED after urethroplasty for radiation-induced BMS (Strong), and offer salvage prostatectomy to motivated, fit patients with adequate bladder function and a prostatic stricture caused by irradiation or high-energy treatment (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 6.3.5.1.4 Extirpative surgery and urinary diversion for non-traumatic posterior urethral stenosis
document_sections.content: In complex or recurrent disease, severe necrosis, calcification or morbidity—particularly severe pain—may make LUT reconstruction inappropriate or impossible. Intractable haematuria and fistulation are other reasons to abandon the urethral outlet. Such patients commonly have previous pelvic irradiation or high-energy prostate cancer treatment and multiple prior treatment attempts. Preserving the bladder requires adequate capacity, compliance and function, as well as healthy distal ureters. The last-resort option is continent or incontinent urinary diversion, with or without cystectomy; selection depends largely on bladder capacity, local symptoms, performance status and patient expectations. Cystectomy at diversion can relieve otherwise unmanageable bladder pain, spasms and haematuria, especially after pelvic radiotherapy. In Sack et al.’s study of fifteen patients, satisfaction was 100%, and the overwhelming majority would have undergone surgery an average of thirteen months earlier. Faris et al. reported that 27% also needed bowel diversion because of intractable gastrointestinal morbidity. Improved QoL and high satisfaction after diversion, and palliation of pain, spasms and haematuria by cystectomy, each have LE 3. Perform diversion for recurrent or complex disease with reduced bladder capacity and/or incapacitating local symptoms (Weak); perform cystectomy during diversion for intractable bladder pain, spasms and/or haematuria (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 6.3.5.2 Post-traumatic posterior stenosis
document_sections.content: The EAU Guidelines on Urological Trauma address acute and early PFUI management. Non-obliterative stenosis can follow a partial membranous injury or unsuccessful early realignment of a partial or complete injury. Complete injury instead produces an obliterative distraction defect, whose gap fills with dense fibrosis. Deferred PFUI treatment starts no earlier than three months after trauma; by then, the pelvic haematoma has nearly always resolved, the prostate has descended towards its usual position, the scar has stabilised, and the patient is clinically stable and able to assume the lithotomy position.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.5.2.1.1 Endoluminal treatment as primary treatment for post-traumatic posterior stenosis
document_sections.content: Dilatation or DVIU using cut-to-the-light for obliterative stenosis will not succeed and may create a false passage towards the bladder base or rectum. A single endoscopic incision or dilatation can be attempted for a short (< 1.5 cm), non-obliterative stenosis. Kulkarni et al. reported stricture-free rates of 92.3% with “cold knife” and 96.5% with holmium laser urethrotomy, at median follow-up of 61 and 57 months, respectively; Barbagli et al. reported 51% with holmium laser but supplied no follow-up duration. In Cai et al.’s comparison of bipolar plasma vaporisation and “cold knife” DVIU among 53 patients with traumatic posterior (80%) or iatrogenic (20%) strictures, respective stricture-free rates were 81.5% and 53.8% at mean follow-up of 13.9 months. Neither group had severe complications, and operative time was statistically significantly shorter with bipolar treatment. Barratt et al. calculated a composite stricture-free rate of 20% across endoscopic treatments in a population mixing obliterative and non-obliterative stenoses; de novo UI occurred in 4%. Repeated endoluminal treatment is unlikely to cure, delays definitive treatment and can increase complications, so it is discouraged.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.5.2.1.2 Endoluminal treatment after failed urethroplasty for post-traumatic posterior stenosis
document_sections.content: A short (< 1 cm), non-obliterative recurrence after urethroplasty may be treated endoluminally. Reported stricture-free rates for a 1st and 2nd DVIU are 22.9-77.3% and 0-60%, respectively; three or more incisions have never succeeded. Further dilatations or incisions therefore serve only as palliation. The evidence summary rates failure and false-passage risk in obliterative disease, 1st-DVIU outcomes after short non-obliterative recurrence following EPA, and failure of three or more incisions as LE 3. Do not treat obliterative stenosis endoscopically (Strong). Attempt endoluminal treatment once for a short, non-obliterative stenosis (Weak). If durable patency is the aim after EPA for traumatic posterior stenosis, do not perform more than two DVIU procedures and/or dilatations for a short, non-obliterative recurrence (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 6.3.5.2.2 Urethroplasty for post-traumatic posterior stenosis
document_sections.content: Because reconstruction is difficult and the first operation produces the best results, urethroplasty should take place in high-volume centres. For well-resourced countries, an estimate suggests that one centre per twelve million inhabitants could maintain sufficient PFUI reconstruction experience.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.5.2.2.1.1 Indication and technique of urethroplasty for post-traumatic posterior stenosis
document_sections.content: Progressive perineal EPA is standard for obliterative stenosis and for non-obliterative stenosis either initially or after unsuccessful primary endoluminal therapy. Both midline and inverted U incisions provide posterior access, but a midline incision causes less superficial perineal and posterior scrotal neurovascular injury, fewer surgical-site infections (3.1% vs. 16.4%) and a shorter hospital stay. A combined transpubic abdomino-perineal route is needed only for complications such as a para-urethral bladder-base fistula, trauma-related recto-urethral fistula or bladder-neck injury. Total pubectomy increases bleeding, pelvic instability and dead space relative to partial superior or inferior pubectomy without improving exposure. An iatrogenic recto-urethral fistula after misdirected endoscopy, a traumatic recto-urethral fistula < 5 cm from the anus, UCF or a urinoma cavity can usually be repaired through the progressive perineal route alone.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.5.2.2.1.2 Patency rate after urethroplasty for post-traumatic posterior stenosis
document_sections.content: Overall patency after deferred EPA is 85.7%. Complete removal of scar predicts freedom from recurrence, whereas suture number (3-5 vs. 6-7) and size (3.0 vs. 4.0) do not. A retrospective study associated mucosal eversion at both ends before anastomosis with better patency, but prospective confirmation is lacking. Bulbar artery-sparing EPA aims to retain antegrade blood supply and reduce operative trauma; initial patency ranges from 88.5-100% over 20-45 months. Xie et al. applied it only to distraction defects less than 2.5 cm. Evidence does not yet establish superiority over classic EPA for patency, potency or continence. If a deeply situated proximal urethral end cannot be sutured, the Badenoch pull-through technique has reported patency of 33.3-96.5% over 43-126 months. Wong et al. advise a 1.5 cm overlap of the bulbar stump inside the prostatic urethra to limit recurrence. Robotic assistance for deep proximal suturing remains under investigation, without evidence of better outcomes.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.5.2.2.1.3 Sexual function, urinary continence, and rectal injury after urethroplasty for post-traumatic posterior stenosis
document_sections.content: Hosseini et al.’s prospective study found no significant erectile-function difference before EPA and at three or six months afterwards. Another prospective study found no significant overall ED change, but a significant postoperative increase among patients with pre-operative non-vascular ED. A meta-analysis of retrospective studies found ED rates fell from 43.27% before to 24.01% after posterior urethroplasty (p < 0.001). Because erectile function may recover, definitive assessment and treatment, including a possible penile prosthesis, should occur two years after trauma. Antegrade ejaculation after deferred EPA is reported in 98.3-100%; reduced ejaculatory volume and/or force in 17.2-18.7% cannot be attributed confidently to trauma rather than surgery. Continence is generally linked to bladder-neck competence, although part of the external sphincter may survive reconstruction. Incontinence after deferred EPA is uncommon (6.8-8.5%) and usually reflects an incompetent bladder neck, which does not invariably cause incontinence. Rectal injury is uncommon (0-10.2%) but serious; risk appears higher in complicated cases or after previous urethral manipulation.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.5.2.2.2 ReDo-urethroplasty for post-traumatic posterior stenosis
document_sections.content: Recurrent stenosis may undergo ReDo reconstruction, usually another EPA, particularly when the 1st EPA did not employ every length-gaining manoeuvre. Badenoch pull-through remains an option if adequate mucosa-to-mucosa suturing cannot be achieved. Gracilis muscle or omental flaps may fill excessive dead space and support an anastomosis; these, bulbospongious muscle or local subcutaneous dartos flaps may also separate suture lines with a recto-urethral fistula. If tension-free anastomosis remains impossible or the bulbar urethra is ischaemic or necrotic, described options include a tubed preputial island flap, staged BMG urethroplasty with flap, staged buccal mucosa dartos flap, radial forearm free flap urethroplasty and entero-urethroplasty. For entero-urethroplasty, sigmoid colon is preferred to ileum, which is preferred to stomach, because of vascular-pedicle proximity; this operation requires a competent bladder neck because later AUS placement is nearly impossible. Patency across ReDo techniques ranges from 50-100%. Mitrofanoffvesicostomy, PU where perineoscrotal skin is suitable, and permanent suprapubic diversion are alternatives to the usual outlet. Table 6.10 reports outcomes by ReDo technique. The evidence summary grades the better results of 1st urethroplasty LE 4; overall EPA patency of 85.7%, indications for EPA and complex approaches, alternative tissue transfers and use of local flaps LE 3; the comparative benefits of a midline incision LE 2b; and the disadvantage of total pubectomy LE 4. Perform open reconstruction only in high-volume centres (Weak); use progressive perineal EPA for obliterative stenosis and for non-obliterative stenosis after failed endoluminal therapy (Strong for each); use a midline perineal incision (Strong); avoid total pubectomy in abdomino-perineal reconstruction (Strong); reserve that reconstruction for very long distraction defects, para-urethral bladder-base fistula, trauma-related recto-urethral fistula or bladder-neck injury (Weak); offer another urethroplasty after a 1st failure to motivated patients unwilling to accept palliative endoluminal treatment or diversion (Weak); and use a local tissue flap for excessive dead space or a concomitant recto-urethral fistula (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 7. DISEASE MANAGEMENT IN FEMALES
document_sections.content: The following sections address presentation, diagnosis and treatment of female urethral strictures.

document_sections.heading: 7.1 Signs and symptoms of female urethral strictures
document_sections.content: FUS symptoms are nonspecific and generally cannot establish the diagnosis. Reported symptoms are frequency in 63%, urgency in 55%, incomplete emptying in 36%, poor flow in 32%, stress, urge or mixed incontinence in 31%, straining in 21.5%, UTI and nocturia each in 20.5%, and dysuria in 20%. Urethral pain (2.7%), terminal dribble (2%), haematuria (1.6%) and renal failure (0.5%) are rare presentations. Diagnosis is often substantially delayed: reported mean intervals are 4.3-12 years, with a range of 1-30 years.

document_sections.heading: 7.2 Diagnosis of female urethral strictures
document_sections.content: Across Twenty-four studies, assessment always included a complete history and pelvic examination for prolapse, masses, scarring and vulval disorders including LS, lichen planus and vulvo-vaginal atrophy. Flow rate was assessed in nineteen (75%) studies and US PVR in eighteen (71%). Lateral VCUG was routine in sixteen (63%) and used as needed in one (4%); cystourethroscopy was routine in fourteen (54%) and as needed in two (8%). UDS was routine in four (17%) and as needed in seven (30%), while VUDS was routine in three (13%) and calibration in four (13%). Pelvic MRI was used as needed in four series (17%); TRUS and renal US were each routine in two (8%), and IVU in ten (4%). Flow rate and PVR provide non-invasive initial assessment and treatment monitoring. VCUG and/or VUDS can identify BOO, proximal ballooning and coexisting or alternative DO or SUI, but VCUG, VUDS and UDS require insertion of a 6 Fr catheter, which may require preliminary dilatation. Cystourethroscopy also generally requires preliminary dilatation, even with a paediatric uretero-renoscope; it identifies the distal stricture boundary and helps exclude functional BOO. MRI chiefly evaluates alternative disorders such as diverticulum or carcinoma and the associated urethral fibrosis. TRUS proponents use it instead of MRI and to show proximal dilatation. In a preliminary study (n=8), gel-infused USS diagnosed stricture and associated spongiofibrosis more accurately than cystoscopy or videourodynamics.

document_sections.heading: 7.3 Treatment of female urethral strictures
document_sections.content: Treatment evidence is considered by minimally invasive procedure and urethroplasty technique.

document_sections.heading: 7.3.1 Minimally invasive techniques for treatment of female urethral strictures
document_sections.content: Reported minimally invasive options comprise urethrotomy, dilatation, meatotomy and meatoplasty. In the female urethra, meatotomy and meatoplasty are essentially equivalent; the guideline uses “meatoplasty”.

document_sections.heading: 7.3.1.1 Urethrotomy for treatment of female urethral strictures
document_sections.content: No paper specifically reported urethrotomy outcomes for FUS. Massey and Abrams reported symptomatic improvement in 80% after urethrotomy or dilatation for a mixture of causes of obstructed voiding, including FUS. Because their population had varied conditions and urodynamic outcomes were not assessed, the result for true FUS is uncertain. When female urethrotomy is used, incisions are made at three and nine o’clock, sometimes also at twelve o’clock.

document_sections.heading: 7.3.1.2 Urethral dilatation for treatment of female urethral strictures
document_sections.content: Dilatation expands the urethra to between 24 Fr and 41 Fr; some patients subsequently use ISD. Romman et al. and Popat & Zimmern also described suturing bleeding meatal areas when necessary. Four studies of 183 patients receiving dilatation alone reported patency of 7.5-51% after twelve to 59 months. Another four studies involving 31 patients continuing ISD reported stabilisation with “patency” of 37.3-100% after twelve to 21 months. New SUI (1.4%) and other complications are very rare. Given its low complication rate, limited invasiveness and reasonable results, initial dilatation is acceptable for uncomplicated FUS; repeating dilatation after recurrence is unlikely to cure.

document_sections.heading: 7.3.1.3 Meatoplasty for treatment of female urethral strictures
document_sections.content: True meatal stenosis was found in only 2/58 (3%) females assessed for voiding dysfunction. Only one meatoplasty series had more than five patients: at twelve months, 96% of 50 girls had a favourable outcome without reported adverse effects. Forty-eight of 50 had resolution of recurrent UTIs and improved voiding at one year; no incontinence or other acute complications were reported. Meatoplasty is the first-line option for short meatal strictures.

document_sections.heading: 7.3.2 Urethroplasty for treatment of female urethral strictures
document_sections.content: The Panel identified Twenty-five papers involving 253 patients. It assessed outcomes by vaginal graft or flap, labial/vestibular graft or flap, and buccal or lingual graft. In female urethroplasty, a dorsal approach opens at twelve o’clock, a ventral approach at six o’clock, and circumferential reconstruction involves the full urethral circumference.

document_sections.heading: 7.3.2.1 Vaginal graft augmentation urethroplasty for treatment of female urethral strictures
document_sections.content: Five studies included 72 dorsal vaginal graft procedures. Mean/median patient age was 47.5-60.6 years (range 28-79). At mean/median follow-up of 8.5-24.65 months (range 6-36), 59 (82% range 73-94%) had no recurrent stricture. Neither complications nor new incontinence were reported. Mean/median flow rose from 6.2-8.23 mls/s (2.2-10.2) to 16.64-27.6 ml/s (12-32.7), and mean/median PVR fell from 113.2-187.1 mls (44-420) to 20-90.31 mls (0-122).

document_sections.heading: 7.3.2.2 Vaginal flap augmentation urethroplasty for treatment of female urethral strictures
document_sections.content: Vaginal flap urethroplasty was reported in 150 women, always by a ventral approach. Reports describe an inverted U flap in seven studies (n=96), a lateral C flap in three (n=58), and a vaginal island flap in one patient. After mean/median follow-up of 12- 80.7 months (range 3-198), reported patency was 67-100%. Eight (5.3%) underwent simultaneous PVS, four (2.7%) simultaneous Martius fat-pad flap interposition and one (0.7%) simultaneous diverticulum excision. Fourtheen (9.3%) developed new UI, and fourtheen (9.3%) had other acute complications, including UTI or an intravaginally directed urinary stream.

document_sections.heading: 7.3.2.3 Labial/vestibular graft augmentation urethroplasty for treatment of female urethral strictures
document_sections.content: Four papers covered 42 graft procedures: fifteen ventral labia minora, thirteen dorsal labia minora and fourtheen dorsal labia majora. Ventral grafting yielded 75-86% patency after mean follow-up of 18 to 24 months; dorsal grafting yielded 100% after twelve to ninetheen months. One (2.4%) ventral-graft patient developed postoperative UTI, with no other complications, including UI, reported. Following dorsal labia minora onlay grafting, PVR changed from 141.9 +/- 44.2 mls to 24.5 +/- 2-.9 ms.

document_sections.heading: 7.3.2.4 Labial/vestibular flap urethroplasty for treatment of female urethral strictures
document_sections.content: Two papers described twenty-one patients, including seventeen dorsal vestibular flaps and twelve dorsal labia minora flaps. At mean/median follow-up of 24 months, two ventral-flap patients (100%) remained stricture-free; fifteen (88%) dorsal-flap patients remained stricture-free at mean follow-up of twelve months. Neither group reported short- or long-term adverse effects.

document_sections.heading: 7.3.2.5 Buccal and lingual mucosal graft augmentation urethroplasty for treatment of female urethral strictures
document_sections.content: Eleven papers described 234 patients, predominantly receiving BMG; Sharma et al. used dorsal LMG in fifteen. Reported subgroups included 44 DOOMG, 27 VOBMG and two circumferential BMG procedures. DOOMG stricture-free rates were 62.5-100% at mean/median follow-up of six to 33 months; VOBMG rates were 92-100% at mean follow-up of six to 24.5 months. Both circumferential BMG patients were stricture-free at mean follow-up of 21 months. Twenty-four (10.7%) DOOMG patients had a low-grade short-term adverse effect; no subgroup reported new UI. Neither acute complications nor new SUI were reported after VOBMG or circumferential BMG, although only two patients received the latter. After DOBMG, mean/median flow increased from 5.0-12.5 ml/s (range 3-11.2) to 12.1-28 ml/s (range 14-37), while mean/median PVR fell from 101-270 mls (range 90-200) to 6.5-122.6 mls. After VOBMG, mean/median flow increased from 5.1-7.6 ml/s (range 3-11.2) to 18-29.2 ml/s (range 5-33.4), and mean/median PVR decreased from 100-149 ml (range 0-300) to 15-59.2 ml (range 0-360 mls). Flow and PVR results specific to circumferential BMG were unavailable. A prospective randomised trial found comparable stricture-free, maximum-flow, PVR and sexual-function outcomes with VOBMG and DOBMG, but included only twelve patients per group and six months of follow-up.

document_sections.heading: 7.3.2.6 Anastomotic urethroplasty
document_sections.content: Only two cases are described, both with very short mid-urethral strictures. Both remained stricture-free at four and 24-months follow-up, respectively, without postoperative UI.

document_sections.heading: Table 7.1: Summary of available evidence on treatment of female urethral strictures
document_sections.content: The table compares female stricture treatments by study and patient counts, patency, new UI and follow-up. Its note distinguishes a patent urethra maintained by ongoing ISC or dilatation from freedom from stricture. The accompanying evidence summary assigns LE 3 to the nonspecific, longstanding symptoms; mean stricture-free rate of 40.1% after dilatation to 24-41 Fr at mean follow-up of 36 (12-59) months; patency of 26.6% after isolated repeat dilatation versus palliative patency of 97% over mean FU 6-21 months with ISD or planned dilatation; urethroplasty patency of 62.5-100%, including 92-100% for VOBMG and 62.5-100% for DOBMG; and 97% outcome after meatotomy/meatoplasty for short meatal strictures at twelve months. Recommendations: assess flow, PVR and VCUG or VUDS in all women with refractory LUTS (Strong); initially dilate FUS to 24-41 Fr (Weak); for a 1st FUS recurrence, repeat dilatation and begin planned weekly ISD with a 16-18 Fr catheter, or plan repeat dilatation (Weak); offer urethroplasty for a 2nd recurrence when ISD is not possible or definitive treatment is desired, selecting technique by surgeon experience, graft/flap availability and quality, and ventral versus dorsal urethral quality (Strong); and treat meatal strictures with meatotomy/meatoplasty (Weak).
