document_sections.heading: 8. DISEASE MANAGEMENT IN TRANSGENDER PATIENTS
document_sections.content: The following sections address stricture management in trans men and trans women.

document_sections.heading: 8.1 Treatment of strictures in trans men
document_sections.content: For trans men, treatment selection depends on the time since neophallic reconstruction, the stricture’s site and length, and local tissue quality.

document_sections.heading: 8.1.1 Management of strictures early after neophallic reconstruction
document_sections.content: Reconstructed urethral tissues usually require six months to stabilise. Endoscopic incision within six months for short (< 3 cm) strictures, chiefly at the anastomosis, has achieved a maximum stricture-free rate of only 16.7%. For obstruction that severely affects QoL, recurrent UTI or retention, initial treatment is a suprapubic catheter. Perineostomy is an alternative specialist procedure for a urologist experienced in transgender urethral anatomy and may be closed during definitive reconstruction.

document_sections.heading: 8.1.2 Treatment of meatal stenosis in trans men
document_sections.content: Intermittent urethral dilatation can palliate low-grade meatal stenosis. Offer simple meatotomy for high-grade disease, refusal of ISD or preference for a durable result. Reported patency is 50% after metoidioplasty and 75% after phalloplasty, at the cost of a hypospadiac meatal position. Staged urethroplasty is another option.

document_sections.heading: 8.1.3 Treatment of strictures at the neophallic urethra
document_sections.content: Staged urethroplasty, with or without BMG or full-thickness SG augmentation, is standard. Reported patency is 50-88% after phalloplasty and up to 100% after metoidioplasty. For complex, fully obliterated or recurrent disease, complete replacement with a tubularised radial forearm free flap has been proposed, with 67% patency.

document_sections.heading: 8.1.4 Treatment of strictures at the anastomosis neophallic urethra-fixed part of the urethra
document_sections.content: Short, non-obliterative disease can undergo endoscopic incision: a first incision yielded 37-45.5% patency, falling to 0% after three or more attempts at median follow-up of 51 months. Repeat incision is discouraged except for palliation. Heineke-Mikulicz urethroplasty is an option for very short (< 1.5 cm), low-grade strictures, with reported patency of 58-80% after phalloplasty and up to 100% after metoidioplasty. Nearly or completely obliterative disease can receive EPA, graft augmentation or staged urethroplasty. EPA patency is 46-57% after phalloplasty and 78% after metoidioplasty. Graft augmentation, including when EPA is impossible because length is >2 cm, yields 56-100% patency; inadequate ventral tissue warrants support by a local fasciocutaneous flap. Staged repair is another option, particularly after previous techniques fail.

document_sections.heading: 8.1.5 Treatment of strictures at the fixed part of the urethra
document_sections.content: This segment has more dependable vascular supply and dorsal support from the clitoral corporal bodies. Single-stage dorsal inlay graft urethroplasty is therefore possible, particularly after metoidioplasty, with patency up to 100%. Staged reconstruction, with or without a dorsal graft, is an alternative.

document_sections.heading: 8.1.6 Definitive perineostomy in trans men
document_sections.content: Offer definitive perineostomy for refractory strictures or when a patient with a stricture does not want complex reconstruction.

document_sections.heading: 8.2 Peri-operative care after treatment of strictures in trans men
document_sections.content: Anecdotal practice leaves the urethral catheter for two to three weeks after endoscopic incision or urethroplasty. Peri-catheter urethrography before removal is advised because reinsertion after detecting extravasation can be difficult.

document_sections.heading: 8.3 Strictures in trans women
document_sections.content: Initial dilatation is acceptable for short, non-obliterative disease, although long-term effectiveness data are lacking. If dilatation cannot be performed or fails, Y-V meatoplasty for a short (< 1 cm) meatal stricture has an 85% stricture-free rate. For a longer (1-2 cm) meatal stricture, an inverted U or “7-flap” neovaginal advancement flap has been used without observed recurrence at median follow-up of 37 months. The evidence summary rates usual tissue stabilisation at six months, lack of success after two endoscopic incisions in trans men, 50-88% staged-neophallic urethroplasty patency after phalloplasty and up to 100% after metoidioplasty, and 85% stricture-free outcome after Y-V meatoplasty in trans women as LE 3. Do not perform endoscopic incision or urethroplasty within six months of neophalloplasty (Strong); do not exceed two endoscopic incisions in trans men except for palliation (Strong); use staged urethroplasty when open reconstruction of the neophallic urethra is indicated (Weak); and perform Y-V meatoplasty when open repair is indicated for short (< 1 cm) meatal stenosis in trans women (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 9. TISSUE TRANSFER
document_sections.content: The following sections compare grafts and flaps, assess tissue-engineered grafts and discuss care of the oral donor site.

document_sections.heading: 9.1 Comparison of grafts with flaps
document_sections.content: A small RCT excluding LS found no significant patency difference between OMG and PSF, but PSF caused more superficial penile skin necrosis, torsion, hypoesthesia and post-void dribbling, required longer surgery and caused significantly more dissatisfaction. Another small LS-excluding RCT comparing penile skin grafts with PSF found similar patency but longer surgery and more superficial necrosis with flaps. Retrospective comparisons likewise reported comparable patency; Table 9.1 presents those studies. Flaps’ vascular pedicle permits use as a tube or patch in one stage. Castagnetti et al. found greater complications with tubularised than onlay grafts (OR: 5.86; 95% CI: 1.5-23.4); Patterson et al. reported complication and recurrence rates of circa 50% for tubularised grafts. Iqbal et al. reported 87% freedom from stricture among 23 patients after single-stage circumferential skin-flap reconstruction. Where one-stage replacement of an entire urethral segment requires a tissue tube, flaps are generally preferred. Their independent blood supply also makes them relevant to poorly vascularised beds, including after irradiation or dense scarring, and they can survive active urinary infection. Flaps and grafts can be combined for complex, multifocal or penobulbar disease. The evidence summary rates greater flap morbidity but comparable patency, and greater complications with single-stage tubularised grafts, LE 1b; independence of flap survival from recipient-site vascularity is LE 3. Prefer a graft when graft and flap are equally indicated (Strong); do not tubularise a graft for single-stage repair (Strong); use flaps when the urethral bed has poor vascularisation (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 9.2 Comparison of different types of flaps
document_sections.content: Penile skin flaps are generally hairless, although ventral skin around the raphe may contain hair in some phenotypes. Described designs include transverse preputial, transverse distal penile and longitudinal island flaps. Reported patency is 74.2-100%; complications comprise skin necrosis (0-3.8%), fistula (0-7%), deformity (0-7%), post-void dribbling (0-79%) and sacculation (0-16.5%). Without direct flap comparisons, superiority cannot be determined. Fu et al. reported significantly greater patency with PSF than scrotal or perineal skin flaps: 87.7%, 69% and 66.7%, respectively. Hair-bearing scrotal and perineal tissue may produce hairballs and chronic infection and compromise repair. Blandy’s long-term study reported 3% revision for calculi and 3% for diverticula. Alternatives include epilation before transfer or attaching OMG to underlying scrotal dartos after skin incision, then using the patch as a flap at a later operation. Lower patency with hair-bearing flaps has LE 3. Do not use hair-bearing perineal or scrotal flaps unless no other option is feasible (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 9.3 Comparison of different types of grafts
document_sections.content: Buccal mucosa is the most frequently used graft; a systematic review reported 86.6% patency at average follow-up of 31.5 months for anterior strictures. Penile skin, especially foreskin in uncircumcised men, is another source. With LS, Trivedi et al. found significantly higher patency for non-genital mucosa (82.6%) than genital skin (4%), so genital skin is not indicated. The Pee’BuSt RCT found no significant outcome difference between buccal and penile-skin grafts for dorsal onlay repair. A systematic review and meta-analysis suggested possible superiority of BMG augmentation, but confounding precluded a clear conclusion. Foreskin can supply a spiroid graft up to 20 cm, which is harder to obtain from OMG. Buccal harvesting causes oral morbidity, prompting consideration of LMG. A review and meta-analysis of four prospective and two retrospective comparative studies found no significant patency or overall long-term complication difference between LMG and BMG. LMG caused more problems with eating or drinking, speech, tongue protrusion and taste; speech problems persisted beyond six months in 13.8-20%. Xu et al. reported tongue-movement difficulty, donor-site numbness and speech difficulty at twelve months in 6.2%, 4.9% and 2.5%, respectively. BMG caused more oral tightness, present in up to 24% beyond six months. Chauhan et al. found more immediate and early donor-site complications with BMG except bleeding, which was more frequent with LMG; first-week numbness, chewing difficulty, swelling and articulation problems occurred in 61%, 54%, 48% and 40%, respectively, while late problems were rare. Pal et al. found more early tongue-movement and speech problems with LMG, but persistent pain, perioral numbness, mouth tightness, salivary changes and cheek scarring after three months only with BMG. Buccal and lingual mucosa can be combined for long strictures. Lower-lip mucosa can supply smaller grafts, but a narrative review associated it with more donor-site morbidity and possible lasting discomfort, sensory deficits, salivary changes and aesthetic effects not described for lingual grafts. Other described grafts include postauricular, abdominal, thigh split-thickness mesh and inguinal skin, and colonic mucosa; Table 9.2 summarises their series. Postauricular skin was used when genital skin and oral mucosa were unusable, or added to oral mucosa for lengthy defects. Abdominal skin was used for lengthy disease, previous OMG urethroplasty or refusal of OMG. Pfalzgraf et al. reported similar patency with split-thickness mesh and BMG (84 and 83%) but more penile deviation (9% vs. 0%) and lower satisfaction (83.3% vs. 96.7%) with mesh. Xu et al. reported 85.7% patency with colonic mucosa for strictures > 10 cm, but harvesting required abdominal surgery and 1/35 (2.9%) developed a colonic-abdominal fistula. Because experience is limited, other grafts should be considered only if oral mucosa and penile skin are unavailable, inappropriate or unwanted. Evidence summaries give comparable buccal and lingual patency and distinct, sometimes lasting oral morbidity LE 1a; penile-skin patency of 79-81.8% versus BMG patency of 85.9-88.1% and 4% genital-skin patency in LS LE 3. Use buccal or lingual mucosa when grafting is needed and available (Weak); explain potential buccal, lingual and lower-lip donor complications when proposing oral grafting (Strong); use penile skin when buccal/lingual mucosa is unavailable, unsuitable or declined (Weak); and avoid genital skin grafts in LS (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 9.4 Tissue engineered grafts
document_sections.content: The guideline distinguishes cell-free scaffolds from autologous oral-cell-seeded grafts.

document_sections.heading: 9.4.1 Cell-free tissue engineered grafts
document_sections.content: Cadaveric or animal materials, including porcine SIS, acellular bladder matrix and acellular dermal matrix, provide cell-free scaffolds for host-cell ingrowth; ready availability is a proposed advantage. In a small RCT (n=30), acellular bladder matrix yielded 66.6% patency versus 100% with BMG, with particularly poor matrix outcomes in unhealthy urethral beds. Small heterogeneous retrospective series, mostly of porcine small intestinal submucosa, report patency from 20-110%; differences in aetiology, prior treatment, location and outcome definition limit interpretation. Extensive spongiofibrosis, poor vascularity, prior treatment and longer strictures generally predict worse outcomes. Table 9.3 presents the retrospective series. Reduced patency with longer strictures and an unhealthy bed has LE 1b. Do not use cell-free tissue-engineered grafts with extensive spongiofibrosis, after failed urethroplasty or when stricture length is > 4 cm (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 9.4.2 Autologous tissue engineered oral mucosa graftss
document_sections.content: These grafts use a laboratory-manufactured matrix seeded with a patient’s oral mucosal cells following a biopsy at 0.5 cm². Reduced donor-site morbidity is a proposed advantage; costs and a restrictive manufacturing-to-implantation interval are disadvantages. A prospective multicentre study of 99 patients estimated patency of 67.3 and 58.2% at twelve and 24 months, respectively, with minimal oral adverse events. Comparative studies against acellular or native OMG and cost-effectiveness data are unavailable. Safety, patency and cost-effectiveness remain under investigation (LE 3). Do not use autologous tissue-engineered oral mucosal grafts outside a clinical trial (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 9.5 Management of oral cavity after buccal mucosa harvesting
document_sections.content: Prospective RCTs comparing closure and non-closure of the buccal donor site are summarised in Table 9.4. Findings do not justify recommending either approach; the treating physician may decide. Chamomile or chlorhexidine mouth rinses have been suggested during the first postoperative days, but evidence that they lessen pain or other oral complications is lacking.

document_sections.heading: 10. PERI-OPERATIVE CARE OF URETHRAL SURGERY
document_sections.content: Peri-operative considerations comprise urethral rest, antimicrobial use and catheter management.

document_sections.heading: 10.1 Urethral rest
document_sections.content: After a urethral catheter, ISD, dilatation or DVIU, rest permits healing and scar maturation, improving assessment of the true fibrotic extent before urethroplasty. Insert a suprapubic catheter if obstructive symptoms become incapacitating or retention occurs. Terlecki et al. proposed diagnostic assessment after two months and urethroplasty after three months; their wound-healing-based approach permitted reliable urethrographic assessment and outcomes comparable with stable, previously unmanipulated strictures. The ideal duration for every patient is unknown; greater infection or inflammation may warrant longer rest. The evidence summary assigns LE 3 to a minimum three-month rest period after manipulation before urethroplasty. Do not perform urethroplasty within three months of any urethral manipulation (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 10.2 Antibiotics
document_sections.content: Wound infection and UTI are common after surgery, and infection at the repair site may contribute to urethroplasty failure. Most reconstructive urologists obtain culture one to two weeks before surgery; culture is superior to urinalysis, which may be omitted. Give a therapeutic antibiotic course before surgery for infection or colonisation. Even adequately treated pre-operative UTI may increase postoperative UTI risk. With an indwelling catheter, general principles favour attempting to suppress colonisation before surgery. The EAU Guidelines on Urological Infections strongly recommend screening for and treating asymptomatic bacteriuria before mucosa-breaching urological procedures, and treating catheter-associated asymptomatic bacteriuria before traumatic urinary interventions. Intra-operative antibiotic prophylaxis tailored to local resistance reduces surgical-site infection and UTI. Despite common extended postoperative prescribing, evidence does not show that antibiotics continued through or beyond catheter removal reduce infection. Baas et al.’s retrospective comparison found no apparent UTI-rate difference between prophylaxis lasting three weeks until removal and 3 days around removal. The EAU Guidelines on Urological Infections do not routinely recommend prophylaxis against clinical UTI at catheter removal, and there is no evidence that urethral surgery is an exception. Intra-operative prophylactic efficacy has LE 4. Administer intra-operative antibiotic prophylaxis during urethral surgery (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 10.3 Catheter management
document_sections.content: After uncomplicated DVIU, prolonged catheterisation offers no advantage; remove the catheter within 72 hours. After one-stage urethroplasty or closure of the urethral plate in staged repair, transurethral catheterisation or a suprapubic catheter with urethral stent diverts urine to prevent leakage. An underpowered randomised comparison found no significant recurrence or time-to-recurrence difference between silicone and hydrogel-coated latex catheters. Urethral catheter size generally ranges from 14 Fr to 20 Fr. Routine anticholinergics did not significantly reduce involuntary pericatheter voiding. An indwelling catheter commonly remains for two to three weeks after urethroplasty; after three weeks, reported urethrographic extravasation ranges from 2.2-11.5%. Earlier removal has also succeeded: after EPA for uncomplicated anterior strictures, removal at one versus two weeks produced no significant differences in extravasation (6.8% vs. 4.5%) or recurrence (4.9% vs. 5.2%). In Poelaert et al.’s series (n=219), leakage was 3.5% with removal < 10 days and 8.3% with removal > 10 days (p=0.158), although longer and more complex strictures received longer catheterisation. Beiske et al. found more UTI with three weeks than two weeks after open urethroplasty. Evaluate leakage before removal to prevent peri-urethral inflammation, abscess or fistula. Some studies linked leakage to recurrence; others did not, but included minor leaks. Grossgold et al. associated high-grade leakage—length > 1.03 cm and width > 0.32 cm—with significantly more recurrence, and identified length > 1.03 cm alone as an independent predictor. With persistent significant leakage, maintain or reinsert the catheter and repeat evaluation after one week. Minor “wisp-like” leakage does not appear to increase long-term recurrence; removal without another urethrogram is possible. If severity is uncertain, another week of catheterisation and reassessment is safe. pcRUG, RUG or VCUG can assess leakage. A prospective within-patient study (n=80) found pcRUG and VCUG had comparable sensitivity, while pcRUG avoided reinsertion and inability to void during VCUG and used less radiation (120 mGy/cm2 versus 241 mGy/cm2; p < 0.001). Perform RUG if a patient cannot void during attempted VCUG after removal. Limited evidence in trans men includes a recommendation for three weeks of transurethral catheterisation and pcRUG at removal. Following perineostomy or a 1st-stage urethroplasty, removal without urethrography is possible after three to five days. The evidence summary grades pre-removal urethrography to detect leakage LE 2b; lack of benefit from prolonged catheterisation after uncomplicated DVIU and possible early removal in selected uncomplicated short strictures LE 3. Assess leakage with validated urethrography before removing a catheter after urethroplasty (Strong); remove the catheter within 72 hours of uncomplicated DVIU or dilatation (Weak); consider the 1st urethrogram seven to ten days after uncomplicated urethroplasty to assess possible removal, particularly if the catheter is bothersome (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 11. FOLLOW-UP
document_sections.content: Follow-up addresses complications, recurrence, patient-reported outcomes and schedules tailored to recurrence risk.

document_sections.heading: 11.1 Rationale for follow-up after urethral surgery
document_sections.content: Follow-up seeks to detect and manage complications and recurrent narrowing. At short to medium follow-up, complications occur after up to 34-38% of anterior urethroplasties; 92-99.1% are Clavien grade 1 or 2. Recurrence can occur despite urethroplasty offering the highest chance of treatment success, with frequency varying by stricture and procedure (LE 3). Offer follow-up to every patient after urethroplasty (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 11.2 Definition of success after urethroplasty surgery
document_sections.content: The traditional criterion of no intervention for recurrence overlooks patients with symptomatic or asymptomatic narrowing who decline further surgery; definitions also differ on whether endoscopic retreatment counts as failure. Anatomic success concerns a normal lumen on RUG or cystoscopy regardless of symptoms. Some groups define recurrence by inability to pass a 16 Fr flexible scope without force; up to 35% of cystoscopic recurrences after bulbar reconstruction remain asymptomatic. Others count any visible narrowing, including > 17 Fr, as recurrence. Not every anatomical recurrence requires treatment. Intervention has been suggested for recurrent symptoms, stricture-related high PVR or calibre < 14 Fr, even without symptoms. Patient-reported outcomes assess whether voiding, symptoms and HRQoL actually improve; pain, sexual dysfunction or persistently poor urinary function may lead patients to judge a patent reconstruction unfavourably. In one multivariable analysis, uroflowmetry did not significantly explain satisfaction. Kessler et al. found only 78.3% of clinically successful patients were (very) satisfied; curvature, shortening, worse erectile function and impaired sex life were significantly associated with dissatisfaction. Conversely, 80% of clinical failures were (very) satisfied. Postoperative pain, sexual dysfunction and persistent LUTS predicted dissatisfaction independently of anatomic outcome; IPSS improvement alone did not predict satisfaction. After adjusting for recurrence and age, persistent weak stream, genitourinary pain and sexual changes were major independent drivers. Penile shortening (OR: 2.26; 95% CI: 1.39-3.69) and chordee (OR: 2.26; 95% CI: 1.44-4.19) also independently predicted dissatisfaction. Table 11.1 presents study-specific dissatisfaction predictors. PROMs address the discrepancy between patient and surgeon assessments. A comprehensive outcome combines anatomic, endoscopic and patient-reported assessment. For clinical practice, the Panel suggests functional success as absence of symptoms and/or need for further intervention. For academic comparisons, collect standardised subjective and objective outcomes simultaneously but report them separately.

document_sections.heading: 11.3 Follow-up tools after urethral surgery
document_sections.content: Diagnostic tools establish whether recurrence is present; screening tools identify patients who may need diagnostic evaluation. Patient-reported measures assess outcomes not captured by anatomy alone.

document_sections.heading: 11.3.1.1 Calibration during follow-up after urethral surgery
document_sections.content: Calibration may inadvertently dilate a soft stricture, making the distinction subjective. Use it cautiously after urethroplasty and select dedicated calibration bougies rather than dilators.

document_sections.heading: 11.3.1.2 Urethrocystoscopy during follow-up after urethral surgery
document_sections.content: Urethrocystoscopy can confirm or exclude recurrence, including in the up to 35% of patients with asymptomatic re-strictures. Common scopes of 15.7 Fr (5 mm diameter) or 17.3 Fr (5.5 mm diameter) also indicate lumen calibre. Examination can distinguish a diaphragm or cross-bridge amenable to simple treatment from a substantial recurrence needing repeated intervention or ReDo surgery. At three months, endoscopic narrowing predicts reintervention within one year: relative to a normal examination, large-calibre (> 17 Fr) narrowing had HR 3.1 (1.35-7.29), and small-calibre (< 17 Fr) narrowing HR 23.7 (12.44-45.15), adjusted for age, stricture length, location and aetiology. Routine endoscopy has limited acceptance: only 54% underwent it at one year despite its inclusion in a study protocol.

document_sections.heading: 11.3.1.3 Retrograde urethrogram and voiding cystourethrogram during follow-up after urethral surgery
document_sections.content: RUG with VCUG is used to confirm suspected recurrence or within routine protocols to assess postoperative patency.

document_sections.heading: 11.3.1.4 Urethral ultrasound – Sonourethrography during follow-up after urethral surgery
document_sections.content: SUG is infrequently used in follow-up, although it could reliably diagnose recurrent strictures.

document_sections.heading: 11.3.2 Screening tools for follow-up after urethral surgery
document_sections.content: Screening measures identify suspected recurrence that warrants subsequent diagnostic evaluation.

document_sections.heading: 11.3.2.1 Flow-rate analysis during follow-up after urethral surgery
document_sections.content: Qmax is the most common follow-up measure. Suggested failure or confirmatory-test thresholds include 15 ml/s and 12 ml/s, but no threshold is established: 19% with Qmax < 14 ml/s still permit passage of a 15 Fr scope. Results can be influenced by measurement error, BPO/LUTS, bladder dysfunction and bladder-capacity variation; reliable prediction requires at least 125-150 ml voided. Even under controlled conditions, adequate paired pre- and postoperative measurements were obtained in only 31%. A pre-to-postoperative Qmax difference of 10 ml/s or less has been proposed to screen for recurrence, with sensitivity 92%, specificity 78% and reproducibility R=0.52. Age complicates this comparison: patients over 65 years old average less than 10 ml/s improvement, potentially owing to BPO and/or bladder dysfunction. Curve shape is another measure. A flat obstructive curve showed 93% sensitivity for recurrence; symptoms combined with an obstructive curve achieved 99% sensitivity and 99% NPV.

document_sections.heading: 11.3.2.2 Post-void residual ultrasound measure during follow-up after urethral surgery
document_sections.content: US PVR is significantly higher in recurrent than non-recurrent cases, but ascites, diverticula, impaired bladder function, possible BPO and interobserver differences affect interpretation. Combined with uroflowmetry, IPSS and SUG it can predict recurrence adequately; evidence does not support PVR alone for this purpose.

document_sections.heading: 11.3.2.3 Symptom questionnaires during follow-up after urethral surgery
document_sections.content: IPSS was designed for BPO but improves significantly after successful urethroplasty and correlates significantly and inversely with Qmax. Mean improvement is around -11 points (range -19 to -5); Table 11.2 reports study-specific preoperative and postoperative values, changes and p-values. A proposed combination of IPSS 10 points and Qmax > 15 ml/s could avoid invasive studies in 34%, missing 4.3% of strictures < 14 Fr; IPSS 15 points with Qmax > 15 ml/s could avoid testing in 37%, missing 6% of strictures < 14 Fr. VPSS takes significantly less time than IPSS, particularly with illiteracy or limited education, and correlates with IPSS, Qmax and urethral diameter. VPSS > 8 plus Qmax < 15 ml/s yielded 89% NPV and 87% PPV for recurrence. USS-PROM found post-micturition dribble in 73% before and 40% after anterior urethroplasty; 6.3% was new. Neither stricture location nor procedure type predicted it.

document_sections.heading: 11.3.3 Quality of life assessment, including disease specific questionnaires during follow-up after urethral surgery
document_sections.content: EQ-5D-3L evaluation found preoperative anxiety and depression in 29%; new anxiety and depression after urethroplasty was uncommon (10%) and predicted by poorer sexual function and a poor self-reported overall-health image. Assessment specific to the condition is more recommended. USS-PROM has been useful after anterior urethroplasty, although its generic QoL questions have been criticised for not always improving after successful repair. A North American collaborative group is developing and validating another PROM that includes sexual consequences. PROMs should be used at every visit to assess functional outcome over time. With CLSS, most bladder, penile/urethral and perineal/scrotal pain measures improved, although up to 29% reported worse perineal pain. When PROMs do not capture sexual function, use validated assessment; IIEF, SHIM, O´Leary Brief Male Sexual Function Inventory (BMFSI), SLQQ and MSHQ have been used for erectile and ejaculatory outcomes. PUSQ and questionnaires on genital appearance or sensitivity have been suggested but are not validated. Evidence summaries rate RUG or urethrocystoscopy for anatomic assessment, the objective–subjective outcome gap and value of PROMs, and validated sexual-function questionnaires LE 2a. Use cystoscopy or RUG to assess anatomical outcome (Weak), PROMs for patient-reported outcomes and satisfaction (Strong), and validated questionnaires for sexual function after stricture surgery (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 11.4 Ideal follow-up interval after urethral surgery
document_sections.content: Follow-up should measure both anatomy and function without unnecessary invasive tests, costs, discomfort, anxiety or risk. Following anterior urethroplasty, 21% of recurrences are clinically apparent and cystoscopically confirmed by three months, and 96% by one year. Earlier recurrence is more frequent with LS, older age, longer strictures and skin grafts.

document_sections.heading: 11.5 Length of follow-up after urethral surgery
document_sections.content: Median time to recurrence after bulbar urethroplasty is approximately ten months. Series identify 55.4% to 96% of recurrences in the first postoperative year; 23% of bulbar recurrences are detected in the second year, with a decreasing proportion thereafter. Longer observation itself predicts detection of recurrence. Late recurrence beyond five years occurs in up to 15%, particularly after augmentation and use of skin grafts. Patients should seek urological review if symptoms recur late.

document_sections.heading: 11.6 Risk-stratified proposals during follow-up after urethral surgery
document_sections.content: Follow-up costs peak in the first year and, in a literature review, ranged from 205 to 1,784 US Dollars, with posterior repair costing more. A proposed US risk-tailored protocol could save up to 85% over five years: after low-risk EPA without radiotherapy, hypospadias or LS, monitor symptoms using self-administered IPSS every three months for one year and annually afterwards; after standard-risk graft/flap repair or in patients with irradiation, hypospadias and/or LS, combine IPSS and flowmetry on that schedule, adding RUG at three and twelve months. Cystoscopy in this protocol is performed when needed. Another proposal uses cystoscopy or RUG/VCUG at three months, particularly after grafting, to exclude early failure and establish new questionnaire and flowmetry baselines after a good anatomical result. Subsequent non-invasive flow and symptom checks trigger cystoscopy if deterioration occurs. A further suggested protocol compares LUTS, erectile and ejaculatory function, and LUT pain with preoperative PROM findings, performs cystoscopy and flowmetry at three to six months, and uses flow as a new baseline. A later significant decline of 25-30% in Qmax or Qmax - (average flow rate) triggers cystoscopy even without symptoms. Cystoscopy at twelve to fifteen months is left to surgeon discretion according to higher patient risk, partial narrowing at three months or low surgeon volume. Evidence summaries rate concentration of recurrence within twelve months LE 2a and safety and cost-effectiveness of risk-tailored protocols LE 3. Offer at least one year of routine follow-up after urethroplasty (Strong) and adopt a risk-adjusted protocol (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 11.7 Follow-up protocol proposal after urethroplasty
document_sections.content: The Panel proposes separate schedules for low and standard recurrence risk.

document_sections.heading: 11.7.1 Surgeries with low risk of recurrence
document_sections.content: This group consists of anastomotic repairs of the bulbar/(bulbo)membranous urethra without radiotherapy, hypospadias or BXO/LS features. Table 11.3 schedules uroflowmetry and PROM including sexual function at 3 months, 12 months and 24 months. Anatomic assessment by urethrocystoscopy or RUG-VCUG is suggested at three months and otherwise performed when indicated. Follow-up may stop after two years if the patient is instructed to seek urological assessment for worsening symptoms; academic centres may continue longer for research.

document_sections.heading: 11.7.2 Surgical management options with standard risk of recurrence
document_sections.content: Standard-risk procedures include bulbar anastomotic reconstruction with previous radiotherapy, hypospadias or BXO/LS; penile urethroplasty; non-traumatic posterior urethroplasty; and graft and/or flap substitution. Table 11.4 schedules uroflowmetry and PROM, including sexual function, at 3 months, 12 months, 24 months and 5 years. Anatomic evaluation by urethrocystoscopy or RUG-VCUG is scheduled at 3 months, 12 months and 24 months, and at 5 years when indicated. Follow-up may end after five years with advice to return if symptoms worsen; longer observation should be considered after penile or substitution repair, and academic centres may extend it for research.
